Sports.title: How Joe Marler became an unlikely national treasure: Secrets behind rugby star's meteoric rise after Traitors fame - with Prince Harry appearing on his podcast - as he prepares for new Gladiators role
Sports.content:
How Joe Marler became an unlikely national treasure: Secrets behind rugby star's meteoric rise after Traitors fame - with Prince Harry appearing on his podcast - as he prepares for new Gladiators role

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Joe Marler spent most of his rugby career in the dirt, where mud, mauls and mayhem were at the very core of his identity.

But since hanging up his boots, the former England international has swapped scrums for studios, tackling for television and rucks for red carpets to become one the most popular stars of British mainstream media.

From building a successful podcast empire to appearing on a string of high-profile TV shows, Marler, 36, has carved out a new career that few could have predicted, becoming a familiar face far beyond the sport that made him famous initially.

It was announced on Monday that the powerful prop is set to become the first ever celebrity Gladiator when the fourth series of the BBC’s hit TV show returns in 2027, taking on the new identity of ‘Mauler’.

While appearing on Gladiators is not a huge departure from the physical and competitive world of England and Harlequins rugby, it was a very different BBC programme that transformed Marler from a cult figure among sports fans into a household name across the UK.

That popular TV show was Celebrity Traitors, where millions of viewers saw a side of Marler that had often been hidden beneath his rugged, intimidating and formidable appearance.

Joe Marler will be the first celebrity to appear as a Gladiator on the BBC's popular TV series

The former England rugby star has become a national treasure since his retirement

His appearance on the first series of Celebrity Traitors boosted his popularity away from sport

Away from the chaos and carnage of the rugby pitch was a self-deprecating and surprisingly vulnerable character who quickly became one of the breakout stars of the series.

His unlikely friendship with Ted Lasso actor and comedian Nick Mohammed became one of the show’s most memorable highlights, while his blunt observations and mischievous plotting made him a favourite among viewers who had never watched him play a single minute of rugby.

Yet Celebrity Traitors was not the beginning of Marler’s media career. By the time he stepped inside 'the castle', he had already spent years building a platform that would allow him to make the leap into mainstream media.

Rather than following the well-trodden path into rugby coaching or full-time punditry, the forward began cultivating a media career while he was still playing, launching The Joe Marler Show before evolving it into the hugely popular Things People Do podcast.

Co-hosted alongside sports journalist Tom Fordyce, the podcast deliberately avoided becoming another rugby chat show. Instead, Marler leaned into his natural curiosity and self-deprecating humour, eager to learn new perspectives from guests and share unique stories about his life so far.

Boxing promoter Eddie Hearn and Married at First Sight relationship expert Paul Brunson are among those to have joined Marler in the studio since, although the down-to-earth former rugby star continues to invite ordinary people with extraordinary jobs on to the show to share their stories and perspectives as well.

The success of the show opened the door to a second podcast, Joe Marler Will See You Now, which launched in the wake of his appearance on Celebrity Traitors and has quickly become extremely popular, sitting 19th in the charts currently.

Last month, listeners were left stunned when Prince Harry appeared as a guest on the show, adding to an impressive list of celebrities who have joined the ex-England prop on Joe Marler Will See You Now specifically, including Russell Howard, Dani Dyer, Joel Dommett, Joe Lycett, Prue Leith and Stephen Fry.

The rugby star chatted to Prince Harry on his popular Joe Marler Will See You Now podcast

The podcast currently sits 19th in the UK charts after Prince Harry's appearance last month

From raising £64,000 for CALM on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? to featuring at Soccer Aid for UNICEF, Marler does done plenty of charity work after his retirement from rugby too

After proving his credentials behind the microphone, it wasn't long before TV producers came calling. Appearances on Michael McIntyre's The Wheel and Blankety Blank showcased just how comfortable Marler was on the small screen, while reports linking him with Celebrity Bake Off and the recent announcement of his Gladiators role suggest broadcasters increasingly see him as far more than simply a former rugby player.

Marler has never taken himself too seriously, either. During an appearance on Michael McIntyre's Big Show in January, he happily threw himself into a 'lip-sync battle' with RuPaul's Drag Race UK winner Blu Hydrangea, mouthing the words to Tina Turner's Simply the Best while dressed in a wig, skirt and glittery make-up.

His growing popularity has not gone unnoticed commercially too. Away from television, Marler has fronted campaigns for a string of popular brands, from Pringles and Sky Mobile to Jacamo and Sainsbury's.

Humour is often at the heart of these adverts, typified by Durex choosing Marler to front their tongue-in-cheek 'Fit Matters' campaign in July 2022. Filmed relaxing in a hot tub and discussing condom sizes with his trademark deadpan delivery, he played exactly the sort of self-deprecating, slightly absurd role that many former elite sportsmen might have avoided - but one that undoubtedly worked to his benefit.

Brand and Culture Expert Nick Ede believes his honesty and humour has been at the centre of his success post-retirement.

'His success comes from the fact that he has never tried to present himself as a polished media personality. Instead, he's leaned into being authentic, unpredictable and genuinely funny, and audiences have responded to that honesty,' he told Daily Mail Sport.

'What makes Joe so marketable is that he's incredibly relatable. He doesn't fit the traditional mould of the media-trained ex-professional athlete. He's happy to laugh at himself, talk openly about his struggles with mental health, poke fun at rugby culture and show the messy realities of life after elite sport.

'His retirement has actually given him more freedom to showcase that personality. Without the pressures and restrictions of being an active England international, he's been able to embrace opportunities across television, podcasts, radio and entertainment, allowing people who may never have watched a rugby match to discover him.

'His appearance on Celebrity Traitors was a pivotal moment because it introduced him to an entirely new audience who may have had little or no knowledge of his rugby career. Viewers saw his humour, strategic thinking and warmth, proving that his appeal extends well beyond the sporting world. That kind of mainstream exposure has significantly strengthened his profile and demonstrated that he has the charisma to succeed in entertainment as well as sport.

'He's also incredibly versatile. One minute he can be making audiences laugh on a panel show, the next he's having a thoughtful conversation about mental health or fatherhood. That range gives broadcasters confidence because they know he'll entertain while also bringing authenticity when a subject becomes more serious.

He was hailed a national treasure by Celebrity Traitors fans after his memorable appearances

'Brands are increasingly looking for ambassadors who can build trust rather than simply attract attention, and Joe ticks that box. He's imperfect, self-aware and refreshingly honest, which makes him highly credible.

'Consumers are far more likely to connect with someone who feels genuine than someone who appears overly polished, and Joe has built his reputation by never pretending to be anything other than himself.'

Fellow industry expert Rebecca May, Founder of RM Publicity, agreed: 'Joe is seen by audiences as entertaining - audiences see him as funny, quick-witted and honest - a combination that's incredibly likeable and marketable. Audiences respond to him, which is why he does so well on TV and continues to be booked.

'Just because an athlete or sportsperson has had a successful career and is well known doesn't mean that can translate into being a successful TV personality that audiences love. That is what separates Joe Marler apart - audiences automatically like him.

'I'd describe Joe's brand as controlled unpredictability. He’s fun, edgy and relatable but with enough spontaneity to keep people watching, which is why he is becoming a mainstream TV favourite.

'The audience is waiting to see what he says or does next, and that’s part his appeal. That balance is valuable in mainstream TV because it keeps viewers engaged.'

While refusing to take himself too seriously in terms of his public image, Marler has become an ambassador for multiple charities and mental health organisations since his retirement from rugby.

An ambassador for UK suicide prevention charity Campaign Against Living Miserably (CALM), Marler is passionate about breaking mental health stigmas and encouraging vulnerability among men, having raised £64,000 for the organisation during an appearance on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? in 2024 and having starred in Sky's documentary Big Boys Don't Cry.

Marler also made his Soccer Aid debut for UNICEF earlier this year, lining up alongside the likes of Wayne Rooney, Jill Scott, Olly Murs and Robbie Williams. True to form, he stole the spotlight after being thrown on as an emergency goalkeeper, earning the fan-voted 'Moment of the Match' award for his unlikely cameo.

His wide-ranging interview with British GQ in February also showed how Marler's appeal has grown far beyond traditional sports audiences. The former prop discussed everything from retirement and fatherhood to mental health and finding purpose away from rugby, offering the same level of openness that has become a defining feature of his public persona.

It is that combination - the willingness to be both ridiculous and vulnerable - that has separated Marler from many former athletes attempting to build a profile after retirement. He has never tried to reinvent himself as a polished celebrity but instead has taken the same unpredictable personality that made him such a compelling rugby figure and simply moved it into a different arena.

Since walking away from rugby, he has become a reality TV star, podcast host, brand ambassador, mental health advocate and one of the most recognisable figures in British entertainment. Not bad for a 36-year-old who retired fully just two years ago.

A mischievous rogue and joker on the rugby pitch, Marler did not leave behind the personality that made him popular among sports fans. He simply used it to carve out another highly successful career.

Sports.title: Argentina rugby fans display 'Malvinas' banner laying claim to the Falkland Islands - as bad blood lingers after World Cup semi-final
Sports.content:
Argentina continued to cause controversy around the Falkland Islands as fans of their rugby team held up a 'Malvinas' banner at their game against South Africa on Saturday.

During the match, which Argentina lost by a scoreline of 10-17, some supporters were seen with a sign that read: 'Los Malvinas son Argentinas', which translates to 'The Falkland Islands are Argentinian'.

The contention around the banner follows Argentina's World Cup semi-final victory over England at the FIFA World Cup.

After that triumph, their players used it as an opportunity to assert their claim over the Falkland Islands, a self-governing British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean located around 300 miles east of Argentina.

Britain have ruled the Falklands since January 1833 and in 2013 in a referendum, 99.8 per cent of citizens voted to remain as a British territory. The islands were the subject of a conflict between the two nations in 1982.

The lifting of the original banner - which also read 'Los Malvinas son Argentinas' - triggered a fierce backlash in the UK.

Argentina rugby fans held up a 'Malvinas' banner laying claim to the Falkland Islands

It came after their footballers did similar after beating England in the World Cup semi-final

Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer insisted that while 'the World Cup might not be ours, the Falkland Islands definitely are. Self-determination rests with the islanders and our commitment to the Falklands will never waver'.

FIFA subsequently opened an investigation, with the governing body's rules forbidding the use of any political messaging at the World Cup.

They had, however, previously turned a blind eye to continued references to the 1982 conflict in a song sung by the players – and posted on social media by the country’s association – in the dressing room throughout the tournament.

Argentina President Javier Milei described the players' celebration with the banner as 'perfectly valid,' and said the message 'reflects a sentiment shared by all Argentines'.

'I know that for Argentinians, we won the World Cup the moment we beat England because that's really what everyone wanted,' he said.

Tapia added: 'We are proud of our national teams' performance, and of the fact that they created that sense of epic invincibility - that nobody could beat us.'

The banner displayed on Saturday came in Argentina's first rugby game since their badly-tempered defeat by England last month, during which similar signs were displayed.

That was just a few days after the World Cup semi-final and the Pumas appeared to try to mock their rivals by wearing a kit paying homage to Diego Maradona's World Cup-winning 1986 team, a triumph made famous by Maradona's 'Hand of God' goal against England in the quarter-final.

Although England won that match, it ended in chaos when Argentina had a late try ruled out by the TMO, with their fly-half Tomas Albornoz subsequently suspended for four games for allegedly confronting the referee in fury.

Sports.title: Newcastle suffer pre-season injury scare as Anthony Elanga is carried off on a stretcher following horror challenge from Valencia star - but new boss Matthias Jaissle receives positive update on winger
Sports.content:
Newcastle winger Anthony Elanga was stretchered off after a horror challenge that saw Valencia captain Jose Luis Gaya sent off during Saturday night’s friendly at the Mestalla Stadium.

The incident sparked a mass brawl after the home midfielder was given a straight red card for a high lunge that connected with Elanga’s shin just in front of the dugouts. The Swede was left writhing in agony on the turf while his team-mates emptied the bench and clashed with Valencia's players and staff.

Elanga received lengthy treatment to his right leg before a stretcher was called for, and he was clearly still in distress when he left the field. He had been Newcastle’s best player to that point and his loss was a sour end to the first half for new boss Matthias Jaissle, whose side trailed 1-0 at the interval.

However, the 24-year-old was able to walk in the dressing-room during half-time and it is thought he has avoided serious injury.

Sports.title: Big Buck's dies aged 23 as Paul Nicholls pays tribute to one of his greatest horses
Sports.content:
Big Buck's dies aged 23 as Paul Nicholls pays tribute to one of his greatest horses

A fall in the 2008 Hennessy Gold Cup persuaded Nicholls to revert to hurdles with Big Buck’s, who rattled up a then-record 18 straight victories over hurdles, including four successes in the Stayers’ Hurdle at Cheltenham.

View 4 Images Paul Nicholls (arm aloft) and Ruby Walsh celebrate Big Buck's fourth World Hurdle win (Image: Getty)

Paul Nicholls has paid tribute to “invincible” hurdler Big Buck’s after the record-breaker’s death at the age of 23.

‌



A fall in the 2008 Hennessy Gold Cup persuaded Nicholls and owner Andy Stewart to revert to hurdles with Big Buck’s, who rattled up a then-record 18 straight victories over hurdles, including four successes in the Stayers’ Hurdle at Cheltenham.

‌



Big Buck’s was a contemporary of Ditcheat superstars Kauto Star, Denman and Master Minded, and Nicholls said: “Ability-wise, he was probably as good as anything I’ve ever trained. Over hurdles, he was invincible. History tells you how good he was - he won all those Grade 1s on the trot. What a horse!”

‌



Saffie Osborne heads to Shergar Cup believing big wins prove her a future jockeys' title contender READ MORE :

Big Buck's, who formed an exceptional partnership with Ruby Walsh, became a crowd favourite as he would frequently appear to struggle mid-race before surging clear to triumph.

Nicholls said: "He was a wonderful horse for a wonderful owner who deserved to own a great horse like that. Andy enjoyed the whole journey and shared it with everybody.

"The horse had a brilliant life and had a great time with us and then a great time with Mike and Lucy Felton in retirement, but sadly time caught up with him.

‌



View 4 Images Record breaker Big Buck's (Image: Getty)

"I was very lucky to have him at the same time as Kauto Star, Neptune Collonges, Master Minded and Denman. He was definitely as good as any of them."

One of the last surviving stars from that golden era for the Ditcheat trainer, Big Buck's would go on to surpass Sir Ken and claim a then record 18 consecutive National Hunt victories upon returning to hurdles, a feat only bettered by Altior since.

‌



Yet for Nicholls, the nagging question of just how far he could have gone over the bigger obstacles will never truly go away.

View 4 Images Big Buck's winning his fourth Stayers' Hurdle with jockey Ruby Walsh aboard (Image: PA)

"He won the Graded race at Aintree over fences, jumped 18 fences and jumped them 18 different ways and still won," said Nicholls. "It made me think he was a certainty in the Hennessy and he was unlucky that day, but he just wasn't a natural jumper of a fence.

‌



"If Kauto Star hadn't been about at that time then we probably would persevered over fences and he had the ability to win a Gold Cup. If he had won the Hennessy that day it would have definitely given us a headache and it would have been interesting where he would have ended up.

"But over hurdles he was invincible. Andy said I was bonkers, but going back over hurdles was the best thing we ever did.

View 4 Images Rubby Walsh and Big Bucks celebrate winning the Liverpool Hurdle (Image: PA)

Article continues below

When pressed to single out just one race from Big Bucks' illustrious career, packed with so many memorable victories, it was his fourth consecutive triumph in the day three feature that stands out most for Nicholls — seeing off what was arguably the strongest field he ever faced, narrowly beating Irish challenger Voler La Vedette.

"His fourth World Hurdle was the one that sticks out as being very special," said Nicholls. "But we had so many great days with such a brilliant horse and we were all very lucky to be associated with him."

Sports.title: Man Utd forced to field former non-league star as injury crisis deepens vs PSG
Sports.content:
Man Utd forced to field former non-league star as injury crisis deepens vs PSG

Manchester United were in pre-season action against PSG on Saturday, but were hit with two injury worries.

View 2 Images Dermot Mee made his first Man United appearance in the pre-season friendly vs PSG. (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Manchester United were forced to turn to a goalkeeper whose only previous first-team appearance came in a non-league match as their pre-season friendly against Paris Saint-Germain threatened to take a turn for the worst. An injury to Tom Heaton meant they had to turn to academy graduate Dermot Mee.

‌



The 24-year-old was called upon early in the second half when Heaton appeared to injure his hamstring after coming out to clear the ball. The score was locked at 1-1 at the time, and that's how it stayed with Mee getting a clean sheet.

‌



The goalkeeper's appearance comes four years after his only other senior appearances. The shot-stopper made four appearances for National League side Altrincham back in 2022.

‌



Michael Carrick delivers Mason Mount injury update after cruel blow vs PSG READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

He got his chance against PSG with first-choice goalkeeper Senne Lammens given extra time following his return from World Cup action with Belgium. Summer signing Karl Darlow is continuing his recovery from a minor procedure.

Andre Onana has returned to Trabzonspor on loan for the season, while Altay Bayindir has now completed a loan move to Celta Vigo.

‌



Radek Vitek has also completed a permanent move to Championship side Middlesbrough for an initial fee of £7million, which could rise to £14m. The goalkeeper impressed on loan in the Championship with Bristol City last season.

The transfers and injuries meant that United were short on options for the game against PSG, something that gave Mee a chance to show what he can do. The academy graduate recently signed a new two-year contract at Old Trafford.

View 2 Images Tom Heaton suffered an injury in the second half of Man United's friendly against PSG. (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

‌



The injury to Heaton wasn’t the only blow to Michael Carrick’s side during the game, with Mason Mount picking up a problem early in the match. The midfielder has been one of the standout players for United during pre-season so far, but was replaced in the first half and appeared to hold a lengthy discussion with members of the United medical team after making his way off the pitch.

Speaking after the game, Carrick gave an update on Mount. "He got kicked," the manager said.

"We just wanted to be careful and look after him. We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful."

Article continues below

United are back in pre-season action on Wednesday night as they take on rivals Leeds United (7.30pm BST). They then finish their pre-season preparations with a friendly against AC Milan, ahead of the season opener against Hull City on Saturday, 22 August (12.30pm BST).

Sports.title: Diego Simeone confirms Julian Alvarez transfer 'decision' amid Arsenal interest
Sports.content:
Diego Simeone confirms Julian Alvarez transfer 'decision' amid Arsenal interest

Arsenal have long-standing interest in Julian Alvarez, who dropped a bombshell at the World Cup by revealing that he wants to leave Atletico Madrid after two seasons

View 2 Images Julian Alvarez is wanted by Arsenal (Image: Diego Souto/Getty Images)

Diego Simeone has reiterated that Arsenal target Julian Alvarez is not for sale after Atletico Madrid crushed his 'dream' of a transfer. Alvarez, 26, made headlines during the World Cup when he revealed his desire to leave Atletico this summer.

‌



The former Manchester City star has since been the subject of bids from both Barcelona and Real Madrid. Atletico turned them down and CEO Miguel Angel Gil Marin stated that the only way in which Alvarez can be sold is if a club pays his extravagant €500million (£428m) release clause.

‌



Now, Simeone has reminded the likes of Arsenal of his club's stance. "The situation is very clear," the Argentine told a press conference while on the club's pre-season tour of Asia.

‌



"The club took a decision which Miguel Angel explained well. We are very happy with Julian.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

"From the sporting side of things, we will help him keep growing and improving so that he can give us what he has given us over these two years at the club so far, which was a mountain of things."

‌



Alvarez is due to return to training with Atletico next week, having been given extra time off after helping Argentina reach the World Cup final. It was early in the tournament that the forward confirmed that he wanted to leave, having communicated as such to the Atletico board.

"I spoke with people at the club, with those I had to speak with and the best thing for everyone is ‌a transfer and I want to fulfil my dream," Alvarez explained. "It's not the time to talk about this, but I also can't hide ⁠it. I try to ⁠be an honest person."

Arsenal have long admired the 26-year-old and are in the market for a forward after missing out on Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior. It's even been reported that the Gunners would be willing to include £64m signing Viktor Gyokeres in a swap deal for Alvarez, who joined Atletico from City in 2024 for £82m.

Who should Arsenal sign before the transfer window closes? Have your say in the comments section.

View 2 Images Diego Simeone has sent a clear message regarding Julian Alvarez (Image: Joaquin Corchero/Europa Press via Getty Images)

Atletico will drive a hard bargain, though, even filing a complaint to FIFA accusing Barcelona of tapping Alvarez up. "We don't want to transfer him," Gil Marin declared earlier this summer.

"We didn't accept the €100m offer, nor will we accept one for €150m or €200m. I have no doubt that Atletico is the right place for Julian and that Julian is the centre forward for Atletico Madrid. We want to keep him."

Sports.title: 'I negotiated Man Utd transfer – they paid more than double what we expected'
Sports.content:
'I negotiated Man Utd transfer – they paid more than double what we expected'

One of Manchester United's most high-profile signings ended up leaving the selling club delighted with the fee they received

View 2 Images Luke Shaw's move from Southampton to Manchester United in 2014 was blockbuster (Image: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images)

Former Southampton chief Les Reed claims he "pulled Manchester United's pants down" during negotiations for Luke Shaw after selling the defender for more than double the amount the club had expected to receive.

‌



In 2014, Shaw became the most expensive teenager in world football after joining United in a £30million deal. At the time, the transfer was viewed as something of a coup for the Red Devils, who had beaten off competition from several Premier League rivals to land one of the most highly-rated young talents in Europe.

‌



But ultimately, it was Southampton who came away from negotiations rubbing their hands together. Recalling the transfer on the Fozcast podcast after being asked by Ben Foster whether there were any deals where he felt he had got the better of another club, Reed said: "I met with Ed Woodward for the Luke Shaw transfer.

‌



"I came back to the Southampton offices and my office is on the same floor as the finance director and the chief executive. And they had their doors open and we were chatting.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

7 Man Utd players face uncertain futures as part of huge summer overhaul of squad READ MORE :

Jadon Sancho's Man Utd decline and manager trend leaves unwanted star in awkward spot READ MORE :

"They've both gone, 'So, how much [did you sell him for]?' And I went, 'Go on, guess.' So the finance director said £12m and the CEO said, 'Nah nah, more than that. £15m.' And I said, 'Nah, you're both wrong. £30m.' I thought I've done pretty well there."

‌



The deal remains to this day Southampton's most lucrative academy sale, with Shaw having emerged from the club's famed youth system before becoming a first team regular at St Mary's as a teenager.

The full back was one of several high-profile departures overseen by Reed during his eight-year spell at Southampton, which began with him serving as Head of Football Development and Support before later becoming Vice-Chairman.

Between 2010 and 2018, he played a key role in negotiating lucrative deals for the likes of Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain, Adam Lallana, Dejan Lovren, Calum Chambers, Morgan Schneiderlin, Sadio Mane and Virgil van Dijk - with those sales alone bringing in just shy of £250m for the club.

‌



View 2 Images Luke Shaw has been at Manchester United for 12 years (Image: Visionhaus/Getty Images)

Shaw would go on to establish himself as a key figure for both Manchester United and England, cementing his reputation as one of the finest left backs in Europe and ultimately justifying the fee United forked out for him.

However, injuries have repeatedly disrupted his career, with the defender making fewer than 13 Premier League appearances in five of his 12 seasons at Old Trafford.

Article continues below

Now 31, Shaw has entered the final year of his United contract and is expected to leave Old Trafford next summer, with no talks over a new deal currently taking place. Michael Carrick's side are also actively eyeing up long-term replacements for Shaw, with Newcastle's Lewis Hall high on their wish list.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat
