World.title: Community leader recounts Kwara abductees’ ordeal during six months in captivity, seeks support for orphaned children
World.content:
The Kaiama community in Kwara State has called for sustained government support to rehabilitate and reintegrate victims of the February 3 attack on Woro, following the release of 163 of the victims after about six months in captivity.

A retired permanent secretary in Kwara State and vice president of the Kaiama Development Association, Yakub Jaja, made the call during an interview with PREMIUM TIMES in Ilorin on Saturday.

Mr Jaja thanked President Bola Tinubu, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara, security agencies and local vigilantes for the release of the abductees.

He said the community was relieved to see the victims return alive after months of uncertainty. Still, he stressed that their release marked the beginning of another phase requiring coordinated government and community intervention.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, 176 persons were initially abducted during the attack, while 163 have so far returned.

He said the 3 February incident left a lasting impact on Woro and neighbouring communities, with homes, shops and places of worship destroyed in the attack.

Mr Jaja said the rescued victims were currently receiving medical treatment at various facilities, including the Kwara State University Teaching Hospital. At the same time, some were being accommodated at the Nigerian Army’s Sobi Barracks.

He explained that the victims were in different conditions, with some physically and mentally stable, while others were in the intensive care unit and hospital wards.

The community leader also recounted some of the experiences shared by the victims, saying some had spent months under difficult conditions while in captivity.

He disclosed that some of the women gave birth during their captivity.

According to him, 11 children were born during the period, including a set of twins, while six of the children died, and five were brought back alive.

Mr Jaja also alleged that some of the abductees were forced into relationships with members of the criminal group. At the same time, some persons aged 15 and above were allegedly incorporated into their activities.

He said he could not confirm whether a ransom was paid to secure the victims’ release.

“I cannot exactly say what transpired in that,” he said when asked about the circumstances surrounding their release.

Mr Jaja recalled that the abductors had initially demanded a ransom of about N2 billion, adding that the community subsequently attempted to mobilise funds for negotiation.

He said the community later intensified advocacy, protests, and engagement with authorities after it became difficult to raise the demanded amount.

The Kaiama leader identified poor road infrastructure as one of the factors complicating security operations in the area.

He said the major routes linking Kaiama with neighbouring communities were in deplorable condition, making it difficult for security personnel to respond promptly to emergencies.

Mr Jaja said Woro is about 40 kilometres from Kaiama town. At the same time, the route linking the community to Nibusa, where army and air force facilities are located, is also difficult to navigate.

He urged the government to improve road infrastructure in the area as part of broader measures to strengthen security and facilitate economic activities.

Mr Jaja welcomed the federal government’s reported approval of the establishment of a military base in Kaiama, describing it as a significant step towards improving security in the area.

He said the presence of a permanent military formation would enhance the response capacity of security agencies and provide greater confidence to residents.

He also commended Governor AbdulRazaq for visiting some of the rescued victims at Sobi Barracks and the hospital.

According to him, the state government has pledged to provide medical care for the victims.

However, he said government intervention should extend beyond immediate medical treatment to include psychological support, accommodation, education and economic assistance.

Mr Jaja said the attack had significantly affected education and economic activities in Woro and the surrounding communities.

He said some parents had moved their children to Kaiama town and the neighbouring communities because of lingering security concerns.

However, he noted that economic activity was gradually returning but had not yet fully recovered, with residents still leaving their communities early due to concerns for their safety.

According to him, the state government had commenced some interventions, including the reconstruction of shops and the provision of water facilities.

He, however, stressed that more needed to be done to restore confidence and enable displaced residents to return permanently.

Mr Jaja appealed to residents to accept the rescued victims without discrimination or stigmatisation.

He said many of the survivors would return to communities where they had lost parents, relatives and property, making reintegration a major challenge.

READ ALSO: 13 unaccounted for after 163 Kwara abductees rescued Community leader

“Some, their father had been killed. Some of their mother had been killed. And they are small children. They would like to see their parents. Unfortunately, they cannot see them,” he said.

He called for a coordinated rehabilitation programme involving the federal government, Kwara State Government, local authorities, traditional institutions and community leaders.

He said the programme should address healthcare, accommodation, education, psychosocial support and livelihood opportunities.

Mr Jaja also urged security agencies to maintain their presence in Woro and other vulnerable communities around Kainji Lake to prevent a recurrence.

He said the rescue of the abductees should be seen not as the end of the crisis but as the beginning of a long-term process of recovery, rehabilitation and restoration of confidence in the affected communities.

World.title: WAFU B U-20 Preview: Flying Eagles seek revenge against Burkina Faso in showdown
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flying Eagles will have more than the WAFU B U-20 Championship trophy on their minds when they face familiar foes Burkina Faso in Sunday’s 2026 final.

The two sides have emerged as the last teams standing after four matches apiece, setting up a repeat of their Group B encounter and giving Nigeria an immediate opportunity to avenge the only defeat they have suffered in the tournament.

But with the regional title and qualification for next year’s Africa U-20 Cup of Nations in Ghana at stake, there is little room for sentiment when the two West African heavyweights meet again on Sunday.

Speaking ahead of the tie, head coach Abdul Maikaba gave his thoughts on expectations for the game.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I think this is an opportunity for us to redeem ourselves, having lost to Burkina Faso in the group stage. Having played them before, we now have an idea of their shape and structure, and we are working on how to capitalise on their weaknesses, while also capitalising on our own strengths.”

”It has been a gradual process, and we have arrived here against Burkina Faso. We met in the group stage, and we lost; this is the second time in the final. I hope it will be our turn to win the game so that we can round it up with a trophy,” the former Akwa United head coach added.

Two different routes to the final

Nigeria impressively began their campaign, defeating Ghana 4-2 before cruising past Togo with a convincing 3-0 victory.

Their final Group B fixture, however, brought their first setback, as the Flying Eagles were beaten 2-0 by Sunday’s final opponent. This result saw the Young Stallions finish top of the group with seven points, one ahead of Nigeria’s six.

Burkina Faso remained unbeaten throughout the group stage, while Nigeria advanced as runners-up after two wins and that solitary defeat.

Abdul Maikaba’s side responded strongly in the semi-final, producing a dramatic 2-2 draw against hosts Côte d’Ivoire after extra time before winning 4-3 on penalties.

Goalkeeper Clinton Lawani emerged as the hero, saving two spot-kicks to send Nigeria into the final.

Burkina Faso, meanwhile, have been the tournament’s only unbeaten side, with the Young Stallions opening with a 1-1 draw against Ghana before defeating Togo 3-1. They then made their biggest statement by beating Nigeria 2-0, and followed that with another 2-0 victory over Niger in the semi-final.

Meanwhile, the two teams are meeting for the first time in the final of the regional competition, with all previous meetings happening in the group stage.

Flying Eagles have unfinished business

For Nigeria, Sunday’s final offers the perfect opportunity to put the group-stage defeat behind them.

Burkina Faso already know they can hurt the Flying Eagles, having exploited Nigeria’s weaknesses to claim a 2-0 victory on Matchday 3, but this is a different game, with the WAFU B title now at stake.

Nigeria must start with greater intensity, maintain concentration throughout and avoid the defensive mistakes that allowed Burkina Faso to take control of their previous meeting.

Abdulmuiz Adeleke, Oraro Lucky, Habila Simeon and goalkeeper Clinton Lawani are among the players expected to rise to the occasion. At the same time, Maikaba faces another major tactical test against a Burkina Faso side that has yet to taste defeat.

History favours Nigeria

Burkina Faso have reached this stage before, but their only previous WAFU B U-20 final appearance ended in disappointment.

The Young Stallions reached the 2018 final in Togo but lost 2-0 to Senegal. Nigeria, meanwhile, have dominated the competition in recent editions.

The Flying Eagles won the title in both of their last two appearances.

In 2024, Nigeria defeated Ghana 2-1 in Lomé to retain the championship, having previously beaten Benin Republic 3-1 in Niamey in the 2022 final.

The Flying Eagles are therefore two-time WAFU B U-20 champions and will be chasing a third regional crown on Sunday. Burkina Faso, by contrast, is seeking their first-ever WAFU B U-20 championship title.

Nigeria also have another piece of unfinished business after losing 1-0 to Côte d’Ivoire in last year’s edition.

A victory over Burkina Faso would therefore represent another step towards restoring the Flying Eagles’ dominance in regional youth football.

More than a trophy at stake

Sunday’s final carries consequences beyond the regional title.

Victory would crown Nigeria the 2026 WAFU B U-20 champions and secure qualification for the 2027 Africa U-20 Cup of Nations in Ghana.

Burkina Faso have already beaten Nigeria once. Now the Flying Eagles have 90 minutes, or more if need be, to change the story.

One win separates Burkina Faso from a perfect tournament. Meanwhile, for Nigeria and the Flying Eagles, one more victory would deliver the trophy, revenge, and open another chapter in the nation’s proud history at the WAFU B U-20 Championship.

World.title: WAFCON 2026 PREVIEW: Nigeria’s dominance faces Cameroon test with World Cup ticket at stake
World.content:
The Super Falcons of Nigeria will face familiar opponents when they take on Cameroon in the quarter-finals of the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Casablanca on Sunday.

The match, scheduled for 6 p.m. at the Stade Larbi Zaouli, carries a huge prize: the winner advances to the semi-finals and secures a ticket to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Nigeria entered the contest as defending champions and the most successful team in the history of the competition, while Cameroon have reached the knockout stage unbeaten.

But while the numbers strongly favour Nigeria, Cameroon believe they have a chance to produce a different result.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria’s overwhelming WAFCON advantage

There is little to suggest that Nigeria and Cameroon have enjoyed an evenly balanced contest at the WAFCON.

The two teams have met 13 times since 1998, with Nigeria winning nine, Cameroon one, and three matches ending in draws.

The Falcons have also scored 33 goals, compared to Cameroon’s six.

Nigeria’s dominance began at the inaugural edition in 1998, when the hosts defeated Cameroon 6-0 in the semi-final.

They won 3-0 in the 2000 group stage, drew 2-2 with Cameroon in 2004 before winning the final 5-0, and repeated the 5-0 scoreline against the Lionesses in the 2006 semi-final.

Nigeria also won 5-1 in the 2010 semi-final.

Cameroon’s only WAFCON victory over Nigeria came in the 2012 third-place match, when the Lionesses won 1-0. Nigeria had earlier beaten them 2-1 in the group stage.

The Falcons then defeated Cameroon in the 2014 and 2016 finals, winning 2-0 and 1-0 respectively.

The 2018 semi-final ended 0-0, but Nigeria advanced 4-2 on penalties.

The most recent WAFCON meeting came in the 2022 quarter-final in Casablanca, where Rasheedat Ajibade scored the only goal to send Nigeria into the semi-finals and secure qualification for the 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup.

Cameroon arrive unbeaten

Cameroon have been one of the more consistent teams in the tournament.

The Lionesses topped Group D with seven points after beating Mali 2-1, defeating Ghana 1-0 and drawing 1-1 with debutants Cape Verde.

Marie Gisele Ngah Manga has been central to their campaign, scoring three of their four group-stage goals.

She was forced off against Ghana with an ankle problem, but has since been cleared to continue in the tournament.

Cameroon also have the confidence of their 1-0 friendly victory over Nigeria in Yaounde in February. Nigeria responded three days later with a 3-1 win in the return match.

The Lionesses are therefore aware of what Nigeria can offer, but they also know they have beaten the Falcons this year.

Eto: We will give everything

Cameroon midfielder Eto acknowledged Nigeria’s status as the stronger side on paper but insisted that her team would not be intimidated.

“Nigeria is a very great nation in African Women’s Football and deserves all our respect. We know we are not the favourites and, in fact, we never really were in this competition. But we also know what we want to achieve,” she told cafonline.com.

Eto said Cameroon would remain committed to their approach rather than change their style because of Nigeria’s reputation.

“We will not change the way we play. We will continue our work, apply the technical staff’s plan and seek to correct the few shortcomings that we have identified,” she said.

And while she acknowledged Nigeria’s status as favourites, Eto believes the outcome will be decided on the pitch.

“We know there is a favourite, and it’s not us, but in football nothing is a foregone conclusion.”

Nigeria finding their feet

Nigeria’s path to the quarter-finals has been less convincing than Cameroon’s.

The defending champions suffered a 3-2 defeat to Malawi in their opening Group C match before recovering with a 1-0 victory over Zambia.

They then produced their strongest performance of the tournament so far, defeating Egypt 6-2 in their final group match.

Asisat Oshoala has been among the key attacking players, scoring against Zambia and converting a penalty against Egypt.

The veteran forward also scored twice in Nigeria’s two friendly matches against Senegal before the tournament.

Coach Justine Madugu will also welcome back defender Oluwatosin Demehin and midfielder Jennifer Echegini, who missed the Egypt match through suspension.

The return of the two players gives Nigeria more options as they seek to avoid another setback against Cameroon.

History favours Nigeria, but the stakes are different

Nigeria’s record against Cameroon at the WAFCON is clear: nine wins from 13 meetings, one defeat and three draws.

But Sunday’s encounter will not be decided by history.

Cameroon have already shown that they can frustrate Nigeria, while their unbeaten group-stage campaign has given them confidence.

For Nigeria, however, the objective remains straightforward.

“We have to get the World Cup ticket and then go ahead to retain the trophy,” Madugu said.

The Falcons need a victory to keep both ambitions alive.

World.title: MFM win inaugural Louis Edem West Africa Women’s Basketball Championship
World.content:
MFM have emerged champions of the inaugural Louis Edem West Africa Women’s Basketball Championship after defeating record Nigerian Women’s Basketball League champions First Bank 49-41 in the final.

The final, played on Saturday at the Indoor Sports Hall of the National Stadium in Surulere, Lagos, produced a competitive contest before MFM secured victory, adding another title to their women’s basketball achievements.

MFM, two-time winners of the Nigerian Women’s Basketball League, held their nerve against First Bank, who remain the most successful team in the history of the domestic league.

In the third-place match, Victoria Queens of Lagos defeated Ghana’s GRA 54-48 to claim the bronze medal.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The tournament brought together women’s basketball teams from Nigeria and Ghana, providing an opportunity for the participating teams to test themselves against different opposition and promote greater cooperation through sport.

Louis Edem, organiser of the championship, praised the participating teams and described the tournament as another milestone for the Louis Edem Foundation.

“It’s another great moment for all the teams that came for this year’s championship,” Mr Edem said.

He said the participation of GRA from Ghana was particularly significant, noting that playing against established Nigerian teams could help the Ghanaian side improve when it returns to domestic competition.

“For example, the team from Ghana, coming out here to play basketball against all the elite teams in Nigeria, helps them go back and perform in their league. And one important thing that people forget is that it fosters regional cooperation and, you know, fosters youth cooperation and all that,” he said.

Victoria Queens captain, Toluwani Arogundade, described the competition as a valuable experience for her team and commended the organisers for staging the championship.

She said the team would build on its performance as it prepares for a possible return to the Nigerian Women’s Basketball League in 2026.

“It’s been a great experience for us. We appreciate the organisers for allowing us to compete, and we will take the lessons from this tournament and work on our performance ahead of the 2026 Women’s League,” she said.

B4 Sail Finance Ltd, one of the sponsors of the championship, said its involvement was part of its commitment to supporting Nigerian youths through sport.

Oluwatobiloba Oladipupo, Business Development Officer of the company, said the tournament provided an opportunity to support young athletes while promoting values that extend beyond the basketball court.

“Finance goes beyond just giving companies opportunities; it’s a way to promote discipline, teamwork and resilience, and we can see what the girls are doing,” Mr Oladipupo said.

He congratulated MFM on their victory and praised all the participating teams for their performances throughout the tournament.

World.title: NPFL: Shooting Stars part ways with Head Coach Aweroro after historic campaign
World.content:
Shooting Stars SC have parted ways with head coach Nurudeen Aweroro just days before the start of the new Nigeria Premier Football League season, bringing an abrupt end to his time in charge of the Oluyole Warriors.

The Ibadan club confirmed the development in an official statement, announcing that Aweroro, Team Manager Tammy Tamuno and Assistant Coach Shakiru Lawal have all left their respective positions with immediate effect.

Shooting Stars did not disclose the specific reasons behind the decision, describing the departure as a mutual agreement following discussions between the club and members of the technical team.

However, sources indicate that lingering issues between Aweroro and some influential members of the club’s board contributed to the sudden change.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In its statement, Shooting Stars said the affected members of the technical team had agreed to end their contracts amicably.

“We have reached a mutual agreement with Head Coach Nurudeen Aweroro, Team Manager Tammy Tamuno and Assistant Coach Shakiru Lawal to bring their respective contracts with the Club to an end, with immediate effect,” the club stated.

“The decision follows discussions between the Club and the affected members of the technical team, with both parties agreeing to part ways amicably.”

The club also praised the trio for their commitment and contributions, particularly their role in Shooting Stars’ impressive campaign last season.

“Shooting Stars appreciates Nurudeen Aweroro, Tammy Tamuno and Shakiru Lawal for their commitment, professionalism and contributions to the Club during their respective periods of service,” the statement added.

“The Club particularly acknowledges their efforts in helping Shooting Stars achieve a third-place finish in the 2025/26 NPFL season and secure a continental ticket.”

The club wished all three officials success in their future careers before announcing that its remaining assistant coaches would temporarily oversee the technical department.

“In the interim, the other Assistant Coaches have been directed to take charge of the affairs of the Technical Department pending the appointment and announcement of a substantive Head Coach. The Club will communicate further developments in due course.”

Aweroro leaves after historic NPFL campaign

The timing of Aweroro’s departure has added to the surprise surrounding the decision.

Shooting Stars parted ways with the coach on the eve of their participation in the Value Jet Cup pre-season tournament, just 24 hours after the Oluyole Warriors suffered a 3-0 friendly defeat to Ikorodu City.

Aweroro was appointed Shooting Stars head coach in July 2025 and went on to oversee one of the club’s most significant campaigns in recent years.

The Ibadan-based side finished third in the 2025/26 NPFL season, securing a place in the CAF Confederation Cup.

The achievement was particularly significant as it marked Shooting Stars’ first qualification for continental football in 27 years.

The club specifically acknowledged the contributions of Aweroro, Tamuno and Lawal to that historic accomplishment.

Now, however, the Oluyole Warriors must begin the new campaign without the coach who guided them back to continental competition.

World.title: EKO 2026: Sanwo-Olu inspects Lagos facilities ahead of National Intermediate Games
World.content:
Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, has inspected ongoing rehabilitation works at the Teslim Balogun Stadium and other sports facilities ahead of the inaugural National Intermediate Sports Festival, EKO 2026.

Mr Sanwo-Olu, in a post on his social media platforms on Saturday, said the state was making progress with preparations to host thousands of young athletes from across Nigeria.

According to the governor, the natural-grass pitch at Teslim Balogun Stadium has been completed, while work on the new tartan track is expected to be finished in the coming weeks.

He added that indoor halls, swimming pools and other sports facilities were also being upgraded ahead of the Games.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The natural grass pitch is complete, while work on the new tartan track will be finished in the coming weeks,” Mr Sanwo-Olu said.

“Our indoor halls, swimming pools and other facilities are also being upgraded to receive the thousands of young athletes expected from across the country.”

The governor said the rehabilitation of sports facilities was part of the state’s broader investment in grassroots sports development.

“For the past three years, we have been rebuilding sports centres across Surulere, Ikorodu, Epe, Agege and Badagry, because our young people deserve quality facilities close to home,” he said.

“We want them to discover their talents, compete with confidence and see a future for themselves in sports right here in Nigeria.”

EKO 2026 preparations

The inspection comes weeks after Lagos unveiled the official logo and mascot for EKO 2026, marking another milestone in preparations for the maiden edition of the National Intermediate Games.

The Games are scheduled to be held from 1 to 15 October 2026. They are expected to bring together young athletes from all 36 states, the Federal Capital Territory, and eligible Nigerian athletes from the diaspora.

The National Sports Commission conceived the Intermediate Games as a structured pathway between the National Youth Games and the National Sports Festival to identify and develop young talents before they progress to elite competition.

Speaking at the logo and mascot unveiling in July, the Director-General of the Lagos State Sports Commission, Lekan Fatodu, said the state was committed to delivering a successful first edition.

Mr Fatodu said rehabilitation work at the Teslim Balogun Stadium was progressing according to schedule and that the state was also working with private institutions to provide additional venues.

He specifically mentioned the British International School in Lekki as one of the private facilities secured through partnerships for the Games.

The Director-General of the National Sports Commission, Bukola Olopade, had also explained that Lagos was chosen as the host because of its established grassroots sports development structure.

He said the state had demonstrated a system capable of identifying athletes from the school level and developing them towards elite competition.

Mr Olopade said the Games would help bridge the gap between youth-level competitions and the National Sports Festival, providing young athletes with a more structured route into higher-level sports.

The commission also planned diaspora trials in London for eligible Nigerian athletes abroad, with successful participants expected to compete in Lagos.

With less than two months to the opening of the Games, Mr Sanwo-Olu said Lagos was ready to welcome the next generation of Nigerian athletes.

“Lagos is ready, and we look forward to welcoming the next generation of Nigerian athletes,” the governor said.

World.title: ‘We know what is at stake’ — Madugu rallies Super Falcons for Cameroon WAFCON showdown
World.content:
Super Falcons head coach Justin Madugu says his players fully understand what is at stake as Nigeria prepare for a high-stakes Women’s Africa Cup of Nations quarter-final clash against Cameroon in Casablanca.

The defending champions face the Indomitable Lionesses at the Larbi Zaouli Stadium on Sunday, with a place in the semi-finals and qualification for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup both on the line.

Madugu insists Nigeria are ready for the challenge and determined to keep their title defence alive.

“It’s an important match because we all know what is at stake, the ticket for the World Cup. After the World Cup ticket, you have the semi-finals, which will also enable you to continue your quest for retaining the trophy,” Madugu said at his pre-match press conference.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We’ll go in there fully prepared, give it our best and ensure that we carry the day.”

The Super Falcons have already faced Cameroon twice in recent friendlies, but Madugu does not believe those matches provide an accurate assessment of Sunday’s contest.

The coach pointed out that both teams have changed in those meetings, with several players who featured previously now absent, while others have joined the squads.

“The last two games we played against Cameroon were preparatory games, and a lot of things went into those matches,” he explained.

“There were players that were not involved then who are here now for both teams, so we’re not using those games to assess the current team.”

Nigeria have conceded goals during the group stage, but Madugu remains confident his team can tighten up defensively without losing the attacking threat that has kept them competitive.

“There can always be a starting point when you don’t concede goals, and we’re believing it will start from the quarter-final stage,” he said.

“We have been working to ensure that those mistakes and loopholes that caused those goals are corrected. Yes, we conceded goals, but we equally score goals, so it’s still positive for us.”

The coach, however, confirmed that there are injury concerns within the squad ahead of the crucial encounter.

“We have some injury concerns in the team. The medical team is working on that to prepare the players in better shape,” Madugu revealed.

Payne: Super Falcons are ‘just as hungry as ever’

Midfielder Toni Payne shared Madugu’s confidence, stressing that the Super Falcons are focused on securing World Cup qualification and taking another step towards retaining their continental crown.

“Everyone in the team, including myself and the staff, are really confident going into this game,” Payne said.

“It was our goal to get through the group stage and have a chance at qualifying for the World Cup. We did that, so we’re ready to continue to that next step.”

The Inter Milan midfielder expects Cameroon to provide a physical test but believes Nigeria have the experience and preparation required to cope with the challenge.

“We know every game is going to pose a different threat to us. They have their style, and we have our own style,” she said.

“We know it’s going to be a physical game, but that’s something that we’re always prepared for. A lot of us have been playing football for a long time, and we know what it takes to win games.”

Despite Nigeria’s remarkable record at the WAFCON, Payne insists the Super Falcons’ hunger for success has not diminished.

“I don’t think anyone gets tired of winning. We appreciate all the accomplishments we’ve made, but we’re just as hungry as ever,” she said.

“The opportunity to win an 11th title is something we’re all looking forward to.”

Nigeria will take on Cameroon at the Larbi Zaouli Stadium in Casablanca, with victory guaranteeing the Super Falcons a place in the semi-finals and securing their ticket to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup.

World.title: 10 churches with the largest auditoriums in the world
World.content:
Some of the world’s biggest churches are distinguished not only by their congregations but also by the enormous auditoriums built to accommodate thousands of worshippers in a single service.

The trend is particularly striking in Africa, where several Pentecostal churches have constructed or are developing worship centres capable of seating tens of thousands of people. Nigeria, in particular, dominates the global rankings.

For this ranking, auditorium capacity refers to the number of people a main worship auditorium can seat in a single service, rather than total church membership, weekly attendance or the capacity of an entire church campground. Figures can vary between sources, particularly for newer projects.

Here are 10 of the largest church auditoriums in the world based on reported seating capacity.

1. Hand of God Cathedral – 120,000 seats

Location: Port Harcourt, Rivers State, Nigeria

Church: Salvation Ministries

The Hand of God Cathedral, operated by Salvation Ministries, is currently reported as the world’s largest church auditorium, with a capacity of 120,000 worshippers.

Located in Port Harcourt, the massive worship centre is associated with Pastor David Ibiyeomie and was designed to accommodate the church’s growing congregation and large-scale gatherings.

The cathedral was dedicated in November 2025, according to recent reports, and its reported capacity has placed it at the top of current rankings of the world’s largest church auditoriums.

Its size is particularly notable because it surpasses several other Nigerian megachurch auditoriums that previously held the distinction of being among the world’s largest.

2. The Ark – 109,345 seats

Location: Ota, Ogun State, Nigeria

Church: Living Faith Church Worldwide

The Ark, another massive Nigerian church project, is associated with Living Faith Church Worldwide, popularly known as Winners’ Chapel.

The proposed auditorium has a reported capacity of 109,345 seats, putting it among the biggest church auditoriums ever planned. It is being developed close to Faith Tabernacle at Canaanland in Ota, Ogun State.

The project represents an expansion of Living Faith Church’s enormous worship infrastructure at Canaanland, which already includes the 50,000-seat Faith Tabernacle.

Because The Ark has been reported as under construction, its inclusion in a ranking of the largest auditoriums should be understood as a planned/projected capacity rather than that of a completed, regularly operating auditorium.

3. Glory Dome – 100,000 seats

Location: Abuja, Nigeria

Church: Dunamis International Gospel Centre

The Glory Dome of Dunamis International Gospel Centre is one of the most recognisable megachurch auditoriums in Nigeria.

The Abuja facility has a reported capacity of 100,000 people and was completed in 2018. It serves as the headquarters of Dunamis International Gospel Centre.

The church has itself described the facility as a 100,000-seat auditorium, while footage from Dunamis has shown large gatherings filling the venue.

Its completion helped establish Abuja as home to one of the largest enclosed worship auditoriums anywhere in the world.

4. Champions Royal Assembly – 80,000 seats

Location: Abuja, Nigeria

Church: Champions Royal Assembly

The main auditorium of Champions Royal Assembly, also known as the City of Wonders, has a reported seating capacity of 80,000.

The auditorium, associated with Pastor Joshua Iginla, was completed in 2015 and is located in Abuja.

The enormous building has been used for church services, conferences, crusades and other large gatherings. Its 80,000-seat capacity places it ahead of several internationally recognised megachurch facilities.

5. Temple of the Glory of God – 60,000 seats

Location: São Paulo, Brazil

Church: God Is Love Pentecostal Church

Moving outside Africa, the Temple of the Glory of God in São Paulo is one of the largest church auditoriums in South America.

The auditorium belongs to the God Is Love Pentecostal Church, a Brazilian Pentecostal denomination founded by David Miranda.

The church inaugurated the Temple of the Glory of God in 2004, with a reported capacity of 60,000 seats.

Its size makes it one of the few non-African churches in the top tier of the global auditorium rankings.

6. Faith Tabernacle – 50,000 seats

Location: Canaanland, Ota, Ogun State, Nigeria

Church: Living Faith Church Worldwide

The Faith Tabernacle is one of Nigeria’s best-known megachurch auditoriums and was once widely recognised as the world’s largest church auditorium.

Living Faith Church Worldwide says the 50,000-seat sanctuary was built and dedicated between 1998 and 1999, with construction completed in just one year.

The auditorium remains the main worship centre at Canaanland and hosts major programmes, including the church’s annual Shiloh gathering.

Although newer projects have overtaken it in reported capacity, Faith Tabernacle remains one of the largest completed church auditoriums in the world.

7. Nginden Bethany Church – 35,000 seats

Location: Surabaya, Indonesia

Church: Bethany Indonesian Church

The Nginden Bethany Church, also known as Graha Bethany Nginden, is one of the largest church auditoriums in Asia.

The Surabaya-based church originally opened a 20,000-seat temple in 2000. Following subsequent expansion and renovation, the capacity rose to about 35,000 seats in 2009.

The church is affiliated with Bethany Indonesian Church and is associated with a large Pentecostal and charismatic Christian community in Indonesia.

Its presence in the top 10 also makes it one of the biggest church auditoriums outside Africa and South America.

8. International Gospel Centre – 35,000 seats

Location: Warri, Delta State, Nigeria

Church: Word of Life Bible Church

The International Gospel Centre in Warri is the main worship facility of Word of Life Bible Church.

The auditorium has a reported capacity of 35,000 people. The facility is located along Ajamimogha-Ekpen Road in Warri and has become a major venue for worship services and large Christian gatherings.

The church was founded by Pastor Ayo Oritsejafor, and the centre has played an important part in the growth of the ministry.

9. United Family International Church Auditorium – 30,000 seats

Location: Chitungwiza, Zimbabwe

Church: United Family International Church

Zimbabwe also features on the global list through the United Family International Church (UFIC) auditorium in Chitungwiza.

The facility has a reported capacity of 30,000 worshippers and was opened in 2022. The church is led by Prophet Emmanuel Makandiwa.

Construction of the auditorium began in 2011 before encountering regulatory delays. The project eventually resumed, culminating in the opening of the large worship centre more than a decade later.

10. Deeper Life Bible Church Auditorium – 30,000 seats

Location: Gbagada, Lagos, Nigeria

Church: Deeper Christian Life Ministry

The Deeper Life Bible Church Auditorium in Lagos rounds out the top 10, with a reported capacity of 30,000 seats.

The facility serves Deeper Christian Life Ministry, founded by Pastor William Folorunso Kumuyi. The present auditorium was completed in 2018 and replaced the church’s earlier worship centre in Gbagada.

World.title: INEC extends deadline for Guber, assembly candidates’ lists
World.content:
File: INEC chairman Joash Amupitan

…Says stolen Osun PVCs cannot be used to vote

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA — The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has extended the deadline for political parties to submit their lists of candidates for the governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections scheduled for the February 2027 General Election.

The Commission disclosed this in a statement by the National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee, Mohammed Kudu Haruna.

INEC also announced that downloadable replacement Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) are available to voters in Odo-Otin and Ife Central Local Government Areas of Osun State whose cards were stolen during an invasion of the two collection centres.

The Commission warned that the stolen PVCs could not be used to vote.

“The Commission reiterates that the stolen cards cannot be used to vote,” the statement said, while assuring the people of Osun State of its readiness to conduct a free, fair, credible and inclusive governorship election on August 15, 2026.

According to INEC, the submission window, which was originally scheduled to close on Saturday, August 8, 2026, has been extended to Tuesday, August 11, following appeals by political parties for additional time to complete the process.

In a related development, the Commission said voters who applied for replacement of lost, damaged or defaced PVCs have until midnight on Sunday, August 9, to print downloadable copies of their cards.

It said the deadline would enable it to compile data on downloaded PVCs ahead of the August 15 Osun governorship election.

INEC recalled that PVC collection in Osun State commenced at the Registration Area level from July 22 to 28, 2026, but was extended to July 31 following complaints about large crowds and difficulties encountered by voters at collection centres.

The exercise subsequently moved to the Local Government Area level and ran from August 1 to 7, 2026.

World.title: Osun election: Farmers, butchers endorse Gov Adeleke
World.content:
By Shina Abubakar Osogbo

As the governorship election in Osun State is set to hold this weekend, farmers under the aegis of All Farmers of Nigeria, AFAN, endorsed Governor Ademola Adeleke for re-election, describing him as farmer-friendly.

The group, in a statement issued by Governor Ademola Adeleke’s spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, appreciated the governor for his pro-farmers policies, which include the purchase of new tractors, completion of the farmers’ secretariat, distribution of farmers’ inputs and distribution of thousands of cocoa, cashew and palm oil seedlings.

Speaking through their representative, Moshood Adepoju, the group said farmers in Osun had never had it so good, accusing the state APC of arresting their leaders to force the association to work against Governor Ademola Adeleke.

“We endorse Mr Governor for re-election because he did well for Osun farmers. We were neglected for years under APC. Governor Adeleke came and changed our fortunes for the better.

“We were arrested, but we insisted on standing by Mr Governor. Farmers will come out and vote massively for the governor’s second term. We compare the records of previous governors. The Accord candidate is our man within the farmers’ movement”, the AFAN chairman noted.

Also, the State Chairman of the Butchers Association, Amoo Afeez, said his members have resolved to back the governor for a second term because of his achievements across all sectors of society.

Speaking in Yoruba language, Afeez said the governor has positively transformed Osun State, adding that “Osun people will show appreciation by re-electing our governor”

Earlier, the Commissioner for Agriculture, Hon Tola Faseru, briefed the governor on the event, which he said was requested by the various associations to show their appreciation for the good job being done by the governor.

The farmers later moved a motion for the endorsement of the governor for a second term, a motion which was unanimously approved by elated farmers in attendance.

Responding to the endorsement, Governor Adeleke commended the show of love for him and his administration and promised to deliver more once re-elected.

“I am happy that our deliveries in the agriculture sector are recognised by our dear farmers. This will encourage me to do more. We will get more machinery and farm inputs as well as processing factories in our second term”, the governor stated.

World.title: Osun election: NDC chieftain tasks INEC, security agencies on fair, peaceful election
World.content:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and security agencies to ensure a fair and peaceful election in the Aug.15 governorship election in Osun

Mr Ladipo Johnson, NDC candidate for Lagos Central Senatorial District, made the call in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Lagos on Sunday .

He said the election presented another opportunity for INEC to prove its independence and ability to conduct credible elections in Nigeria.

“This election is a major test for INEC before the 2027 general elections. However, INEC alone cannot do it; security agencies and all stakeholders must ensure a level playing field for all political parties,” he said.

According to him, the ruling party at the national level must avoid using state institutions to frustrate opposition parties during campaigns and elections.

He expressed hope that if all stakeholders play by the rules, Nigerians would have more confidence in the electoral process going forward.

On the role of citizens, Johnson urged eligible voters in Osun to come out en masse and vote, saying high voter turnout would reduce the chances of electoral manipulation.

“The more people that vote, the more difficult it becomes for anyone to rig the election. Citizens must take ownership of the process,” he said.

He also advised young people not to allow themselves to be used as political thugs, warning that short-term gains from politicians would not translate into good governance.

“Do not reduce your future to what you get on election day. Stomach infrastructure cannot replace good governance,” he said.

Johnson further appealed to politicians to shun violence, stressing that public office is about service and not a do-or-die affair.

“Once politics becomes violent, it is no longer service. It becomes a struggle for control of public resources,” he said.

He expressed optimism that the will of the people would prevail in the election and prayed for a peaceful process.

“I wish the people of Osun well. I pray that their choice will stand and bring development to the state,” he added.

He also urged INEC, security agencies and other institutions involved in the election not to disappoint.

“If they remain committed to their constitutional duty, we will have a free and fair election,”he said.

Johnson wished Osun residents a peaceful poll and expressed hope that the outcome would lead to greater prosperity for the state.

World.title: Nigeria’s Samuel becomes president of Commonwealth Fencing Federation
World.content:
Nigeria has recorded a historic achievement in international sports administration with the election of Adeyinka Samuel as President of the Commonwealth Fencing Federation (CFF).

This is contained in a statement issued by the federation on Sunday in Lagos.

Samuel defeated the incumbent, Marie-France Dufour, at the federation’s elective Annual General Meeting, held at Rugby School Nigeria, Atlantic City, Lagos, on Saturday.

He secured 14 votes against Dufour’s six.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Samuel has become the first Nigerian and African to lead the CFF, breaking the long-standing tradition of leadership from countries such as Scotland, Australia and Canada.

“This is a great honour and a responsibility that I do not take lightly,” the statement quoted Samuel as saying.

“I am grateful to the Commonwealth fencing family for the confidence placed in me,” Samuel added.

He said his election would provide an opportunity to further develop fencing across the Commonwealth and create greater opportunities for athletes.

“I believe we can work together to grow the sport, support our athletes and make fencing more accessible and inclusive across the Commonwealth,” he said.

Samuel said the election also highlighted the growing influence of Africa in international fencing and marked a new era for the sport across the Commonwealth.

According to him, the election came as Nigeria hosts the Senior and Veteran Commonwealth Fencing Championships in Lagos, with more than 20 countries participating.

He said, for the first time, the Under-23 and Wheelchair Fencing events would be recognised as medal-yielding competitions, further promoting inclusivity in the sport.

Delegates praised Samuel’s leadership and vision, as well as his journey from a world-class athlete to President of the Nigeria Fencing Federation.

Under his leadership, Nigeria has successfully hosted International Fencing Federation-sanctioned Junior World Cups and African Championships.

Nigeria has also become the first African country to host the Senior Commonwealth Fencing Championships.

Samuel said his election was not only a personal achievement but also a major step forward for African representation in international sports leadership.

World.title: Lekki residents decry two-week power outage, urge EKEDC to restore supply
World.content:
Some residents of Lekki Phase 1 have decried the prolonged power outage that has crippled activities in parts of the neighbourhood for almost two weeks following a transformer fault.

The residents also condemned what they described as negligence, poor communication and indifference on the part of the Eko Electricity Distribution Company (EKEDC) during the blackout.

They expressed their displeasure in separate interviews with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Sunday, saying the prolonged outage had imposed significant financial burdens on residents.

According to them, the blackout has resulted in spoiled food items, while residents who depend on private generators have been forced to spend more on fuel.

The residents appealed to the management of EKEDC to urgently restore electricity supply to Alhaji Hakeem Odumosu Street and other affected parts of the Lekki 1 area.

One of the residents, Mr Taiwo Bolodeoku, described the situation as disturbing and disheartening.

“It has been almost two weeks now since a transformer blew up with a loud bang. The transformer services our home and quite a number of other houses in the area.

“No information has been given, no apology has been sent out, and we wonder what is going on as we continue to wait endlessly.

“EKEDC has just been going back and forth without providing information or a plan on when the transformer will be fixed,” Bolodeoku said.

Another resident, Mrs Margaret Sogbesan, accused the EKEDC management of playing politics with the situation.

“The system is somehow. We have spoken to everyone that needs to be spoken to; they have given updates and made promises to restore power, but here we are, still without a solution. So, it is really frustrating,” she said.

Similarly, another resident, Mr David Nezaya, said life had become unbearable since the area was thrown into darkness nearly two weeks ago.

“I work from home, and it is so terrible that I have to power my generator for hours. It is very frustrating.

“We appeal to EKEDC to do the needful and restore our electricity to enable us to live comfortably.

“It is bad enough that the price of petrol is high, yet there is no electricity to cushion the effect of having to buy petrol almost daily just to survive,” Nezaya said.

Also, Ms Efe Obiomah said she had been forced to switch off her refrigerator because of the prolonged power outage.

“It is a terrible and uncomfortable situation. We appeal to the electricity managers to restore power,” she said.

However, an EKEDC official, Mr Adeyemi Razaq, told NAN that the company was working to restore electricity supply in the area during the week.

Razaq said the workers had requested the materials needed to repair the transformer and that the request had been approved by the head office.

He, however, said the materials had yet to be released to the workers.

“Hopefully, I am promising next week. The materials may arrive on Monday. Hopefully, by Tuesday, they will come and carry out the job, before Wednesday or Thursday next week,” he said.

World.title: 10 countries where getting citizenship is difficult for Nigerians, others
World.content:
For millions of people around the world, obtaining citizenship in a second country can provide greater security, mobility and long-term opportunities.

While many countries have established routes for foreign residents to become citizens, others impose lengthy residency periods, strict language and integration requirements, limited eligibility or highly discretionary approval processes.

In some cases, simply meeting the legal requirements does not guarantee success. Authorities may retain broad powers over who can ultimately be granted citizenship, while countries such as Japan and China also place restrictions on dual nationality.

Here are 10 countries where obtaining citizenship can be particularly difficult for foreigners.

Qatar

Qatar has one of the world’s most restrictive naturalisation systems. Foreign applicants generally need to have lived in the country for 25 years before becoming eligible, alongside requirements including Arabic proficiency and good conduct.

Even after meeting the conditions, citizenship is not guaranteed, with approvals tightly controlled by the authorities.

Vatican City

Vatican City does not operate a conventional citizenship-by-residency system.

Citizenship is generally connected to specific positions or official responsibilities within the Holy See. It can therefore end when the individual’s qualifying role comes to an end, making it fundamentally different from traditional naturalisation systems.

Liechtenstein

Liechtenstein is known for its lengthy route to citizenship, with naturalisation potentially requiring decades of residence.

Applicants can also face local and national approval procedures, making citizenship a highly selective process in the small European principality.

Bhutan

Bhutan maintains strict citizenship rules aimed at protecting its national identity and culture.

Foreign applicants face demanding residency, cultural and integration requirements, while final approval is subject to government scrutiny. The country’s approach makes naturalisation considerably harder than simply establishing long-term residence.

Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabian citizenship is generally far easier to obtain through family heritage than through naturalisation.

The kingdom has opened limited opportunities for certain highly skilled professionals and individuals with exceptional expertise. However, applicants still face demanding requirements and decisions remain heavily dependent on government approval.

Kuwait

Kuwait maintains tight controls over who can become a citizen.

Naturalisation is restricted to specific categories and can involve lengthy residency and other eligibility requirements. The country’s restrictive nationality framework has also contributed to longstanding debates surrounding its sizeable stateless population.

Switzerland

Switzerland has a demanding naturalisation system that combines federal requirements with assessments at cantonal and municipal levels.

Foreign residents generally need around 10 years of residence, as well as evidence of language ability and successful integration. Local authorities can play an important part in deciding whether an applicant qualifies.

China

China rarely grants citizenship to foreign nationals and does not generally recognise dual citizenship.

Foreigners seeking naturalisation typically need Chinese family connections or another legally recognised basis for their application. Because approvals are uncommon and the criteria are narrowly applied, acquiring Chinese citizenship can be extremely difficult.

North Korea

North Korea has no widely accessible or transparent naturalisation route comparable with those found in many other countries.

Citizenship is predominantly determined by birth and state classification, leaving foreign nationals with very limited opportunities to obtain citizenship through ordinary residency.

Japan

Japan has a formal naturalisation process, but applicants must satisfy a range of conditions.

Foreign residents generally need at least five years of continuous residence, financial stability and evidence of good conduct. Japan also generally requires applicants to give up their existing nationality when naturalising, making the process particularly demanding for people seeking to retain dual citizenship.
