That history is part of why the volume of activity in the current scandal has not, on its own, reassured a skeptical public: dismissals across five agencies, a five-month purge, and a summer of headline arrests have so far produced only a handful of formal courtroom prosecutions, chief among them LDEA officer Moses Jallah and Paynesville bar owner George “Leroy” Harris, both charged but neither yet tried. Mark Kuiah, named in a writ of arrest since June and holding a letter tied to a vessel now under search-and-seizure orders, remains uncharged more than a week after his dismissal. Inspector General Coleman, who himself alleged trafficking “sanctioned at very, very senior level,” has faced no formal charges over the escort and protection allegations swirling around his own office, which he denies.

None of that is necessarily the judiciary’s fault in the narrow sense — cases move from investigation to indictment to trial on a timeline set as much by prosecutors and police as by judges. But it is precisely the gap Boakai’s speech was aimed at closing. A court system already associated, fairly or not, with cases that stall, get delayed, or end in acquittals gives Boakai’s “no sacred cows” promise very little room for error. Every week that passes between an arrest and a verdict is a week in which skeptics can point to 2022 and ask whether this summer’s cases are headed anywhere different. The president’s appeal to the incoming judges to avoid becoming “revolving doors through which criminals repeatedly pass without consequence” reads, against that backdrop, less like a stock line for a commissioning ceremony and more like a direct response to the exact criticism his own government’s track record has invited.

What the Speech Leaves Unsaid

For all its rhetorical force, the speech is most interesting for what it does not do. It does not address Coleman’s claim of senior-level sanction, made weeks earlier and never followed by a name. It does not mention Mark Kuiah, whose case has become a running symbol of the gap between dismissal and prosecution. It does not address the specific allegations against Coleman himself, or the question of whether any foreign suspects might eventually face trial abroad. In a speech built around the promise that no one is beyond the law’s reach, the absence of any single concrete example is conspicuous — whether by design, out of legal caution, or simply because a commissioning ceremony is not the venue for naming names.

What the speech does leave behind is a standard the president has now set publicly and repeatedly, in front of the judges who will decide many of these cases and the country watching to see whether “no sacred cows” survives contact with the specific, uncomfortable cases already sitting in front of Liberia’s investigators. Before closing, Boakai paused to wish his wife of 54 years, First Lady Kartumu Y. Boakai, a happy birthday — a brief, warmer note that briefly softened a speech otherwise built almost entirely around warning. Whether that warning holds up will be measured less by Thursday’s applause than by what happens the next time a case with a senior name attached to it lands on a prosecutor’s desk.

World.title: Liberia: IG Coleman Rejects Any Ties To Liberia’s Cocaine Cartel
World.content:
Monrovia – Coleman’s statement, posted to his personal Facebook page, reads less like a routine institutional update and more like a man answering a question nobody asked him directly, because everybody has been asking it indirectly for weeks. “Criminal organizations thrive where fear, silence, and institutional weakness prevail. They will not prevail in Liberia again,” he wrote. “The Liberia National Police will not be intimidated, distracted, or deterred from enforcing the law.”

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

He was explicit about where his loyalties sit, in language built to preempt exactly the kind of insinuation that has followed him for weeks: “Our commitment is not to personalities, political interests, or public applause. It is to the Constitution, the laws of Liberia, and the safety and security of the Liberian people. No individual, network, or organization is above the law, and every case will be pursued based on credible evidence, due process, and lawful authority.”

The statement then turned forward-looking, framing the police force’s mission in terms that doubled as a personal pledge. “We will continue to identify and disrupt narcotics networks, protect communities, strengthen cooperation with national and international partners, and bring those responsible before the courts,” Coleman wrote. “We will remain professional, impartial, and accountable, but we will also remain resolute.” He closed with the line that has since traveled furthest online: “We will not retreat. We will not be distracted. We will continue to work firmly, lawfully, and without fear.”

A Statement Aimed at Doubt, Not Just Critics

What makes the post notable is not simply what it says, but what it doesn’t: at no point does Coleman name an accuser, cite a specific allegation, or address any of the individual claims that have circulated about his own conduct in recent weeks. Read one way, that is restraint — a chief declining to dignify speculation with a point-by-point rebuttal. Read another way, it is a statement carefully built to sound like an answer without engaging the specific questions that prompted it. Both readings have circulated freely since the post went up, which is itself a reflection of how contested Coleman’s standing has become in the middle of the very investigation he leads.

The Allegations That Won’t Go Away

Coleman’s position in this scandal has been complicated from multiple directions at once. He was the one who put the phrase “sanctioned at very, very senior level” into public circulation in the first place, describing the trafficking network’s protection in terms serious enough to implicate senior officials without ever naming one — a claim that, however he intended it, has also been read by critics as circling uncomfortably close to his own office. Separately, Coleman has faced allegations, aired by critics and unnamed sources rather than proven in any court, that he personally gave the order for his own deputies to escort cocaine shipments, that suspects were promised freedom in exchange for silence, and that a protection arrangement shielded at least one implicated officer from the consequences facing others in the case. He has denied all of it, framing himself instead as a target of the corruption he is trying to root out.

None of those allegations has been substantiated in the reporting available to this newspaper, and Coleman is entitled to the same presumption of innocence as anyone else named in this scandal. But the fact that a sitting Inspector General has had to publicly deny personal involvement in the very network his department is prosecuting says something on its own about how deeply this case has unsettled public confidence in Liberia’s security leadership — regardless of where the facts ultimately land.

How Liberia Got Here

Coleman’s Facebook post did not emerge from nowhere; it is the latest data point in a scandal that has been widening for two months. It began with the June 8 seizure of roughly $19.2 million in cocaine at Roberts International Airport and grew dramatically in July with the discovery of a $317 million cocaine haul in a Duazon warehouse — a seizure large enough that the government eventually destroyed it in public. In the weeks since, two police commanders have been accused of personally escorting cocaine through the capital in marked cruisers, an LDEA officer named Moses Jallah has been charged with obstructing the investigation, Paynesville bar owner George “Leroy” Harris has been charged with drug trafficking and money laundering after his venue was tied to the case, and a Monrovia Central Prison operations chief was arrested over allegations his phone was used to keep suspects in contact with their financiers. RIA deputy director Mark Kuiah was dismissed, along with three other officials, in a five-agency purge that has become the most visible symbol of the government’s response so far.

At the center of nearly all of it sits Coleman’s own police force — the agency that arrested some of the officers now implicated, and the one whose own leadership has been publicly accused of shielding others. Deputy Inspector General Nelson Freeman has defended the department’s willingness to prosecute its own, telling the public to judge the force “by the evidence, not the emotion.” Coleman’s own Facebook statement reads, in many ways, like an extension of that same argument — a plea to be judged on results rather than rumor, at a moment when the line between the two has grown genuinely difficult for ordinary Liberians to see.

A Chief Investigating Himself?

The uncomfortable structural reality underneath all of this is one Coleman’s statement does not resolve and perhaps cannot: he is simultaneously the chief overseeing Liberia’s response to this scandal and one of the people whose own conduct within it has been publicly questioned. That is not, by itself, evidence of wrongdoing — someone must lead the police through a crisis inside the police, and stepping aside is its own kind of statement most chiefs are reluctant to make absent a formal charge. But it does mean that every claim of progress Coleman makes on behalf of his department will continue to be read, by at least some of the public, through the lens of the questions still hanging over him personally. “No individual, network, or organization is above the law,” he wrote. Whether Liberians read that as a chief’s genuine conviction or a chief’s most convenient possible defense may depend less on the words themselves than on what, if anything, this investigation eventually turns up about the man who wrote them.

World.title: ECZ confirms tick and cross both valid at Thursday’s polls, defends late clarification
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia has confirmed that voters may mark their ballot papers with a tick, a cross, or any other clear mark, provided it stays within the box of their preferred candidate. The clarification came days before Thursday’s general election and departs from years of voter education material built entirely around the X.

Brown Kasaro, the Commission’s Chief Electoral Officer, gave the clarification during a stakeholders’ meeting with political parties at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka.

“Traditionally, the Commission, in its public information and so forth, has used the X as the correct mark in terms of the voter’s choice when voting, but that is not the only way to mark for a ballot paper to be valid,” he said.

Mr Kasaro said a tick, a cross, or a line drawn across the ballot paper next to a candidate’s name would all count as valid, so long as the mark did not extend into another candidate’s space.

“An X, yes, or a tick, or a line crossing from right across the ballot paper along that candidate. As long as that marking does not cross over to any other candidate, it’s restricted within the particular area for that candidate, it is a valid mark,” he said.

That position sits uneasily against Regulation 33(d) of the Electoral Process (General) Regulations of 2016, which sets out the procedure for casting a vote. It states that a voter must mark the ballot paper with a cross before folding it so the official stamp is visible but the mark itself is not.

A tick, under the printed regulation, would ordinarily render a ballot spoilt. ECZ has not publicly named which legal provision it is relying on to extend validity to other marks this close to polling day.

For years, the Commission’s own radio, television and print voter awareness campaigns have taught the public to use only the X. Nothing in that material prepared voters for a tick or a dash being accepted this year.

That gap has drawn pointed questions from commentators. A widely circulated piece by Linda Banks, titled “ECZ, the X, and the Eleventh-Hour Changes,” asked why the Commission was altering settled procedure so close to polling day without consulting political parties and election monitors beforehand.

A KBN TV editorial put the question to ECZ directly, asking which law permits a tick to be treated as valid this year. The editorial argued that if the Commission cannot point to a legal basis, the position ought to be withdrawn rather than defended.

The editorial also noted that the clarification was first raised with international observers, not with political parties, whose supporters will be most directly affected by how their votes are read at counting.

Some commentary has urged opposition parties, including the Tonse Alliance, to test the change in court rather than raise it only in public statements, on the reasoning that a judicial ruling before polling day would settle the matter for every candidate and every polling station.

Separately, the planned announcement of results in blocks on 17 August has drawn similar calls for transparency, with critics of that approach saying a detailed, station-by-station results trail makes it easier for parties and the public to verify the national count once it begins.

Mwangala Zaloumis, the ECZ chairperson, has urged political parties and other electoral stakeholders to familiarise themselves with the Commission’s guidelines so they can pass accurate information to their supporters ahead of the vote.

Mr Kasaro used the same meeting to address other last-minute concerns, including reports that voters with artificial nails could be turned away from polling stations.

“No one will chase you because you have artificial nails,” he said, adding that polling officers had been instructed to apply indelible ink appropriately regardless.

He also repeated the Commission’s standing instruction that voters must not sign the ballot paper or write their initials on it.

With polling four days away, the Commission has not said whether it will issue a written amendment to reconcile the new position with the printed regulations. Political parties, election monitors and voters are left to work from Mr Kasaro’s verbal clarification in the meantime.

World.title: VEEP Pledges action on Chienge development needs
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has reaffirmed government’s commitment to addressing key development challenges facing the people in Chienge district.

Mrs Nalumango said government remains determined to improving the road infrastructure, education, healthcare and agriculture in the district as part of efforts to improve the livelihoods of local communities.

Speaking when she graced the 2026 Builile Traditional Ceremony of the Bwile people in Chienge, the Vice President stressed that government recognises the importance of the Nchelenge-Chienge Road as a catalyst for economic growth, trade and social integration in the district.

Mrs Nalumango noted that once upgraded to bituminous standard the road will unlock the agricultural, trading and fishing potential of Chienge while also facilitating trade with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

” Construction works to tar the road have already commenced and are progressing well for this road which is very vital for the development of Chienge,” Mrs Nalumango said.

Ms Nalumango also said government is assessing school infrastructure in the district, including Ponde, Lunchinda and Lambwe Chomba Day Secondary Schools, with a view to progressively improving facilities and expanding boarding access for learners.

Meanwhile, Mrs Nalumango disclosed that the Ministry of Health has been directed to prioritise the equipment of mortuary facilities at Lambwe Chomba and Twaileta Mini-Hospitals.

Meanwhile, Mrs Nalumango, who is the matron of the Builile Traditional Ceremony, praised the Bwile people for preserving their rich cultural heritage and promoting unity through the Builile Traditional Ceremony.

” Culture remains an important pillar of national identity and unity and government remains committed to supporting traditional institutions that promote peace, community cohesion and development,” Mrs Nalumango said.

The vice President further urged the people of Chienge to maintain peace and unity and to participate in the August 13, 2026 general elections by exercising their constitutional right to vote.

She stressed that development can only be achieved through collective effort, patriotism and peace.

And the Bwile Royal Establishment has commended the New Dawn Administration for implementing various developmental projects aimed at improving the welfare of people in Chienge District.

Delivering a speech on behalf of Senior Chief Puta, National Chairperson for the Builile Traditional Ceremony Organising Committee, Kalunda Chomba, cited the commencement of works on the Nchelenge-Chienge Road as one of the key projects being undertaken by government.

Mr Chomba also commended government for the provision of free education, school meal allowances, boarding school bursaries and the construction of Chienge Boarding School.

He said the delimitation of Chienge Constituency into Chienge and Kalunguisha constituencies would help improve representation and service delivery.

Mr Chomba further said the Royal Establishment appreciated government’s continued support to farmers as a way of strengthening food security and preserving the traditional practice of Chayenkuwo, which promotes maintaining food reserves.

The 2026 Ubuilile traditional ceremony was held under the theme, “Uwa Kwensha Ubushiku Ba Mutasha Nga Bwacha,” resonating with the country’s resilience amid various economic and climatic challenges and government’s commitment to finding solutions.

World.title: 40 pallets of ballot papers arrive in Lusaka
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has delivered 40 pallets of ballot papers to Lusaka District ahead of the August 13, 2026 General Elections.

The ballot papers, transported in seven trucks from the ECZ central warehouse, will cater for 10 constituencies, 38 wards and 1,246 polling stations in Lusaka District.

Lusaka District Electoral Officer Oliver Muuka said the ballot papers will be securely stored at the district Civic Centre before being dispatched to polling stations on Tuesday and Wednesday, ahead of Thursday’s polls.

Mr Muuka said the ballot papers will be kept under 24-hour security until dispatch and will be escorted to the respective polling stations where they will remain secured until they are used.

“These ballot papers will be stopped here until we dispatch them to these polling stations on Tuesday and Wednesday, in readiness for the polls on Thursday 13th,” he said.

He said of the 40 pallets, Lusaka Central has four, Munali six, Lima two, Roma four, Matero three, Makeni four, Mandevu five, Kanyama four, Chawama four and Kabwata four.

Mr Muuka also apologised for the delayed receipt of the ballot papers, which was initially scheduled for yesterday Friday, attributing the postponement to logistical challenges.

Meanwhile, Roma Constituency parliamentary candidate Chilando Chitangala, said she was satisfied with the security arrangements after stakeholders were allowed to inspect the storage facility.

And Tonse Alliance representative Evelyn Banda commended the ECZ for what she described as transparency in the handling of ballot papers, saying stakeholders had witnessed their movement from the airport to the central warehouse and subsequently to the Lusaka Civic Centre.

Another stakeholder, Foundation for Democratic Process (FODEP) Provincial Chairperson Clement Zulu, also expressed satisfaction with the process.

Mr Zulu further urged stakeholders who may be suspicious of the handling of electoral materials to physically witness the process, saying transparency can best be established by observing the process firsthand.

“Those of us that are suspicious with the process, the best thing is to come and witness and see by ourselves what is happening here,” Mr Zulu said.

World.title: President Hichilema assures accelerated infrastructure development in Lupososhi
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has assured the people of Lupososhi District of accelerated infrastructure development.

Mr Hichilema underscored government’s commitment to ensure that the District Administration and other key infrastructure are built.

Speaking during a community engagement meeting at Katuta Primary School ground this afternoon, the President announced that works on Katuta Boarding Secondary School will soon be completed.

He also assured the residents that government will improve the road network in the area.

“We know the problem of roads here and we will soon begin to work on the Sunday-Chungu Road, Nsombo – Luwingu- Lupososhi road and Katuta – Sobongi road,” President Hichilema said.

The Head of State also pledged to improve mobile phone network in Lupososhi District.

And the President has urged the people of Lupososhi to re-elect him and the UPND for continued development.

He said his government has recorded numerous successes among them the free education policy that has seen over 2.5 million children going back to school.

“That is the reason why you are voting for the UPND because of free education,” President Hichilema said.

Mr Hichilema further cited the peace that the country has seen since 2021 as one of the reasons for Zambians to rally behind the ruling party.

He also said voting for the UPND will allow for the employment of more civil servants such as health workers, teachers and other departments.

“We are continuing with cash for work and we have also increased the social cash transfer programme,” he said.

President Hichilema announced that all volunteer health workers and teachers in Lupososhi will be employed.

Earlier, UPND Acting Provincial Chairperson Cephas Bwalya assured the President of maximum support in next Thursday’s General Elections.

And UPND Lupososhi parliamentary candidate Shadreck Mwansa thanked President Hichilema for ensuring more young people are adopted at various levels.

Mr Mwansa said the move reflects President Hichilema’s commitment to enhance youth participation in governance.

World.title: President Hichilema Pledges State-of-the-Art Hospital for Luwingu
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has pledged to construct a state-of-the-art new district Hospital to cater for the growing population of Luwingu

President Hichilema said plans are underway to improve the current state of the Luwingu district hospital to a much bigger and improved facility.

The Head of State noted that government was aware that the current hospital is inadequate to meet the demand of the district.

“I am aware that the hospital is in bad shape and I can assure you that we have plans to build a new hospital,” he said

President Hichilema also extended his powers to have the health volunteers who gathered to listen to his developmental plans at kapisha school grounds in Luwingu district to be considered for recruitment.

Mr Hichilema further pledged to rehabilitate the Luwingu -Nsombo road, Luwingu- Chaba-road and Luwingu- Kasama road.

Other projects planned for in the district include expansion of the current skills center into a skills college.

He said Government has more development planned for Luwingu district but the projects can only be implemented if the people vote for the vision carriers.

“We have a lot of projects that we want to undertake for you the lovely people of Luwingu but this can only be done if next week you vote for the UPND,” he said.

He reminded the people of the many projects that government has implemented in the past 4 years citing the free education, school feeding and increase of the CDF among other programmes.

Mr Hichilema further asked the gathering whether they would like to go back to paying school fees adding that his government signed into law the free education and hence children will forever attend school for free.

World.title: President Hichilema Pledges Government Offices, Housing for Lunte
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has promised to construct government offices and housing units for civil servants in Lunte District, Northern Province.

‎Mr Hichilema said his government will construct these infrastructures so that civil servants should be staying in the district.

“Your vote will allow us to build district offices and houses for civil servants in the area” he said

The president has also promised to work on the Zacharia Chanda road that connects Lunte from the main Kasama-Mporokoso road and other roads in the area.

Mr Hichilema said this when he addressed residents of Lunte District during the community engagement held at Mukupa Kaoma School Grounds.

‎And the President has urged the people of Lunte to vote for the UPND in next week’s general elections.

He stated that his government has delivered massive developments across the country in the last four years of being in office.

“Vote for the UPND because of the developments it has delivered in the last four years it has been in office. We have delivered developments in several areas” he said‎

‎‎He cited the implementation of free education, the delivery of social cash transfer and the many other developments that government has delivered.

‎‎He said his government is not segregating the selection and issuance of social cash transfers to vulnerable people.

‎‎He has asked all vulnerable elderly people to register with the department of Social Welfare so that they can be added to the social cash transfer programme.

‎‎‎He adds that their vote will allow the UPND to continue with developments, and continue to deliver social cash transfers.

‎‎He added that voting for UPND will allow government to continue the employment of people as teachers, health workers, defense and security wings and other government departments.

“Your vote will allow us to employ more teachers, other than the 45,000 we employed, we will employ more health workers than those we have employed. We will also employ people in ZNS, police and others sectors” he said

‎‎He also directed the employment of all volunteer health workers and teachers in Lunte who attended the community engagement.

‎And former Minister of Technology and Science Felix Mutati who once served as Lunte Member of Parliament asked the people to vote for President Hichilema.

Mr Mutati stated that President Hichilema is the first head of state to visit the area.

World.title: Government invests US$84.2 million in Kasama solar
World.content:
Government has invested 84.2million United States dollars in the construction of 100MW Kasama Solar photovoltaic power project in Northern Province.

President Hakainde Hichilema says the investment is a step towards building an energy secure Zambia.

The President who spoke through Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa at the ground breaking ceremony of the Kasama 100MW solar project said the project will reduce the existing pressure on power generation.

“Today, we are not simply launching the construction of a solar power plant, we are essentially taking another step towards building an energy-secure Zambia,” Mr Hichilema said.

Mr Hichilema said the goal is to increase Zambia’s electricity-generation capacity to approximately 10,000 megawatts within the next five years.

“Ten thousand megawatts means more than additional power, it means mines operating and expanding, factories producing Zambian goods, businesses creating employment and communities gaining access to economic opportunity,” he explained.

He explained that the period of extensive power management was a lesson that Zambia cannot continue depending predominantly on one source of electricity.

“Hydropower remains an important natural resource, however, the changing rainfall patterns have demonstrated the risks of excessive dependence on water for electricity generation,” he said.

“We must, therefore, build a balanced and diversified electricity system comprising solar, hydropower, wind, appropriate base load generation, energy storage, stronger transmission, and distribution networks,” Mr Hichilema added

And ZESCO Managing Director Justin Loongo said the objective of the Kasama Solar Project is to enhance the generation mix and improve the reliability and supply of electricity.

Mr Loongo said the project will also create employment opportunities during construction and operation, contribute to the reduction of carbon emissions and support socio-economic development in Kasama and surrounding areas.

He said Electricity generated from the plant will be evacuated through an approximately 5.7-kilometre, 330 kV transmission line to the Kasama 330/66 kV Main Substation and thereafter supplied into the national grid.

“The power generated here will therefore not only benefit Kasama, it will strengthen the wider electricity system and contribute to improved supply in Northern Province and other parts of the country,” he explained.

And Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Beauty Undi Phiri observed that the project will stimulate economic activities in the province.

“For Northern Province, this project is not only about the electricity that will be generated, it is also about the economic activity that will take place during the twelve-month construction period and throughout the operational life of the plant,” she said.

She explained that investors considering the establishment of a factory or processing facility have an interest in whether a place has sufficient and reliable electricity.

“Our Province has significant potential in agriculture, fisheries, tourism, commerce, manufacturing and value addition. However, that potential cannot be fully realised without adequate and reliable energy infrastructure,” Ms Undi-Phiri emphasized.

Meanwhile China Machinery Engineering Corporation Representative Hu Guangyi said the Kasama project will not only provide clean energy to the people of Zambia but also contribute to the country’s sustainable development goals.

Mr Hu said the Kasama 100MW Solar PV Project is a continued testament to the strong bilateral relations between China and Zambia.

He reaffirmed the company’s’ commitment to continue sharing its expertise and technology to support Zambia’s energy transition.

Meanwhile Senior Chief Mwamba of the Bemba people of Kasama District praised government for investment in his chiefdom.

The traditional leader explained that the project will not only address power cuts but also create job opportunities for the local people.

The US 84.2million Kasama 100MW solar photovoltaic power project is being developed in Sombe village, in Senior Chief Mwambas chiefdom on approximately 150 hectares of land.
