World.title: Trump's latest push to reshape U.S. history? Signs at the Smithsonian
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On any given day at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., Americans and visitors from all over the world file in to see the red slippers Dorothy wore in the Wizard of Oz, the inaugural gowns of U.S. first ladies and the garrison flag that inspired the Star-Spangled Banner.

These days, though, it's not uncommon to also find several protesters outside the entrance, holding up signs that read "Truth Matters" or "History does not belong to rich old white men!"

The museum is currently at the centre of an effort by the Trump administration that observers say is part of a broader attempt to reshape the stories of the United States as told by the country's cultural institutions.

"I think this set of actions fall sort of at the confluence of two trends," said Suse Anderson, an associate professor and head of museum studies at George Washington University in Washington, D.C.

"The first is the longer-term, right-wing project aimed at gaining more control over cultural institutions really since the 1980s to ensure that exhibits and educational programs are more aligned with conservative values. And the second is an attempt to reduce the influence of independent experts in areas where the administration would like more control."

In late July, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered that signs be put up outside the museum warning visitors about "inaccurate information" presented inside.

The National Museum of American History is part of the Smithsonian, the world's largest museum system. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

The signs aren't up yet, but they are supposed to point visitors to a 162-page report the White House released on America's 250th anniversary. The report largely focused on the National Museum of American History and accused the Smithsonian's leadership of "extreme political activism" and prioritizing a narrative of shame and division over more celebratory and patriotic narratives.

Last year, in a Truth Social post, Trump said: "The Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been — Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future."

The recent developments are all part of an overall initiative by the Trump administration to "review" the Smithsonian's exhibits and programs.

The Smithsonian itself is the world's largest museum system. It includes 21 museums, 14 research centres and the National Zoo. It holds more than 150 million items, including historical objects and works of art.

The July 4 report — titled Saving America's Story: How Ideological Capture at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History Erases Our Heritage— echoes Trump's complaint that the Smithsonian focuses too heavily on the legacy of slavery in the U.S.

It also alleges, for example, that there is an overemphasis on the plight of Indigenous people during the country's founding and "identity politics," including materials that "present gender as fluid."

Anthea Hartig, director of the National Museum of American History, testifies during a subcommittee hearing in Washington on July 21. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

The Smithsonian response

The Smithsonian has spent the summer fighting to maintain its independence.

Anthea Hartig, director of the National Museum of American History, faced heavy questioning by Republicans over two days in late July at a House oversight committee, where she was asked questions like "Do you love America?"

"Unconditionally," she said.

WATCH | Questioning a museum director: History museum’s director testifies in Washington | Duration 2:09 Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado questions National Museum of American History director Anthea Hartig at a hearing in Washington, D.C.

In a memo to staff after the White House report's release, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian's secretary, said it was "not a fair characterization" of the work the National Museum of American History does.

"At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America's story."

James Millward, a history professor at Georgetown University and co-founder of Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian, a group created over fears of political censorship of the museums, said he's been impressed by the Smithsonian's unwavering defence of the work it is doing, given how other institutions, such as some universities or big law firms , "caved almost immediately" to similar White House pressures.

"I think history will recognize its backbone in the face of political pressure," he said in an interview.

Millward also said he is concerned this recent flurry of activity — the report, the committee hearings, the executive order for the signs — is setting the stage for attempts by the administration to "stack the board" of the Smithsonian in the coming months with members more sympathetic to its cause.

Millward is also concerned that Trump's attack on the Smithsonian could be seen as "weird things having to do with Trump's own narcissistic goals," similar to his pre-occupation with turning the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall "American flag blue" or the East Wing renovations.

"It really does tie into something that transcends Trump," he said of the fixation on museums, adding that it is part of a long-term effort by various groups to define the U.S. as a country of European settlers by playing down slavery and colonialism and opposing immigration that is ongoing, as well as trying to reassert traditional gender roles and the traditional family.

Millward also cites comments made by U.S. Vice-President JD Vance last year, where he said Americans who have ancestors who fought in the Civil War have "a hell of a lot more claim over America" than those who question their belonging to the country or the work of Project 2025 , a conservative vision and policy plan to reshape American culture through the expanded powers of the executive.

Dorothy's ruby slippers from the Wizard of Oz are displayed at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C., on April 11, 2012. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Mike Gonzalez, a contributor to Project 2025, testified at the same committee hearing as Hartig did.

"Teaching lessons about American wickedness is now the mission of the Smithsonian," he told the hearing.

A trusted institution

The Smithsonian has been around for nearly 180 years.

Susie Wilkening, founder of Wilkening Consulting, has been conducting industry research for the American Alliance of Museums. She said that year after year Americans are increasingly supportive of "inclusive content," including people of colour, women and religious minorities.

At a time when Americans are losing faith in many institutions, museums still rank high in polls, right under family and friends and public libraries and above non-governmental organizations, the media, social media and the government.

"What we're seeing is that most people do want the Smithsonian to have what we refer to as curatorial independence," said Wilkening, adding it cuts across the political spectrum.

Wilkening said polling she did in January from a representative sample of 2,045 U.S. adults shows 63 per cent of conservatives disagree with political pressures to remove content from museums.

Among liberals, she said, that number is higher, at 83 per cent, although there is a segment of the conservative base that supports it — 17 per cent — as well as some liberals — eight per cent.

An exhibit is seen inside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on July 7. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Early this week, on her way out of the National Museum of American History, Amy Carlson Miesel reflected on her first visit. The West Virginia native found it "disappointing" and "a little tinged with leftist ideology."

She said she found the museum pointed out many times that "in American history, Christians had mistreated the Native Americans."

For Carlson Miesel and her husband, Richard Carlson Miesel, neither of whom are fans of Trump, it was a question of emphasis.

"It seemed to me that what you saw was all true stuff," he said. "But it just kind of felt like a hodgepodge of differences while there was not a 'Well, this is all where we came from. Now, what is it that unites us?'"

Tan Tran, a student at George Washington University who is studying museum education, had just come from meeting a friend by the the museum's Jerome and Dorothy Lemelson Hall of Invention, which celebrates American ingenuity.

"Any self-directed educational experience, you get out what you put into it," Tran said, listing several examples of exhibits that celebrate accomplishments of individual Americans.

"But it's all history," said his friend, Rebecca Hill. "Good, bad, ugly, it's all the American history."

World.title: Adult summer camps offer grown-ups a chance to get away from it all
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Every year, kids across the country spend part of their summer at camp. Whether they're staying at cabins in the forest, or spending days at local community centres, camp is usually filled with crafts, snacks and laughter.

Sounds like fun, doesn’t it? Shelby Sanford thinks so, and she says grown-ups deserve some of that joy, too.

“I wanted to relive the summer camp that I enjoyed when I was a kid,” Sanford told The Current guest host Piya Chattopadhyay.

Sanford is the co-founder of Camp Rewind, an adult summer camp for women and non-binary people held in the East Kootenays region of B.C. This year, it will take place at Blue Lake Camp, near Canal Flats, about 80 kilometres from Cranbrook. The camp is into its second year and Sanford says its guests range in age from 19 to 60-something.

Camp Rewind participants do activities like friendship-bracelet-making, capture the flag, yoga, and tie-dye. (Submitted by Adrienna Elcome)

Camp Rewind and others like it are taking off, capitalizing on a desire to recreate the magic of summers you enjoyed as a kid. According to Yelp, searches for adult summer camps in the U.S. were up 300 per cent this year compared to 2025.

While there is no comparable Canadian data, some adult summer camps have been around for years, like Canadian Adventure Camp and Two Islands. Both are based in Ontario cottage country, as is the so-called Zombie Survival Camp in Cardiff, Ont.

It’s also an idea people are embracing around the world. There's the women-only Camp Chateau that’s hosted in the French countryside. Meanwhile, Book Club Summer Camp in the Poconos in Pennsylvania caters to readers. And Black-owned Camp Yoshi in Portland, Ore., is a space for racialized people to reconnect with nature.

Camp Yoshi is a Black-owned summer camp based in Portland, Ore. Its founders say their goal is to bring racialized people together to embrace nature and take part in outdoor expeditions. (Griffin Christensen & Finn Peterson)

Sanford says camp gives grown-ups a chance to simplify their lives for a few days.

“There are no kids pulling at your shirt or partners asking you to do XYZ or work e-mail dinging in the background,” she said.

Finding friends IRL

Adult summer camps also offer people a chance to make friends in ways they can’t when they’re busy with work or running around to get the children to and from school and extracurricular activities, says Sanford.

While the activities are fun — like capture the flag or friendship bracelet-making — and let adults tap into their inner child, she says Camp Rewind guests told her connecting with others was their biggest takeaway.

The activities encourage guests to get out of their shells and interact with others, says Sanford.

According to a 2025 Statistics Canada survey, less than 20 per cent of Canadians saw their friends on an average day in 2022, down from 47.9 per cent in 1986.

Matt Cullen spent a week at Maine’s ‘Camp’ Camp for 2SLGBTQ+ adults. He says he was craving connection and looking for fun ways to meet people.

“My job as a content creator can be quite lonely sometimes because I'm at home all the time just editing by myself,” said Cullen, who is based in Los Angeles.

Matt Cullen is a content creator. He documented his experiences at the 'Camp' Camp in Maine for 2SLGBTQ+ adults. (Submitted by Matt Cullen)

Cullen says while he documented the experience for his social media channels, he avoided his devices as much as he could because he wanted to be present with the group.

The commitment to being connected felt intentional and rare, he says.

“It made us able to bond with each other and reach a different level of understanding,” said Cullen. “We were all there choosing to be there for that week.”

‘Play is essential’

Clinical psychologist Lara Hiseler says she isn’t surprised adult summer camps are becoming so popular.

“Play is essential, relevant, and at the core of who we are as human beings."

Adult summer camps let participants tap into positive experiences like joy, connection and creativity, she says, and important for people's social development.

“These camps are sort of like a safe space for adults to learn and be able to be OK with connecting with these parts of themselves that they would’ve known as children, but maybe haven’t been as in step with as they entered adulthood,” she said.

Lara Hiseler is a clinical psychologist who served as the president of the Ontario Psychological Association. (Submitted by Lara Hieseler)

Hiseler says while play is considered essential for children’s development, it’s often deemed frivolous for adults.

“Engaging in play can come with this almost type of stigma when you become an adult,” she said.

Most people don’t have a reference for what play looks like as an adult, Hiseler says. But she encourages adults to re-engage with their fun-loving side.

“Think about who you were as a child, what you were interested in, then extrapolate. Are those things still of interest?”

It can feel emotionally risky to show up places and put yourself in front of strangers, Hiseler says, but by following your interests — for instance, enrolling in a camp that’s more artsy than sporty, if that’s your jam — you have a higher probability of meeting more like-minded people.

But keep open to possibility, says Sanford. She says one Camp Rewind guest initially "drew the line" at lip syncing, then ended up giving three performances.

Lifelong friends Ruth Krulitsky and Shelby Sanford (right) are the founders and co-directors of Camp Rewind. (Submitted by Adrienna Elcome)

Some guests want to make returning to the camp an annual tradition, Sanford says. She says a few of them have organized events outside of camp, like a trip to Disneyland and starting a book club.

Sanford says the relationships that were formed are heartwarming.

“These are people we met for just a couple of days, but it does feel like we've made these lifelong connections."

World.title: What lives in the rivers near you? Why scientists want you to know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a suburban creek steps from busy roads, biologists sent a mild, electrical current into the water and waited to see what surfaced.

The stunned fish they scooped up included spiky mottled sculpins, blacknose dace with striking red racing stripes and chunky creek chub — residents of the largely hidden freshwater world in and around Ontario's towns and cities.

Scientists are using techniques such as electrofishing and environmental DNA sampling to uncover that biodiversity. They are finding far more species than traditional methods have detected, even as many are disappearing or being replaced by invasive species.

Scientists say protecting creatures from dace and mayfly nymphs to mussels starts with knowing what is there.

But identifying and measuring freshwater life is challenging.

Physid pond snail. (Anthony Ricciardi/McGill University)

Uncovering little creatures — and bigger ones

A recent study published by University of Guelph biologist Mehrdad Hajibabaei and his team searched for environmental DNA (eDNA) in water from 18 Ontario rivers.

Organisms shed DNA through skin, scales and feces. Using those traces, researchers identified hundreds of aquatic invertebrates that had not been found through traditional methods.

Only 22 species identified through traditional methods were not detected by the DNA survey. Many species were found at just one site, showing how much river life can be missed.

Northern virile crayfish (Faxionius virilis). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Nautilus ramshorn snail (Armiger crista). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Last year, CBC News accompanied a team using another technique — electrofishing — to count fish in Tannery Creek in Aurora, Ont., near busy streets and subdivisions.

Wearing hip waders, gloves and battery-powered backpacks, Ontario Streams staff dipped pole-mounted rings into the creek, delivering mild electrical shocks that briefly stunned nearby fish. They netted, counted and measured the fish before returning them to the water.

To electrofish, scientists dip a ring into the water that delivers a mild shock from a powered backpack, stunning nearby fish. In this photo, Ontario Streams staff were teaching the technique to other biologists at Tannery Creek in Aurora, Ont., the spring of 2025. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

Kat Lucas, then the group's outreach co-ordinator and spokesperson, said passersby often ask what crews are doing when they see them electrofishing in urban parks around Toronto.

"They'll be surprised to hear that there are fishes that live in these rivers right through our big cities," said Lucas, who is now an outreach specialist with Credit Valley Conservation.

Urban creeks are even home to critically endangered species such as redside dace and an Ontario population of Atlantic salmon that went locally extinct a century ago and is now being reintroduced.

Kat Lucas, former outreach co-ordinator and spokesperson for Ontario Streams, peers at a mottled sculpin collected during the group's electrofishing workshop. Lucas is now an outreach specialist with Credit Valley Conservation. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

A 'silent mass extinction'

Scientists who compiled data from freshwater surveys around the world reported last year that one-quarter of freshwater animals on Earth are threatened with extinction .

Although half the world's population lives within three kilometres of freshwater , the researchers noted that "declines are continuing, generally out of sight and out of mind."

McGill University Prof. Anthony Ricciardi does research on the Richelieu River in Quebec. (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Anthony Ricciardi, a McGill University biology professor who studies freshwater biodiversity, said North America has already lost many species.

"At least 120 extinctions of freshwater animals in North America were recorded over the past 125 years," he said. "Hundreds of mussels, gastropods, fishes, crayfishes and amphibians are at risk of future extinction."

Ricciardi calls it a "silent" mass extinction because even conservation biologists "do not seem to be aware or paying much attention to it," he said.

That's partly because freshwater biodiversity has traditionally been difficult to measure, as Hajibabaei's findings show.

Water penny beetle larva. (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

'What's going on underwater is dramatic'

People who work, play or live beside the water may know little about its inhabitants. That can put species at risk, Ricciardi suggested.

"How would people who don't know what's living underwater feel any empathy or any sense of loss?"

As a boy, he waded waist-deep to collect native crayfish and mussels in the St. Lawrence River near Lachine, Que. Many of those species are disappearing, pushed aside by invasive spinycheek crayfish and zebra and quagga mussels.

"Even if the river looks more or less the same," he said, "what's going on underwater is dramatic and rapid."

Eastern lampmussel (Lampsilis radiata) with some invasive zebra mussels attached. (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Freshwater species are going extinct five times faster than animals on land, Ricciardi said. Pollution, invasive species and dams have all taken a toll.

Why we need mussels — and other aquatic creatures

Each species disappearing from rivers and lakes has a job, Ricciardi said, "and as we lose species, some of those jobs don't get done."

Native mussels burrow into lake and river beds, helping replenish oxygen needed by other creatures. Insect larvae, including dragonflies, mayflies and caddisflies — groups experiencing " significant" species declines — are essential food for fish.

Mayfly nymph (Stenonema). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

Hajbabaei said many freshwater species are also important indicators of water quality.

"They are much more sensitive than any other chemical test or physical test," he said.

Knowing what lives where, and what is disappearing, is "critical" to their conservation, Hajbabaei said.

"You can't manage something that you cannot measure."

Freshwater sponge (Eunapius fragilis). (Submitted by Anthony Ricciardi)

He said greater public awareness of freshwater neighbours is key. When people know which species live nearby, "they can actually come up with creative ways to protect biodiversity."

Ricciardi said many declining freshwater creatures could still be saved by reducing polluted runoff, removing dams from rivers and fighting invasive species.

Migratory fish are returning to rivers where dams have been removed, he said, and no new invasive species have been recorded in the Great Lakes since ballast-water regulations were introduced in 2008.

"There are success stories," he added, "when we intervene to reverse a problem."

WATCH | Watch these endangered mussels return home to Canadian waters: Watch these endangered mussels return home to Canadian waters | Duration 1:57 Nearly 800 kidneyshell mussels were released in the Medway Creek in London, Ont. on Wednesday. This is the first time a freshwater mussel species has been reintroduced to a lost habitat in Canada. Find out how these little creatures protect biodiversity.

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

World.title: On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Clad in a black bulletproof vest, a gun clasped to his hip, Tim Thayer gently pushes down the throttles of four 350-horsepower engines — and the 18,000-pound U.S. Customs and Border Protection boat jumps to life on the Detroit River.

Thayer is a marine interdiction agent, part of a team that patrols the waterways that make up the Canada-U.S. border in this part of the country.

He's assigned to the Detroit sector, an area that encompasses Michigan, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. The border with Canada here is entirely water — all 1,388 kilometres of it — which poses a unique challenge.

A peculiar quirk in the geography of the two countries is that Windsor, Ont., lies south of Detroit, separated by the river and connected by two bridges and a tunnel, with some seven million people crossing back and forth here alone annually.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection boat is shown navigating the Detroit River, near Windsor, Ont., on Aug. 4. (Willy Lowry/CBC)

On a warm Wednesday afternoon, Thayer scans south, looking toward the Windsor shoreline, his eyes searching for anything out of the ordinary.

"When we do our enforcement patrols out here on the Detroit River, what we're seeing is both people, narcotics and guns going back and forth between the U.S. and Canada," he said.

During the Prohibition era of the 1920s and '30s, the Windsor-Detroit corridor was the main route smugglers used to bring alcohol into the U.S. illegally from Canada.

While illegal activity on the Detroit River is perhaps not nearly as bustling today, the sheer number of recreational boaters who are frequently out presents a challenge for law enforcement.

WATCH | Trump's fentanyl claims aren't materializing at this Canada-U.S. crossing: Trump’s fentanyl claims aren’t materializing at this Canada-U.S. crossing | Duration 2:05 U.S. President Donald Trump declared a national emergency at both the northern and southern borders in 2025, citing the fentanyl crisis to justify tariffs levied against Canadian and Mexican imports. Ottawa, for its part, has committed roughly $1.3B in multi-year investments to beef up border security with the U.S. At the Detroit-Windsor border, the CBC’s Willy Lowry takes a look at how the U.S. handles things on their side of the fence.

"We saw how many boats today? And every boat could be a smuggler unless we stop every single boat," asked Kris Grogan, chief of external communications at CBP's air and marine operations.

"You have to use intelligence and partnerships to be able to secure this area up here."

Trump's claims aren't materializing

Just days into his second term in 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump accused Canada of failing to prevent drugs, especially fentanyl and human traffickers, from entering the U.S., using the flow of drugs as justification to declare a national emergency and slapping 25 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977.

In February of this year, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down those tariffs.

And while Trump has painted a picture of a porous and dangerous border, the reality is much more complicated.

In 2025, U.S. border officials in the Detroit sector seized more than 4,200 kilograms of illegal drugs, including nearly 15 kilograms of fentanyl, according to statistics provided by CBP. But the statistics don't reveal the direction the drugs were travelling.

"It's really not that big of a problem for inbound," said Lavarah Miller, a CBP watch commander on duty when CBC News toured a brand new American port of entry facility at the newly opened Gordie Howe International Bridge.

"A lot of the stuff that we actually get, we get a lot of it going out."

A view from the new American port of entry facility at the just-opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, which runs between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit. CBC News recently spent two days with U.S. Customs Border and Protection agents stationed in the region. (Willy Lowry/CBC)

And guns, too, are travelling north, recent statistics show.

In 2024, 87 per cent of the guns recovered in crimes in Ontario were traced back to the U.S, according to figures compiled by Ontario Provincial Police. In Toronto, police say 88 per cent of guns recovered were illegally smuggled into the country.

"Firearms, for sure. But also, the United States is the middle ground for drugs coming up into our country from Mexico and South America," said Kelly Sundberg, a professor of criminology at Mount Royal University in Calgary.

While the flow of drugs and weapons between the two countries is primarily northward, Sundberg said, Canada still poses a threat to the U.S. — just not the one Trump continues to accuse Canada of.

"There is virtually no fentanyl getting smuggled into the United States, especially when you compare it to what's coming in from Mexico," he said. "Nevertheless Canada does have some serious issues with staffing [at our border] — we don't have enough officers.

"The officers we do have need to be better educated, better trained, better selected, better equipped. There needs to be a significant investment in the human side of our border security."

A tale of 2 borders

Canada's fentanyl czar — a role created in the early days of the trade war to try and assuage Trump's concerns about the northern border — has also pushed back against suggestions that Canada poses a major drug-trafficking threat.

In an interview with CBC's The House in June, Kevin Brosseau pointed to new data from CBP that shows less than half a kilogram of fentanyl was seized at the Canada-U.S. border in May, compared to 358 kilograms at the Mexico-U.S. border.

The total amount of fentanyl seized by U.S. officials so far this year at the Canadian border is approximately three kilograms. At the Mexican border, it's approximately 3,221 kilograms.

Despite ongoing political tensions between Washington and Ottawa, the U.S. border agents who spoke with CBC News over our two-day tour insisted the working relationship with their Canadian counterparts has remained unchanged over the last 18 months.

"Locally, we still have great partnerships with those agencies right across the water," said Tim Balkus, the patrol agent in charge of the Detroit sector.

Meanwhile, Thayer nods his head as an RCMP boat flies past, the Gordie Howe bridge looming large in the distance — a symbol of both how strong and strained the bond between the two countries is today.

World.title: U.S. booze might end up back on Canadian shelves, but have we lost the taste for it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Deb Anderson can't remember the last time she bought a product from the United States.

Like many Canadians, the 65 year old from Prospect, N.S., said she's been alarmed by U.S. President Donald Trump's repeated threats against Canada — and she's been boycotting American goods in protest.

So when she read on Friday that Canada was prepared to lift a ban on American alcohol sales as part of its trade negotiations with the Trump administration, Anderson says she felt disappointed.

"But just because it goes back on the shelves doesn't mean that sales are going to go back to where they were. The damage has been done," she told CBC in an interview.

Anderson says the "constant badgering and unfair negotiation practices" from the U.S. have "really give us a bad taste for all things American."

Anderson doesn't appear to be alone in her feelings: Sixty-nine per cent of Canadians said they weren't likely to buy American alcohol if it goes back on store shelves, according to a Nanos Research poll published last month.

Support for a continued boycott of U.S. alcohol was highest in British Columbia, where 80.9 per cent of respondents said they were unlikely or somewhat unlikely to buy U.S. booze again if it's made available.

That was followed by 74.7 per cent of people in Ontario and 73.9 per cent of Quebecers who said the same, the poll found.

WATCH | Are the booze bans an effective pressure tactic?: Is the U.S. booze ban working? | Duration 3:31 With most Canadian provinces vowing to keep U.S. alcohol off store shelves in response to President Donald Trump’s latest tariff threats, CBC’s Eli Glasner asks: are the booze bans an effective pressure tactic or merely political symbolism — and an inconvenience for consumers.

Steep decline in U.S. alcohol imports

Industry sources with knowledge of Canada-U.S. trade negotiations told CBC News that the Canadian government was prepared to lift bans on alcohol sales as it negotiates possible concessions in exchange for U.S. tariff relief.

Trump has threatened to impose 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods on Aug. 19 if Canada fails to lift some retaliatory trade measures against the U.S., including the alcohol bans.

Those bans date back to early last year, when several provinces removed U.S. alcohol from the shelves at their respective liquor boards in response to Trump slapping a 25-per-cent tariff on Canadian goods.

Ivan Gedz, who owns the bar Union Local 613 in Ottawa, says his stockpile of American booze ran out two months after U.S. supplies were taken off the shelves at the Liquor Control Board of Ontario (LCBO) last year.

But Gedz says customers at the bar, which had previously offered a wide range of American spirits, didn't bat an eye at not having access to bourbon and other alcohol made south of the border.

Instead, the U.S. alcohol ban encouraged patrons to try booze they'd never had before.

"There's nothing I love more than giving someone an Indian whisky and they're like, 'India? I didn't even know India made whisky,' " Gedz told CBC News in an interview. "They're producing excellent stuff — it's just we don't get a ton of it."

A proposal to halt provincial bans on American booze was revealed Friday as negotiators race to reach a deal before new U.S. tariffs take effect on Aug. 19. However, a poll last month suggested 69 per cent of Canadians said they weren't likely to buy U.S. alcohol even if it returns to shelves. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Changing tastes?

The need to seek out alternatives is something that was seen in other parts of Canada, too.

Quebec's liquor board, the Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ), said in its 2026 annual report that "fans of U.S. wines have turned to counterparts from other regions" amid the ban.

"Canadian wines, including Quebec wines, have gained popularity and now rank ahead of Australia's," the report said, adding that Austrian wines were also becoming more popular in "a sign that customers are curious and open to discovering new countries of origin."

Nicole Raufeisen is director of operations at Grape Witches, a bar and wine bottle shop in Toronto that continued to sell U.S. wines it already had stocked when the ban came into effect.

"We've slowly ticked away through those products. I think we're down to maybe just one or two different wines," she told CBC in an interview on Friday.

If the ban is lifted, Raufeisen says she expects customers will again reach for wines they enjoy from the U.S., such as fuller-bodied reds from California. "People will go back because those wines are good, that market share is well-trodden, so to speak, and the visibility there is high."

But she added that demand for American wines can also be attributed to trade barriers between provinces.

While nine provincial premiers announced last month that they would introduce direct-to-consumer alcohol sales between provinces, Raufeisen says restrictions on wholesale wine sales between provinces remain a major challenge.

"If there were no interprovincial barriers to the wholesale movement of wines, then it's possible that no one would miss any of the American wines," she said, noting that B.C. wines are comparable to those from California.

WATCH | Trump said Canada has 'nasty leadership': Canada has 'nasty leadership,' says Trump as he praises U.S. tariff policy | Duration 0:40 U.S. President Donald Trump, speaking from Las Vegas on Wednesday, praised his government's use of tariffs and once again mentioned Canada, saying, 'I love the people' but that the country has 'nasty leadership.'

Back in Ottawa, Gedz says Union Local 613 would probably bring U.S. booze back if the ban is lifted as part of a wider trade agreement between the two countries.

But he says he doesn't expect American alcohol to be as popular as it once was because many Canadians "have exposed themselves to products that they may not have tried" without the ban in place.

"I'm just hoping that those customers maintain their willingness for experimentation," Gedz said. "And you know what? If we stick it to the Americans for a little while longer, I'm cool with that."

World.title: Flight to Toronto cancelled over child standing on seat: Porter Airlines
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A flight bound for Toronto was cancelled Thursday evening after a young child refused to secure their seatbelt, Porter Airlines has said.

Flight PD444 from Victoria International Airport in B.C. to Toronto's Pearson International Airport did not take off as a safety precaution, a spokesperson for Porter Airlines told CBC Toronto in a statement Saturday.

The aircraft left the terminal and headed to the runway for departure but a young child standing in their seat did not secure their seatbelt, despite attempts by the accompanying parent and cabin crew, Brad Cicero said.

The unsafe situation meant the aircraft could not takeoff, so flight attendants opted to return to the terminal and disembark passengers, he added.

The time required to bridge the aircraft, deplane the child and parent, retrieve their baggage and refile paperwork meant the plane would have departed too late, according to Cicero, who said Victoria's airport runway closes at 12:30 a.m.

"We apologize for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day," Cicero said.

The aircraft departed the following afternoon, Cicero said.

World.title: The air travel industry was on the brink of disaster, but travellers are still taking to the skies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It seemed like airlines were on the brink of disaster heading into the peak summer travel season, with the Middle East war causing chaos and uncertainty, closing airspace in many areas and sending fuel prices soaring.

For weeks, headlines seemed to point toward a doomsday scenario. Fuel prices more than doubled in April. Europe was on track to run out of jet fuel by June, the International Energy Agency warned. Many airlines — including those in Canada — cut less profitable flights as a result. Florida-based Spirit Airlines fully shut down in May.

Despite all those headwinds, the industry — and passengers' desire to fly — appears to have rallied. Europe avoided its crisis by finding other sources of fuel , while passenger traffic has held steady, expected to increase by 2.1 per cent this year.

This summer even saw a new record: July 23 had the most global commercial flights ever tracked — a whopping 153,359, according to Flightradar24, a live flight tracker.

"What we're seeing is increased scheduled air traffic," said Ian Petchenik, Flightradar24's communications director. "It's really as simple as that."

Peak travel season

Total air passenger demand fell 1.7 per cent in June, according tothe International Air Transport Association (IATA). However, this was a smaller drop than the preceding months, and much of it was concentrated in the Middle East, which saw a 13.9 per cent fall year over year.

There isn't one single explanation for the July record, experts told CBC News. But it was likely fuelled by demand from the Northern Hemisphere, Newsweek reported , as airlines have been deploying maximum capacity for the season when travel typically peaks.

The last Thursday or Friday of July is usually the busiest, says Petchenik, as many see it as the peak of the summer season, just before school begins in August in much of the U.S.

For this summer in particular, he says, many of those flights were likely booked well in advance.

LISTEN | Canada's domestic tourism boom: The Current 18:53 Why Canadian tourism is booming At a time when the overall economy is sluggish, the Canadian tourism sector is bucking the trend and projected to grow by 6% in 2026. We hear from some innovative Canadian travel businesses that are cashing in and from tourism and hospitality professor Wayne Smith about what is driving the growth — and what it would take to build on it.

"A lot of people looking at the state of the world … before prices really spiked and saying, 'Maybe we should book now to get ahead of any incoming price increases.' "

Canadian commercial flights increased over the summer, as well, by Flightradar24's count, rising by 16 per cent between April 1 and July 23 to hit 5,558. Global commercial flights increased by 11 per cent that same time period.

But the number of flights alone doesn't always paint the full picture, said Amra Durakovic of Flight Centre Travel Group Canada. That's because our total annual commercial flight count remains 20 per cent below 2019, she said, citing data from analytics firm Cirium.

The global increase in flights is likely driven by large, emerging economies like China and India, which are increasing their flights as their markets grow.

However, countries with more established flight industries — like Canada — have instead increased the size of the average plane, while phasing out smaller ones. That means more people are served in the end.

Tourists take selfies with a reflection of the Eiffel Tower in the Champ-de-Mars garden in Paris on July 28. Canadians heading to Europe this summer have tended to book flights last minute, adopting what industry experts refer to as a wait-and-see approach. (Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images)

Where Canadians are going

On July 23, most Canadian travel was domestic, accounting for more than a third of all bookings, according to Flight Centre data.

Durakovic says her firm hasn't seen that happen since before the COVID-19 pandemic, and she notes it's likely that people are rerouting trips that originally would have been to the U.S.

Still, the U.S. was the second most popular destination that day, at 19 per cent, followed by European countries like the U.K., Italy and Spain, at 18 per cent combined.

Durakovic also noted an interesting trend among Canadians heading to Europe: They tended to book their flights last minute, as opposed to the typical approach of booking in advance.

"They've adopted what we refer to as a wait-and-see approach," said Durakovic, who attributed the trend to ongoing uncertainty around factors impacting the industry, like fuel costs and contract disputes.

Meanwhile, summer travel through Flight Centre Canada to Japan is up 37 per cent year over year — a significant sum considering the East Asian country is a long-haul flight away, at a time when cost remains a priority for many.

Notably, that demand is extending into the winter months, Durakovic says, as Canadians are finding it can be more affordable to ski in Japan, largely due to the weak yen.

"That's what is largely driving a lot of Canadians' travel decisions is where are they going to find the best value?"

Tourists ride on horses at the fifth station of Mount Fuji in Fujiyoshida, Yamanashi prefecture on July 23, 2026. Japan has become a popular tourist destination for travellers seeking good value for their money. (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images)

What lies ahead

So far, the Middle East war hasn't seemed to significantly affect summer plans outside that region. But that may change the longer it goes on, alongside events like the recent WestJet strike , for example, which can erode confidence in travelling.

"I think that the more uncertainty there is and the higher prices rise … we will see a pullback in demand," said Petchenik of Flightradar24.

He says that could also trigger a shift to more local travel: "You know, 'I am buying a ticket, but … I'm flying somewhere where the prices are reasonable and I have certainty that my trip isn't going to be affected by world events outside of my control.' "

WATCH | How the war affected flight prices in March: How is war in the Middle East affecting flight prices for Canadians? | Duration 3:37 The costs of the war in the Middle East keep adding up as gas and diesel prices have risen sharply around the world; the cost of jet fuel has also increased. For people planning trips, it can be a scramble to find something less expensive. McKenzie McMillan from The Travel Group Ltd. explains how the war is affecting flights and by how much.

As for ticket prices, expect them to continue increasing, according to IATA. Airlines are still profitable, but their margins are under severe pressure due to fuel prices and with few ways remaining for them to cut costs.

Durakovic says she still expects demand to remain high in the near future.

"Look, it's a lot, but when we travel, we all love it, right?" she said, noting that people are generally willing to cut other costs to afford travel. "It says a lot about how important travelling is."

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: As De la Espriella takes office, his US-backed security policy for Colombia is raising questions
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella assumes office on Friday, after elections with a razor-thin margin. He brings with him promises to wield “iron fist” policies against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and organized criminal organizations in the country.

He has also promised to dismantle ongoing peace talks initiated by outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro, including groups that are currently disarming. De la Espriella made scores of hardline promises on the campaign trail, many of which he will likely not be able to achieve with a minority coalition in the legislature, such as withdrawing Colombia from the United Nations.

On security issues, however, Colombia’s constitution grants the president broad unilateral powers. De la Espriella has promised to “end” armed groups within a month, an extremely unlikely goal. Despite the broad powers of the presidential office, De la Espriella faces historical and logistical limitations.

Despite claims from right-wing parties that Petro has gone easy on armed groups, Colombia’s military has been fully deployed against NSAGs in the country for the last two years.

As conflict expert Thomas Garrison reported for news website Pirate Wire Services in June, Colombia has ongoing and large military operations against FARC dissident group Estado Mayor Central (EMC), the National Liberation Army (ELN), and EMC splinter-group EMBF.

Colombia’s security forces are “already operating on all cylinders,” and “stretched to their limit,” according to the International Crisis Group. It isn’t clear how deployments can be increased without increasing the numbers of security forces themselves — hardly a goal that can be achieved in his first month in office.

Nonetheless, there are strategic changes that de La Espriella can impose to chart a more aggressive course. As part of those plans, the president-elect has promised to implement a “Plan Patriota remixed”, an allusion to highly aggressive US-backed military operations against armed groups under then-President Alvaro Uribe in 2003.

Uribe’s allies to this day hail Plan Patriota as a great success that forced the FARC to the negotiating table in 2016.

Critics, however, point to rampant human and civil rights violations, including working with paramilitary forces to kill thousands of civilians and frame them as guerrilla fighters to increase casualty counts.

The US, however, is pushing Latin America towards increased military spending and Bukele-style crackdowns on organized crime, and de la Espriella plans to comply.

What was Plan Patriota and how will Abelardo’s version be ‘remixed’?

Plan Patriota involved aerial bombardments, large-scale military deployments in FARC-controlled areas, and aggressive intelligence gathering against FARC guerrillas at the height of Colombia’s civil war.

Although paramilitary groups were not officially part of Plan Patriota, they cooperated closely with regular military forces during the operation, functioning as spies, informants, and death squads — ostensibly killing alleged guerrillas, but just as often murdering leftists in general, as well as non-politically involved civilians.

The operation, which continued until 2010, weakened the FARC considerably, but at a great price: gross human rights violations including massacres, torture, and using sexual violence against civilians as a weapon of war.

Paramilitary structures were also greatly empowered across the country, sowing the seeds of groups that still exist today, such as the Ejercito Gaitanista Colombiano (EGC) — often referred to in Western media as ‘the Clan del Golfo.’

The full extent of the atrocities committed by both sides of the war would not become clear until Colombia launched its Truth Commission in 2017. (De la Espriella wants to disband the Truth Commission as well as the Colombian Peace Court, which prosecutes the worst offenders of the civil war.)

Any new version of Plan Patriota would look very different. Colombia is not the same country it was in the early 2000’s. Modern armed groups are not interested in clashing with state forces on the battlefield. Most are not interested in overthrowing the state at all, and certainly not via military victory.

Technology has also advanced considerably. Drone warfare is a dangerous new weapon in the arsenal of NSAGs who wage asymmetrical attacks on state forces as well as one another. Digital surveillance and satellite optics also mean that unlike the FARC, which often relied upon jungle canopies to hide large training and logistics camps, modern NSAGs instead blend into civil society in the communities where they operate.

They do not wear uniforms to distinguish themselves and avoid direct confrontations with the military, which means there are no large targets to bomb, nor columns of marching fighters for the state to confront.

Modern NSAGs are far more flexible, transnational, and relatively decentralized in their operations compared to FARC at the height of the civil war.

De la Espriella’s security program is more likely to look like Daniel Noboa’s policies in Ecuador than the 2002 Plan Patriota. It will likely include US cooperation on target-finding, naval cooperation on drug trafficking, and joint US-Colombia operations within the country.

Most of those dynamics already exist. Despite a rocky relationship with Washington, D.C, Petro continued to cooperate with the US on intelligence-sharing and anti-narcotics operations.

Critics of de la Espriella, however, fear that logistics won’t be the only similarity to Ecuadorian-US operations, which have resulted in the murder of civilians by security forces, torture, arbitrary detentions, and bombings of civilian infrastructure.

One factor that may keep de la Espriella somewhat in check is a lack of a clear mandate. He won elections by less than 1%, and has already clashed with more established right-wing political parties, who will not be forming part of his coalition in the legislature.

De la Espriella signals he will follow Washington’s lead

On a recent trip to the U.S, de la Espriella’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo, met with US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph M. Humire, who spoke of investment by US companies in hydrocarbon and energy sectors as well as cooperation on security and migration issues.

“Colombia is historically one of the U.S. strongest security and defense partners,” he wrote on X on July 21. “Under the leadership of incoming President Abelardo De La Espriella, we plan to take this partnership to new levels with Plan Patriot 2.0.”

Before Humire joined the War Department, he worked as an anti-migration lobbyist propagating conspiracy theories that cartels have “weaponized” migrants as part of “asymmetrical warfare” against the U.S.

He falsely testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee in February that Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua had “opened” the Darien Gap to migrants during the Biden administration as part of a Venezuelan plan to destabilize the US.

De la Espriella has already signalled that he looks forward to closer cooperation with the administration of US President Donald Trump and largely follow the US lead on regional issues. Trump has made migration a key facet of his domestic and foreign policy.

The ultra-right Colombian president-elect has also promised to “secure” the country’s borders. Migrants “who are here illegally, or committing crimes will be deported to their countries of origin without delay,” he said in a press conference on July 13.

He has agreed, however, to keep commercial and migratory pathways open on the Venezuelan border. Petro re-initiated diplomatic and commercial ties with Venezuela in 2022.

De la Espriella has not criticized Chavista governments as heavily as many other right-wing politicians in the country, and provided legal representation for Maduro loyalist Alex Saab, who has been extradited for a second time to the US to face money laundering and corruption charges.

Aggressive military strategies have failed in the past

The nature of conflict has changed drastically in Colombia since the civil war, and presidents have tried aggressive military tactics against criminal organizations and NSAGs before.

Former President Ivan Duque failed to slow the rapid growth of either during his time in office from 2018 to 2022.

The Colombian state failed to fulfill its promises to invest in legitimate economies and develop regions long ignored by Bogotá. Regions that had previously been governed by the FARC became power vacuums that were quickly filled by other criminal organizations and NSAGs.

Duque left office the least popular president in the country’s history since records have been kept, in part because of his security policy. Bombings on rebel camps that killed minors created significant public controversy. When Petro turned to similar strategies, the military inadvertently killed children in bombings in children as well.

Armed groups have continued to grow under Petro despite his employment of increasingly aggressive military strategies. De la Espriella has not offered details about his plans, and it is unclear what he could do that Duque and Petro did not, or why the results would be any different for his administration when similar tactics have failed before.

Trump, however, has gained a new ally in the region. The US president has often shown that projection of US power is an end in and of itself, and de la Espriella is likely to allow Trump to do exactly that.

World.title: Colombia Reports and 21st-century fascism
World.content:
The coming four years will probably be the toughest yet and I will need your support to keep Colombia’s longest-living news source alive.

The Espriella administration will be the third far-right government I have reported on since I started Colombia Reports in 2008.

I expect the incoming government to be the worst because it seeks to undo socio-economic policies that pulled 4 million people out of poverty and end peace processes that kept us safe.

Independent journalists (and the New York Times) have criticized Abelardo de la Espriella for his ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC and drug traffickers, and his alleged corruption of the judicial system, specifically in Colombia.

Many of these journalists have been harassed by De la Espriella’s law firm through at least 109 frivolous lawsuits, and the publication of their private information.

I can only guess what’s ahead for us after De la Espriella appointed reported frauds as his spokespersons and put a conspiracy theorist in charge of my visa.

I will need your support as what’s coming is probably going to be expensive. The last time I reported on a far-right government, I was forced to spend months in my native country, the Netherlands.

If you are not yet a paid subscriber, please become one. If you don’t want to commit to a monthly contribution, please make a one-time donation.

I promise I will continue reporting on Colombia and will update you on the political situation in Colombia through my podcasts with Richard McColl of Colombia Calling.

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky
World.content:
The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance.
