03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — THE FREE CENTRO AXIS From the CCBB to the Paço Imperial, without spending a real on entry Start at the Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil on Rua Primeiro de Março, which opens at 9 am and is free every day it trades. The building is a converted 1906 bank, and its circular glass-roofed rotunda is worth the trip on its own, before you reach a single exhibition. The programme rotates constantly across several floors, so it rewards going in without a plan. One thing to note for later in the week: the CCBB closes on Tuesdays, so this is not a stop to postpone. Walk ten minutes to Praça XV and the Paço Imperial, the colonial palace where Dom João VI governed and Princesa Isabel signed the law abolishing slavery in 1888. Its exhibitions run noon to 6 pm and entry is free, and the thick stone rooms are a cool, quiet contrast to the square outside. One correction worth carrying: the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes is still largely shut for restoration. Only its Galeria de Moldagens 2 has reopened, weekdays from 1 pm to 5 pm, so save it for a weekday rather than building a Sunday around it. The same applies to the Real Gabinete Português de Leitura, which despite its permanent presence on every Rio photo feed keeps weekday hours only. Both are five minutes from this walk on any Monday to Friday morning. For lunch, the Bistrô do Paço sits inside the palace courtyard and serves through the afternoon on Sundays. The whole loop is flat, under two kilometres, and easily reached by metro to Carioca or by the VLT to Praça XV.

OUTDOORS — PARQUE LAGE BEFORE THE HEAT Morning coffee under the imperial palms, then the sand Parque Lage in Jardim Botânico opens early and stays free, and it is the best first move on a warm morning. By nine the light through the mansion arcades is made for photographs, and the café tables around the courtyard pool are still quiet. The short forest trail toward the Corcovado side takes about fifteen minutes at a gentle incline and needs no guide. Go early, because the park fills as the day warms and the shade thins out by late morning. With 27°C and clear skies, this is also the week’s one obvious beach day, and the city knows it. Ipanema and Leblon will be busy from mid-morning, and the stretch between postos 9 and 10 is the liveliest end of the sand. If you want more space, walk west toward Leblon and the Posto 12 end, where the crowd thins and the view back toward Dois Irmãos is the better one. Vendors work the whole strip, so you need very little beyond cash and sunscreen. Whatever the water looks like, check the lifeguard flags before going in. Winter swells around Arpoador can pull harder than the surface suggests, and the currents shift through the day.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO & BOTAFOGO Where a laptop is welcome when the Sunday city goes quiet Curto Café in Centro is the reliable option near the museum circuit, a small, serious espresso bar that has been a fixture of the neighbourhood’s coffee scene for years. It is a short walk from Cinelândia and pairs naturally with a morning at the CCBB. Over in Botafogo, Urban Bean is the better bet for a longer sit with a laptop, with room to spread out and a steadier weekend rhythm. Sunday hours across Centro cafés can be shorter than the weekday listing suggests, so it is worth a quick check before crossing town. Formal co-working is mostly shut today. If you need a proper desk to start the week, WeWork at Porto Maravilha and Como Coworking in Botafogo both sell day passes you can arrange online for Monday morning.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — BOTAFOGO CINEMA An indoor afternoon at the Estação in Botafogo If you want an hour out of the sun, the Estação cinema on Rua Voluntários da Pátria has been the city’s reference point for arthouse film since the eighties. Three screens, a café, and a programme that leans Brazilian and European rather than blockbuster. It is a five-minute walk from Botafogo metro, which makes it an easy pivot if the afternoon plan falls apart. Check the day’s listings and buy ahead online, since Sunday sessions in the smaller rooms do sell out. The cinema also helped turn this corner of Botafogo into one of the better evening neighbourhoods in the city, so the surrounding blocks are worth a wander either side of a screening. Bars and small restaurants run the length of the street. The attached café is a decent place to sit before or after a film. It is also a sensible rehearsal for Monday and Tuesday, when the cold front makes indoor plans the obvious ones.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM The Maracanã, or a Santa Teresa sundowner Tonight splits cleanly in two. Flamengo host Vitória at the Maracanã at 7:30 pm to close the round, and a Sunday night with the Rubro-Negro at home is one of the great cheap spectacles of the city. If you would rather watch it from a bar stool, the botecos around Lapa and Botafogo will have it on every screen they own. Arrive well before kickoff, because tables with a decent view go early on a Flamengo night. For the other kind of evening, start at Bar do Mineiro in Santa Teresa for a cold chope and a shared bolinho. It fills by eight, so get there around 7 pm if you want a decent table. From there it is a short walk downhill to the terrace bar at the Hotel Santa Teresa, which pours a serious caipirinha with the bay laid out below. Aprazível, under its mango trees, is the option to book ahead for a proper dinner, and Sunday tables up the hill go quickly once the light starts to fade.

ALSO ON TODAY Museu do Amanhã — Praça Mauá — open until 6 pm, last entry 5 pm. R$40 full, R$20 half. Note for tomorrow: on the 10th of each month, entry is R$10. Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR) — Praça Mauá — 11 am to 6 pm, last entry 5 pm. R$20 full, R$10 half, and free every Tuesday. The rooftop view is worth the ticket alone. Jardim Botânico — Rua Jardim Botânico — open through the afternoon, with separate resident and visitor pricing at the gate. The orchid house and Amazon section are in good form. Paço Imperial — Praça XV — exhibitions noon to 6 pm, free entry. The historic building itself opens from 11 am. Sunset at Arpoador — Arpoador rock — sunset at 5:35 pm. Arrive by 5 pm with a maté and a light layer for afterwards.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

The metro runs a Sunday timetable across its lines, with trains every seven to ten minutes for most of the day. A single journey is R$7.90, paid by contactless card or with a Giro card from any station machine.

The VLT tram links Santos Dumont, Praça XV and the Praça Mauá museums, and it runs on its own municipal fare, which is lower than the metro’s. Buy or tap at the platform validator rather than assuming your metro fare carries over.

Expect heavier movement around the Maracanã from late afternoon on a match night. The seafront cycle path from Leme to Prainha is open all day, and it is calmest before 10 am.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Bistrô do Paço, in the courtyard of the Paço Imperial, is the natural stop mid-circuit and serves through Sunday afternoon. For something quicker and older, Confeitaria Colombo near Rua Gonçalves Dias is worth a standing coffee for the mirrors and the jacaranda alone.

Dinner: Aprazível in Santa Teresa is the long-table splurge, with bay views and a menu built on Brazilian ingredients — book ahead for a Sunday evening. In Botafogo, the strip around Rua Nelson Mandela covers everything from a quiet tasting menu to a table with the football on.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry sunscreen, a hat and a refillable bottle — Centro has few public fountains and today is genuinely warm. Almost every museum and café takes Pix and contactless, but keep around R$50 in cash for a beach vendor or a tapioca cart.

Book Santa Teresa dinner tables by WhatsApp before late afternoon, because Sunday night up the hill fills with locals. For the cinema, buying online saves standing in a queue for a sold-out room.

Centro is calm on a Sunday but empties out early. Keep your phone in a front pocket, stick to the Praça XV and Cinelândia corridor where foot traffic is steady, and take a ride rather than walking long empty blocks after dark.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Rio’s international crowd tends to scatter on Sundays rather than gather formally, and that is not a bad thing for a newcomer. The beach posto system does the work for you — postos 9 and 10 in Ipanema are where the mix of Cariocas and foreign residents is thickest through the afternoon.

If you would rather have a fixed point, take a maté up to Arpoador for sunset. It is the fastest, lowest-effort way to feel plugged into the city, and the applause when the sun drops is a genuine local ritual rather than a tourist one.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

The Brasileirão’s twenty-second round runs across this weekend, and Rio has the closing fixture. Flamengo, second in the table, host Vitória at the Maracanã tonight at 7:30 pm.

Earlier in the day, Vasco are away at Bahia with a 4 pm kickoff. Palmeiras against Internacional goes at the same hour, and Santos and Bragantino close out the afternoon at 6:30 pm.

Yesterday delivered the derby, with Botafogo hosting Fluminense at the Nilton Santos. Fluminense arrived in a difficult run, having gone out of the Copa do Brasil to Vasco earlier in the week, and the result reshapes how both sides look at the table this morning.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Instrument Level Session Ibovespa (Brazil) 172,513 -1.73% USD/BRL 5.0826 -0.54%

Source: B3 close, Friday, August 7, 2026.

The week ended under pressure rather than in a lull. The Ibovespa fell 1.73% on Friday to 172,513 points, a fourth consecutive decline that left it roughly 3% lower across the week, its weakest stretch since May.

The move originated in Washington. A weak United States jobs report pushed global money out of emerging markets and back into American shares, and Brazil lost ground even as Petrobras reported one of the largest profits in its history. The real went the other way, with the dollar easing to R$5.0826.

The week ahead turns on United States inflation data due Wednesday, the main event for global rates. Locally, Brazil’s monthly IPCA reading is the next signal on the Copom‘s path, and a soft print would give domestic buyers a reason to step in front of the outflows.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD Sun Aug 9 — Today — Free Centro axis and the beach at 27°C, then Flamengo at the Maracanã, 7:30 pm. Mon Aug 10 — Cold front lands — Down to 22°C and wetter. Museu do Amanhã charges just R$10 today, being the 10th; the CCBB is open, MAR is not free. Tue Aug 11 — Coolest day — Around 20°C. MAR is free all day at Praça Mauá, but the CCBB is closed on Tuesdays, so plan around it. Wed Aug 12 — US CPI day — Back to 22°C and drier. Note that both MAR and the Museu do Amanhã close on Wednesdays. Thu Aug 13 — Warming again — Clear and near 26°C. A good morning for the Real Gabinete or the reopened gallery at the Belas Artes, both weekday-only.

Background: Brazil Stocks Post Worst Week Since May as Petrobras Slides — August 8, 2026.

Background: Brazil Markets: Ibovespa & the Real — August 7, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

What can I do on a Sunday in Rio without a beach day?

Start in Centro, where the best of it is free. The CCBB opens at 9 am with no admission charge, and the Paço Imperial on Praça XV runs its exhibitions from noon to 6 pm, also free of charge. The two sit a ten-minute walk apart across the old centre. From there the VLT tram takes you out to Praça Mauá, where the Museu do Amanhã costs R$40 and the MAR R$20, both open through the afternoon. Between them that makes a complete, walkable day of culture for very little money, and almost all of it is indoors and cool.

Is the Real Gabinete Português de Leitura open today?

No, it is closed today. The Real Gabinete opens Monday to Friday from 10 am to 5 pm and shuts at weekends, so a Sunday visit is not possible however good the photographs online look. Plan a weekday morning instead — entry is free, it is a short walk from Carioca or Cinelândia, and the reading room genuinely earns its reputation as one of the most beautiful libraries anywhere. Going early on a weekday also means far fewer people in the way of the view upward.

Can I visit the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes right now?

Only partly, and not on a Sunday. The museum has been closed for a long restoration, and so far just one space has reopened to the public: the Galeria de Moldagens 2, showing newly restored plaster casts of classical sculpture alongside a photography exhibition. It opens on weekdays only, from 1 pm to 5 pm, and entry is free of charge. Full reopening of the building is still expected further ahead, so for now treat this as a short weekday stop rather than a main destination on your itinerary.

Is there football in Rio today, and can I still get in?

Yes, and it is the pick of the evening. Flamengo host Vitória at the Maracanã tonight at 7:30 pm, closing the twenty-second round of the Brasileirão, while Vasco play away at Bahia earlier at 4 pm. Tickets for Flamengo home games are sold through the club’s own official channels and are often still available on the day for a routine league fixture like this one, though prices vary a lot by sector. Get to the stadium well before kickoff, and take the metro rather than trying to drive or park nearby.

Sources: CCBB Rio — official site, IPHAN — Paço Imperial hours, Museu do Amanhã — official visit page, MAR — hours and tickets, The Rio Times — Brazil markets, August 8, 2026

World.title: São Paulo Daily Brief — Sunday, August 9, 2026

São Paulo — A mild, part-cloudy Sunday around 23°C makes for an easy day on foot before the week turns colder. Carry a light layer and keep a small umbrella handy for a passing shower.

The headline culture play is today’s free admission at the Pinacoteca in Luz. The museum opens its doors free to everyone on the second Sunday of each month, and that falls today.

Markets closed the week on the back foot rather than steady. The Ibovespa finished Friday sharply lower and posted its worst week since May, and the board carries every figure.

Make today about a slow morning in Pinheiros, an art afternoon in the centre, and a late wander through Ibirapuera. Get your outdoor time in now, because Monday brings a cold snap.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — PINACOTECA FREE DAY — LUZ The Pina opens free for the month’s second Sunday, then a wander through Bom Retiro Head to the Pinacoteca de São Paulo in Luz, which opens free to everyone on the second Sunday of each month. That is today, so you can walk into all three buildings without paying the usual admission. The 1905 brick building is the oldest art museum in the city, and its permanent collection leans heavily on Brazilian names — Tarsila do Amaral, Almeida Júnior, Anita Malfatti, Portinari, Lasar Segall. The galleries run roughly in chronological order, so a slow walk through reads almost like a short course in the country’s art, from nineteenth-century painting through to the modernists. The building itself is part of the pleasure. Its glass-roofed inner courtyards are calm, light-filled spaces that reward a pause between rooms, and a single ticket covers all three of the museum’s buildings around the Luz gardens. The museum runs 10 am to 6 pm today, with last entry at 5 pm. It is a five-minute walk from Luz station, so getting there is simple from almost anywhere on the metro or CPTM network. Afterwards, walk ten minutes into Bom Retiro. The neighbourhood’s Korean bakeries and old-school snack bars stay lively on Sundays, and a counter on Rua Prates is a fine spot for a coffee and a pastry while you plan the next move. To reach Luz from Pinheiros, take Metro Line 4 to República, then Line 3 to Luz — about 25 minutes, R$5.40 single fare. It is worth booking a free timed ticket on the Pinacoteca website this morning, as the free days draw a crowd.

OUTDOORS — PARK & SKYLINE Ibirapuera in the late afternoon, then a rooftop in Jardins Parque Ibirapuera is São Paulo’s great green lung and it is open daily, staying busy all Sunday. Rent a bike near one of the main gates or simply walk the loop around the lake as the light softens after 4 pm, when the runners, families and picnic blankets are at their best. The park is also an architecture lesson in its own right, built around Oscar Niemeyer’s sweeping white pavilions and their connecting canopy. It is an easy place to spend a couple of unhurried hours before the week’s cold front rolls in. When you want a break from the open air, the MAC USP inside the Niemeyer pavilion is free and open on Sundays. The upper-floor terrace gives you one of the best skyline views anywhere in the park, well worth the trip up. From the park, walk or take a short ride into the Jardins district. The rooftop bars around Rua Oscar Freire serve cold drinks with a breeze, and most stay relaxed and cover-free in the early evening.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — PINHEIROS & VILA MADALENA Two calm Sunday cafés where a laptop is welcome Coffee Lab on Rua Fradique Coutinho in Pinheiros roasts its own beans and is one of the city’s benchmark specialty cafés, a reliable spot for a slow Sunday work session with wifi and a rotating single-origin filter list. A filter coffee runs around R$15, and the room has the kind of steady hum that makes an hour with a laptop pass easily. Further into Vila Madalena, Suplicy Cafés Especiais is another dependable option for a quiet morning over a strong flat white. Both cafés fill up by late morning, so arrive early if you want a comfortable table and a plug within reach. Most co-working spaces close on Sundays, so plan around a café today. If you need a proper desk before the week starts, Spaces and WeWork around Pinheiros and Faria Lima sell day passes you can book online for Monday.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — CENTRO HISTÓRICO QUIET Downtown on its calmest day, with a rooftop finish Centro empties out on Sundays, which makes it the best day to walk the viaducts and old arcades without the weekday crush. Start at Farol Santander on Rua João Brícola, open through the afternoon, with a viewing deck at the top. A couple of blocks away, the Mercado Municipal winds down by mid-afternoon on Sundays. Get there before noon for the famous mortadella sandwich on the mezzanine, and bring some cash for the fruit stalls downstairs, where the vendors are generous with samples of whatever is in season. At sunset, head up to one of the terrace bars near Praça da República. The Sunday evening crowd is small, the drinks are unhurried, and the downtown skyline lights up gradually as the sky fades from gold to deep blue — a quietly spectacular way to close a day in the centre.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM A Vila Madalena dinner, then jazz in Pinheiros Settle in for a slow Sunday feijoada at one of the long-running spots on Rua Aspicuelta in Vila Madalena, where service usually runs into the early evening. Two people eat well for around R$140 with drinks. For something lighter, Tan Tan Noodle Bar on Rua Fradique Coutinho in Pinheiros serves steaming bowls into the night. Counter seats face the open kitchen, and there are no reservations, so aim to arrive by 7:30 pm. Live music starts around 8:30 pm at Jazz nos Fundos on Rua João Moura, one of the more characterful small rooms in the city for a Sunday set. Cover runs roughly R$40 to R$60 depending on the act, and the courtyard bar stays open late — worth booking a table online this morning, as the good nights sell out. If you would rather a quieter night, a natural-wine bar around Rua dos Pinheiros is an easy call, with a short, well-chosen list and a few small plates to share. It is a gentle way to round off the weekend before the cold front and the working week both arrive on Monday morning.

ALSO ON TODAY MASP — Avenida Paulista, open 10 am–6 pm — R$85 full price, free on Tuesdays and Friday evenings. The suspended Lina Bo Bardi building on Paulista is worth the visit for the architecture alone. Japan House — Avenida Paulista, open until 7 pm — Free entry, open weekends. The ground-floor exhibition rotates every few months and the building itself is a draw. Beco do Batman — Vila Madalena, open-air all day — Free and always open. The graffiti alley shifts constantly as artists paint over older work. Museu da Língua Portuguesa — Luz, open until 4:30 pm — Interactive exhibits on the Portuguese language inside the restored Estação da Luz, a short walk from the Pinacoteca. Museu do Ipiranga — Ipiranga, open 10 am–5 pm — Recently restored, with formal gardens out front that are a fine Sunday stroll in their own right.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Sunday means no rodízio, so any plate can circulate freely all day. The metro and CPTM run their usual Sunday frequencies, roughly every six to eight minutes on the main lines.

The single rail fare is R$5.40 and the Bilhete Único works as normal. One nice Sunday perk: city buses run fare-free on Sundays under the Domingão Tarifa Zero programme, so short hops around the centre cost nothing.

Luz and Sé interchange stations are quieter than on weekdays. There are no scheduled line closures today, but it is always worth a glance at the operators’ live updates before a longer trip.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Consulado Mineiro near Praça Benedito Calixto in Pinheiros is a reliable Sunday choice for hearty Minas cooking, and the surrounding square has a relaxed weekend market feel. For something lighter, Z Deli on Rua dos Pinheiros does an excellent pastrami sandwich for around R$40.

Dinner: Mocotó, up in Vila Medeiros, is worth the ride north for its northeastern cooking — the dadinho de tapioca and slow-cooked mains run around R$120 for two. Closer to the centre, a grilled-fish menu in Jardins is an easy, quieter option to round off the weekend.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a small umbrella and a light layer today — the middle of the day is mild, but a shower is possible and the evening cools off. Most museums take Pix or card, though it is worth keeping R$80 in cash for the fruit stalls at the Mercadão and the odd street vendor.

Book dinner tables by WhatsApp this morning. Sunday evening tables in Pinheiros and Jardins tend to fill by early evening, especially on a mild night like this one.

Stick to the main avenues in Centro after dark. The area around Luz is busy and well-patrolled during museum hours but empties quickly after 6 pm, so it is worth taking a ride from the Pinacoteca rather than walking to a distant station.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

São Paulo’s international crowd tends to gather around the specialty cafés of Pinheiros and Vila Madalena on Sunday mornings, and Coffee Lab is a natural meeting point if you want to fall into conversation over a good filter. The various nomad and expat WhatsApp groups usually post informal weekend meetups worth checking.

For newcomers settling in this week, the regular language-exchange nights around Itaim Bibi and Vila Madalena are the fastest way to meet people. They are usually free and casual — turn up early, order a drink, and you will find a table to join.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

The Brasileirão rolls through another weekend round, with the big four São Paulo clubs — Corinthians, Palmeiras, São Paulo and Santos — spread across the fixture list. Kickoff times and venues shift week to week, so check the CBF site or the clubs’ channels for today’s exact schedule.

If you would rather watch European football, the sports pubs around Vila Madalena and Itaim Bibi screen the weekend’s Premier League and other continental fixtures, several with English commentary. They are an easy, sociable way to pass a rainy Monday too.

For live football in person, tickets to the São Paulo clubs are generally affordable and easy to buy online through each club’s platform. The women’s Brasileirão is also in full swing, and Corinthians in particular draws strong crowds at the Neo Química Arena.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Instrument Level Session Ibovespa (Brazil) 172,513 -1.73% USD/BRL 5.0826 -0.54%

Source: B3 close, Friday, August 7, 2026.

Markets closed a difficult week rather than a calm one. The Ibovespa fell 1.73% on Friday to 172,513 points, a fourth straight daily decline that left the index down about 3% for the week — its weakest five-day stretch since May.

The trigger came from Washington rather than São Paulo. A weak United States jobs report sent global money rotating out of emerging markets and back into American shares, and Brazil was on the losing side of that move even though Petrobras had just reported one of its largest profits ever. The real, by contrast, firmed a touch, with the dollar easing to R$5.0826.

The week ahead brings US inflation data on Wednesday, the main event for global rates. Locally, traders will watch Brazil’s monthly IPCA figures for the next read on the Copom‘s path. Expect a quiet start to the week with the exchange closed today and tomorrow’s session shaped by those foreign flows.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SUN 9 — Today — Pinacoteca free day in Luz, then Ibirapuera late afternoon. Mild and part-cloudy, sunset 5:51 pm. MON 10 — Cold front arrives — Sharp drop to around 16°C. Paulista museums are closed Mondays, so make it a work-from-café day in Pinheiros. TUE 11 — Cool and grey — Around 16°C. Free entry Tuesday at MASP all day — a perfect indoor culture day on Avenida Paulista. WED 12 — Warming, US CPI day — Back up near 23°C. A good day for the Museu do Ipiranga gardens, with markets watching the US inflation print. THU 13 — Bright and warmer — Clear skies returning. A fine afternoon for Beco do Batman and the Vila Madalena cafés.

Background: Brazil Stocks Post Worst Week Since May as Petrobras Slides — August 8, 2026.

Background: Brazil Markets: Ibovespa & the Real — August 7, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is anything free to visit today, Sunday, in São Paulo?

Yes, and today is a good day for it. The Pinacoteca in Luz is free to everyone because it is the second Sunday of the month, a courtesy of its sponsor B3, and the museum is also free every Saturday. MAC USP inside Ibirapuera is always free, as is Sesc Pompeia. One to plan around: MASP is not free on Sundays — it costs R$85, with free admission reserved for Tuesdays all day and Friday evenings after 6 pm, so it is worth saving Paulista’s flagship for one of those two windows instead.

Can I use the metro to get around on Sunday?

Yes, and Sunday is one of the easiest days to do it. The metro runs normal Sunday service from early morning until around midnight, though trains come a little less often than on weekdays, roughly every six to eight minutes. The single rail fare is R$5.40 and the Bilhete Único works exactly as usual. As a bonus, the city’s buses run fare-free on Sundays under the Domingão Tarifa Zero programme, and the trains are far quieter than weekday rush hour, so crossing town is genuinely comfortable and cheap today.

Do restaurants take cards or should I carry cash?

You can lean on cards for almost everything. Nearly every restaurant, café and museum takes credit and debit, contactless included, and Pix is everywhere too — from a coffee cart to a sit-down dinner, vendors will happily take an instant transfer straight from your phone. Even so, it is worth carrying around R$80 in cash for the Mercado Municipal fruit stalls, the occasional street vendor, a market snack, and the odd taxi driver who still prefers notes over a card machine. A small cash cushion just smooths out the day.

What is the weather doing this week?

Today is the mild one to make the most of, part-cloudy and near 23°C, with only a small chance of a passing shower. A cold front then arrives on Monday and drops the daytime high to around 16°C for a couple of chilly, grey days, so it will feel noticeably colder to start the week. Temperatures climb back toward 23°C by Wednesday and the skies clear later on. In short, spend today outdoors while it lasts, and treat Monday and Tuesday as the museum-and-café days, when a warm room is the nicer option.

No consensus has been published. —Peru Rate The central bank decides late Thursday from a 4.25 percent starting point, with no published forecast either way. —Euro Area GDP Friday’s second estimate for the second quarter is seen confirming 0.4 percent growth, alongside July retail sales in the United States.

The week turns on a trio of inflation prints from Colombia, Brazil, and the United States, with the dollar’s reaction to the US core rate likely dictating the direction of Latin American currencies and equities.

Latin American markets enter the week with the dollar and global rate expectations as the dominant external forces, capable of overriding decent local fundamentals. Regional inflation is no longer moving in one direction: Colombia is drifting up, Brazil is running near the top of its target band, and Argentina’s monthly pace has settled below 2 percent.

The domestic calendar is headlined by inflation data from Colombia and Brazil, the Copom meeting minutes, and a late-week rate decision in Peru. These provide fresh clues on the pace of monetary easing, but the pivotal release for regional assets is the US consumer price index on Wednesday.

Three Themes for the Week

Latin American disinflation is diverging rather than stalling uniformly. Colombia’s annual rate is forecast to rise to 6.20 percent, Brazil enters the week at 4.64 percent, and Argentina’s monthly pace has fallen to 1.9 percent. Three countries, three different problems for three central banks.

The dollar’s trajectory hinges on the US core reading, not the headline. Headline inflation is forecast at 0.1 percent monthly after a negative June, but core is seen at 0.2 percent with the annual rate slipping to 2.5 percent. A firmer core would tighten financial conditions across the region regardless of what the headline does.

Producer prices are turning in opposite directions across the world. Japanese wholesale inflation is forecast at 7.4 percent annually and Indian wholesale prices at 10.25 percent, while German wholesale prices fall 0.2 percent monthly and Swiss producer prices decline again. The split matters for how long imported inflation persists in emerging markets.

The Week, Day by Day

Monday, August 10, 2026

Ecuador, South Africa, and Singapore are closed. Trading starts quietly with Norwegian inflation and the Brazilian central bank’s weekly survey of economists, but the release that matters for Latin American desks arrives at 11.00 pm, when Colombia publishes July inflation. The annual rate is forecast to rise for a second month, which would complicate the case for further cuts.

The Week in Context

The backdrop for Latin American assets remains one of modest regional growth and tight-to-neutral monetary policy, leaving the asset class sensitive to the dollar and US real yields. A firm dollar tightens financial conditions and can override decent local fundamentals, while a softening greenback gives the Brazilian real, Mexican peso, and Andean currencies room to appreciate.

One number frames the whole week. US headline inflation fell 0.4 percent in June and is forecast to rise 0.1 percent in July, while core went from flat to a forecast 0.2 percent. That pattern, a soft headline with a firming core, is the hardest configuration for markets to price, because it pulls the two halves of the Federal Reserve’s mandate in opposite directions.

Regional divergence is the second story. Colombia’s annual rate is forecast at 6.20 percent, more than double Brazil’s June reading of 4.64 percent and running against the direction of Argentina’s monthly pace, which has fallen to 1.9 percent. Mexican industrial production contracted in May on both measures. Peru enters its rate decision with growth at 1.80 percent and unemployment at 4.9 percent, the region’s most stable combination.

The Bottom Line

Wednesday’s US core reading is the single most consequential release for Latin American portfolios this week, and the headline is likely to mislead. A core print above 0.2 percent would firm the dollar and tighten conditions across the region regardless of what happens to the headline rate. Colombia’s Monday inflation and Brazil’s Tuesday IPCA determine how much room the two largest Andean and Latin American central banks have left, while Peru’s Thursday decision and Argentina’s July print round out a week in which regional inflation is moving in three different directions at once.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most important event for Latin American markets this week?

The US inflation report on Wednesday at 12.30 pm UTC. The core rate is forecast at 0.2 percent monthly and 2.5 percent annually. A deviation from those figures will reset Federal Reserve expectations and drive the dollar, directly affecting every Latin American currency and equity index.

Why does the Colombian inflation print on Monday matter?

It is the first major regional data point of the week and the forecast points the wrong way for policymakers. Annual inflation is seen rising to 6.20 percent from 6.14 percent, a second consecutive increase that would narrow the room for further rate cuts and weigh on Colombian peso-denominated bonds.

What should I watch in Brazil on Tuesday?

The Copom meeting minutes at 11.00 am and the July inflation rate at noon, four hours apart. The minutes reveal the committee’s balance of risks, and the IPCA follows immediately. June inflation was 0.16 percent monthly and 4.64 percent annually, near the top of the tolerance band.

Editor’s note, 9 August 2026. An earlier version put the first-quarter profit increase at 26.8 per cent and, in the headline and summary, at 27 per cent. MBRF reported 26 per cent, which is what its own figures of R$111 million against R$88 million imply. All references have been corrected.

Earnings · Brazil

Key Facts —Q4 2025 Net Profit net profit fell 92% to R$91 million (US$17.9 million) in Q4 2025, down from R$1.125 billion (US$221.3 million) a year earlier. —Q1 2026 Net Profit profit rose 26% in Q1 2026 to R$111 million (US$21.8 million), recovering from R$88 million (US$17.3 million) in the same quarter of 2025. —Company MBRF Global Foods Company S.A., the entity formed by the combination of BRF and Marfrig, trades on B3 under the ticker MBRF3. —Q1 2026 Release Date The first-quarter 2026 results were published on 14 May 2026. —Exchange Rate Figures in reais are converted at R$5.0826 to one US dollar, the closing rate on 7 August. —Key Driver The sharp turnaround was driven by easing integration costs, stronger processed-food margins, and expanding export volumes, particularly to the Middle East.

MBRF Global Foods Company S.A. saw net profit fall 92% to R$91 million (US$17.9 million) in the fourth quarter of 2025 before swinging to a 26% increase in the first quarter of 2026, as the colossal integration of Marfrig and BRF moved from a heavy cost phase into early operational gains.

The Two Quarters in Sharp Contrast

The fourth quarter of 2025 delivered a sobering set of numbers for the newly merged protein giant. MBRF reported a net profit of R$91 million (US$17.9 million), which represented a decline of 91.9% from the R$1.125 billion (US$221.3 million) recorded in the same period a year earlier, according to company filings and Brazilian financial media coverage published in March 2026.

The swing was not merely a margin squeeze but a reset of the earnings base. Financial expenses tied to the complex BRF-Marfrig combination, along with restructuring charges, pulverised the bottom line even as gross revenues held relatively steady, leaving the company with one of its weakest quarterly performances since the merger was conceived.

The Q1 2026 Recovery and Its Components

By the time MBRF reported first-quarter 2026 results on 14 May 2026, the picture had brightened considerably. Net profit reached R$111 million (US$21.8 million), marking an increase of 26% compared with the R$88 million (US$17.3 million) posted in the first quarter of 2025, a figure sometimes rounded up to 27 per cent in the business press.

The recovery was underpinned by a distinctly improved operational performance. Export volumes climbed as the company redirected more shipments to the Middle East, where elevated demand and a favourable pricing environment for halal poultry and beef products supported a healthier mix, while domestic processed-food margins expanded on the back of easing grain costs.

Significantly, the first-quarter gain was not driven by one-off accounting items. The company attributed the profit rise directly to stronger operating income and a reduced drag from merger-related expenses, suggesting that the heavy restructuring work undertaken in late 2025 was beginning to generate a tangible payback.

The Integration That Is Reshaping Latin America’s Protein Trade

MBRF Global Foods Company S.A. is the product of a landmark tie-up between Marfrig Global Foods and BRF, two of Brazil’s oldest and largest protein processors. The combination, finalised after years of regulatory scrutiny, created a behemoth with an unrivalled portfolio spanning fresh and processed beef, pork, and poultry, along with a deep footprint in the Middle East and Asia.

The integration has been a capital-intensive undertaking. In the fourth quarter of 2025, financial restructuring charges and the costs of unifying back-office systems, logistics networks, and supplier contracts weighed heavily on the income statement, producing the dramatic 92 per cent profit drop that alarmed some foreign investors who had bought into the merger thesis.

By the first quarter of 2026, however, the narrative shifted. Management signalled that the heaviest phase of IT system convergence and plant rationalisation was largely complete, freeing management attention to focus on commercial strategy and allowing the combined entity to start extracting the synergies that were promised when the deal was first announced.

Beef, Poultry, and the Export Engine

Brazil’s protein sector has been navigating a turbulent global market defined by shifting trade flows and heightened geopolitical risk. MBRF’s export performance in early 2026 reflected a deliberate pivot toward the Middle East, where demand for Brazilian halal-certified chicken and beef has remained resilient despite regional instability, including the conflict in Iraq.

Domestically, the poultry cycle provided a tailwind as feed input costs, particularly corn and soymeal, retreated from the peaks seen in mid-2025. Lower production costs fed directly into improved margins in the processed-foods segment, which includes branded products sold across Brazilian supermarkets, a channel that accounts for a substantial share of the company’s recurring revenue.

Beef operations, meanwhile, continued to benefit from strong Chinese demand, though logistics bottlenecks at key ports periodically tested the company’s capacity to ship full volumes. The first quarter saw a net improvement in the beef division’s contribution, with higher average selling prices compensating for a modest decline in slaughter volumes.

Balance-Sheet Strains and the Debt Overhang

For all the operational progress, MBRF carries a heavy debt load inherited from the merger, and that leverage remains the single largest concern for investors watching the stock. Fourth-quarter interest expenses ballooned, eroding earnings and pushing the net profit to just R$91 million (US$17.9 million), a level that left scant room for shareholder distributions or aggressive capital investment.

The company’s management used the first-quarter earnings release to emphasise a disciplined approach to deleveraging. The improved operating cash flow in the first three months of 2026 allowed a modest reduction in short-term liabilities, though gross debt remained elevated by historical standards, leaving the firm sensitive to movements in the Selic rate and to the real-dollar exchange rate.

For a foreign investor, the debt profile translates into a binary risk-reward equation. A sustained period of lower US dollar-denominated input costs and strong export demand, combined with falling Brazilian interest rates, could rapidly lift net income above the R$111 million (US$21.8 million) quarterly run-rate; conversely, any disruption to trade flows or a fresh spike in borrowing costs would squeeze the company at precisely the moment it needs to demonstrate it can stand on its own as a merged entity.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did MBRF’s profit drop so sharply in Q4 2025?

Net profit fell 92% to R$91 million (US$17.9 million) in the fourth quarter of 2025 because of heavy financial expenses and restructuring costs tied to the Marfrig-BRF merger, which overwhelmed operating earnings.

What drove the 27% rebound in Q1 2026?

Profit rose 27% in Q1 2026 to R$111 million (US$21.8 million) as integration charges eased, export volumes to the Middle East increased, and lower grain costs improved processed-food margins.

How does the MBRF merger affect a foreign portfolio investor?

The combined entity offers exposure to Brazil’s dominant protein export platform but carries elevated debt; success depends on delivering promised cost synergies and managing currency and interest-rate risks.

World.content:

Investors are betting on continuity but analysts flag a debt time bomb. Here’s what to watch before October.

Brazilian markets are starting to price in a fourth term for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but a warning from UBS about a 2027 fiscal reckoning highlights the risk baked into that bet. For foreign investors and expats holding Brazilian assets, the contradiction is stark: stocks and the real are holding up even as analysts flag a debt trajectory that could double in six years. Understanding what a ’fiscal bomb’ really means — and why markets can rally on a result they also consider fiscally risky — is key to navigating the months ahead. The 2027 fiscal reckoning looms as the central uncertainty, yet the market seems to be looking past it for now.

The Brazilian real and B3 stock exchange trading screens are shown in São Paulo, reflecting market jitters ahead of the Oct. 4 election, with gross public debt at 81.9% of GDP. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What is the 2027 fiscal reckoning?

When analysts talk about a ’fiscal bomb’ in Brazil, they mean a scenario where public debt grows unsustainably fast, forcing a future crisis. The numbers are already worrying: the Central Bank reported gross debt at 81.9% of GDP in June/July 2026, and the 12-month consolidated public sector result showed a primary deficit of 1.19% of GDP and a nominal deficit of 9.99% of GDP.

A primary deficit means the government isn’t even covering its operating costs before interest payments. Adding interest, the nominal deficit exceeds 10% of GDP. If nothing changes, independent commentary suggests debt could double by 2032 — a path that would undermine investor confidence and potentially trigger capital outflows.

UBS, in a note reported by O Globo on Aug. 6, 2026, linked the fiscal situation directly to inflation. The bank argued that if fiscal problems are solved, the inflation target becomes reachable again in 2027. Unsolved, the ’fiscal bomb’ detonates via higher interest rates and a weaker currency.

Why do markets rally on Lula 4 despite the 2027 fiscal reckoning?

At first glance, it seems paradoxical: investors worry about Lula’s spending record, yet they price in his victory. The key is that markets hate uncertainty more than they hate a known outcome. With Lula leading in polls and a 64.5% implied probability on Polymarket for the Oct. 4 vote, investors are effectively pricing continuity.

Continuity means they expect Lula’s government to follow the current fiscal framework — even with its flaws — rather than a drastic regime change. That expectation keeps the Ibovespa from crashing and the real from sliding further. On Aug. 6, the index closed at 175,546 points, still strong but 10.5% below its April record of about 195,000.

However, this is a fragile equilibrium. If polls tighten further — and they have already narrowed from an 8-point lead to just 1 point in one survey — markets could reassess quickly. The real weakened to R$5.13 (about US$1.00)per dollar on Aug. 5, down from less volatile levels earlier in the year, reflecting the jitters.

Markets are now pricing in a fourth Lula term with remarkable calm – but UBS’s warning about 2027 is the quiet tremor beneath that surface. The fiscal problem is simple: by then, the vast bulk of mandatory spending – pensions, salaries, social security – is already legally committed to grow at or above inflation, leaving almost no room for discretionary investment. The fiscal framework demands a primary surplus of 0.25% of GDP that year, yet current projections show a deficit of around R$40bn (roughly US$7.8bn) – a gap that cannot be closed without cutting entitlements or raising taxes, both politically radioactive in an election’s aftermath. The pressure lands in 2027 because this year’s budget was already passed with band-aids and extraordinary revenues; next year, those tricks run out.

What to watch between now and October

First, watch the polls. The gap between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro is closing, and the Oct. 25 runoff (if needed) could be a nail-biter. A highly contested race could increase volatility, as markets price in different policy outcomes.

Second, track fiscal announcements. Any sign that the government is loosening spending to win votes — like new social programs or tax cuts — would raise concerns about the 2027 budget. Conversely, a commitment to austerity could calm markets.

Third, monitor the Central Bank. With inflation above target, the Copom is under pressure to keep rates high. The real’s value and the Ibovespa’s performance will hinge on whether fiscal and monetary policy align.

Finally, watch UBS-type warnings. If major banks formally release reports with ’fiscal bomb’ language, expect a sell-off. For now, the market’s bet is that Lula wins but moderates his spending. That bet is paying off.

The market’s calm in the face of a likely fourth Lula term is not denial — it is the pricing of a specific, known scenario. Investors are betting Lula wins but governs within the existing fiscal framework, flaws and all, and that bet is keeping the Ibovespa around 175,500 points and the real from sliding much past R$5.13 per dollar (US$1.00). What UBS flags for 2027 is the moment that scenario gets tested: mandatory spending is already locked in, the framework demands a 0.25% of GDP primary surplus, and the projected shortfall is roughly R$40bn (US$7.8bn) — a gap that needs either entitlement cuts or tax rises, both toxic after an election. That reversal risk is real, but it is not today’s trade; it is tomorrow’s problem.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is a ’fiscal bomb’ in Brazil? A ’fiscal bomb’ refers to a situation where public debt grows so fast that it becomes unsustainable. In Brazil’s case, that means the government’s primary deficit — where spending exceeds revenue before interest — continues, and the nominal deficit (including interest) reaches nearly 10% of GDP. If unresolved, debt could double by 2032, leading to higher interest rates, a weaker currency, and potentially a debt crisis. Why would markets rally if Lula wins, given fiscal risks? Markets prefer certainty. When Lula leads in polls, investors price in the most likely scenario — continuation of current policies. This reduces the risk premium. Even if Lula’s fiscal record is concerning, a known outcome is less risky than an unpredictable change. So, markets can rally because the alternative (a contested election or policy shift) could be worse for asset prices. What should an investor watch between now and October? Key indicators include: 1) Polling trends — a narrowing gap could increase volatility. 2) Fiscal announcements — any pre-election spending promises that worsen deficits. 3) Central Bank decisions on interest rates, which affect the currency and equities. 4) Reports from major banks like UBS that may use ’fiscal bomb’ language, which could trigger sell-offs. Monitoring these will help you anticipate market moves. How is the Brazilian real performing against the dollar? As of early August 2026, the real traded at about R$5.13 (about US$1.00)per dollar, slightly weaker than earlier in the year. This reflects investor caution ahead of the election. If fiscal concerns escalate, the real could depreciate further; if the market gains confidence in the fiscal path, it could strengthen. Keep an eye on the exchange rate, as it directly affects foreign investors’ returns.

Earnings · Brazil

Key Facts —The deal JBS and PT Danantara Investment Management (DIM), an arm of Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund, agreed a joint venture worth up to US$5 billion on 7 August 2026. —Equity component Danantara will invest US$2.5 billion in equity for a 25% stake, phased with US$800 million at closing and up to US$1.7 billion over three years. —Debt capacity The venture plans to raise up to an additional US$2.5 billion in debt financing after the equity is fully funded. —Geographic scope For the first two years after closing, the sovereign fund capital may be invested only in Indonesia; expansion to other Southeast Asian markets, Australia and New Zealand is possible only after that period. —JBS contribution JBS will contribute 100% of its Australia and New Zealand businesses into the new structure. —Citi rating Citi reiterated a buy rating on JBS shares, citing the deal as a capital-light growth avenue.

JBS has agreed a deal worth up to US$5 billion with an Indonesian sovereign wealth fund to form an Asia-Pacific protein joint venture, the Brazilian meatpacker’s largest strategic partnership in the region.

Structure of the venture

JBS SA (NYSE: JBS; B3: JBSS3) and PT Danantara Investment Management, an arm of Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund Danantara, announced on 7 August 2026 that they had signed a binding agreement to create a joint venture focused on protein production across the Asia-Pacific region. The venture will be capitalised through a US$2.5 billion equity injection from Danantara for a 25% stake, with JBS contributing the entirety of its Australia and New Zealand operations.

The equity component will be delivered in two phases: an initial US$800 million at closing and the remaining US$1.7 billion over a period of up to three years, according to statements from both companies. After the equity is fully funded, the joint venture intends to raise up to an additional US$2.5 billion in debt financing, lifting the total capital available to the venture to as much as US$5 billion.

Who Danantara is

PT Danantara Investment Management is the operational investment arm of Danantara, Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund, which was established in early 2025 to manage state assets and attract foreign co-investment into strategic sectors. The fund’s mandate includes food security and protein supply chains, making the JBS partnership a direct fit with its national investment priorities.

For JBS, the arrangement provides a state-backed partner with deep access to Southeast Asian markets and a long-term capital commitment without requiring the Brazilian parent to dilute its own equity or take on additional consolidated debt. The joint venture will be governed as a separate entity with its own balance sheet, ring-fencing the Australian and New Zealand assets that JBS is contributing.

Asia-Pacific growth strategy

The joint venture is explicitly aimed at expanding protein processing and distribution capacity in Indonesia and neighbouring Southeast Asian markets, while also strengthening JBS’s existing footprint in Australia and New Zealand. Reuters reported on 7 August 2026 that J.P. Morgan analysts described the structure as a mechanism that allows JBS to pursue M&A and organic growth while preserving its own cash reserves.

By folding its wholly-owned Australian and New Zealand subsidiaries into the venture, JBS retains a 75% economic interest and operational control while bringing in a partner that can unlock political and commercial doors across the Indonesian archipelago and the wider ASEAN region. The dual focus on developed-market processing assets and emerging-market consumption growth mirrors the playbook JBS used successfully in Brazil and the United States.

Citi reiterates buy rating

Citi reiterated its buy rating on JBS shares following the announcement, characterising the transaction as a capital-efficient path to expansion in high-growth Asian protein markets. The bank’s analysts pointed to the structure’s limited upfront cash outlay for JBS and the strategic logic of pairing Brazilian operational expertise with Indonesian state capital.

The stock reaction on the B3 exchange in São Paulo showed a positive bias in early trading on 7 August, although the full session’s close was not available at the time of reporting. JBS American depositary receipts traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker JBS also edged higher in pre-market activity, reflecting investor support for a transaction that does not require issuing new JBS equity.

What it means for foreign investors

For foreign holders of JBS paper, the deal represents a significant de-risking of the company’s Asia-Pacific ambitions by attaching them to a sovereign-backed vehicle with its own financing capacity. The structure keeps JBS’s consolidated leverage in check while opening a conduit to one of the world’s fastest-growing protein consumption zones at a time when demand in developed markets is flattening.

The transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, and Reuters noted that the deal was not yet complete as of its 7 August report. Investors will be watching for confirmation of the initial US$800 million closing tranche and for any conditions imposed by Australian or New Zealand foreign-investment review bodies, given the contribution of strategic agricultural assets into a partly foreign-state-owned venture.

Brazilian protein exporters have faced a more complex global trade environment in 2026, with shifting sanitary protocols and regional trade agreements altering market-access terms across Asia. A locally domiciled joint venture backed by an Indonesian sovereign fund provides JBS with a structural hedge against future trade frictions, positioning production capacity inside the consuming region rather than relying solely on cross-border shipments.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is JBS receiving in cash from the Danantara deal?

The joint venture itself will receive US$2.5 billion in equity from Danantara, phased as US$800 million at closing and up to US$1.7 billion over three years, with the venture planning to raise up to an additional US$2.5 billion in debt later.

Will JBS sell its Australian and New Zealand businesses?

No, JBS will contribute 100% of its Australia and New Zealand operations into the new joint venture but will retain a 75% stake and operational control.

Is the deal already closed?

No, the transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions and was not yet complete as of 7 August 2026.

Recurring EBITDA reached R$712 million (US$140.1 million), a figure the company called a quarterly record. At the prevailing exchange rate of R$5.0826 to the US dollar as of 7 August 2026, that performance translates to roughly US$140 million, underscoring the size of the operation for international investors.

Profit and Why the Stock Declined

The bottom line showed a net profit of R$204 million (US$40.1 million) in Q2 2026, an 8 per cent rise from the same period a year earlier. That result, however, did not insulate the stock from a sharp sell-off, with shares falling about 8% on the day after the numbers were released and touching a level not seen since August 2025.

Analysts cited by Brazilian business outlets pointed to earnings below the EBITDA line that disappointed, even as headline revenue and profit grew. Citi called the quarter mixed: revenue and earnings came in below its estimates, while the cash gross margin strengthened to 51.9 percent and cost control tightened. Morgan Stanley focused on the lines below EBITDA and on weaker cash conversion.

World.title: Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack
World.content:
Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A quiet walk along the Philip Goldson Highway turned to tragedy on Friday, August 7, 2026, when a 17-year-old girl drowned in the Belize River after she and her father were attacked by a swarm of bees near mile 7, sending the teen into deep water from which she never resurfaced.

The attack came at about 1:00 p.m., as the girl and her father, residents of Lord’s Bank who often walked that route together, passed a tree stump where the bees were nesting. The swarm descended on them both, and in the chaos that followed, as passersby rushed to assist her father, the teen went into the river, likely to escape the stings. That stretch of the river is said to be about 20 feet deep, and the girl, who could not swim, was unable to get back to the surface.

What followed was an hours-long search that drew together the Belize Coast Guard and eight civilian volunteers from 501 Lifeguard, who waded and dove through dark, murky water until about 3:30 p.m., when her body was finally recovered.

Tevin Conorquie, the 501 Lifeguard swimming instructor who first located her, described the ordeal, speaking to local media. “All we could have done was free dive and try to scan the area,” he said. “Due to the darkness of the water, it was intense for us to see but we still pulled through, we had the faith and the courage and we did what we had to do.” The team spent some three to four hours in the water, in conditions Conorquie called very difficult, “due to the fact that we know there may be crocodiles with us as well.”

When the teen’s brother arrived and the loss became real, the rescuers’ work turned from search to solace, the 501 Lifeguard team circling him in prayer. “With our team it’s just love,” said the organization’s owner, Andrew Gentle, noting that his instructors left their swimming classes to answer the call, and the whole team came.

The recovery weighed on the professionals too. “It’s never easy because you’re talking about the loss of life,” said Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis, Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, which responded to the request for dive operations. “There were times when I myself shed tears because of the situation. Especially when you’re talking about a young person such as the one today.”

The girl’s father is currently recovering in hospital. The family shared that the teen was living with autism and resided with her father. Officials have since sprayed the area where the bees were nesting.

Breaking Belize News extends its deepest condolences to the family, and its gratitude to the divers and volunteers who refused to leave the river without her.

World.title: The 80 million dollar question, a ledger for Belizeans to judge the BTL Speednet deal
World.content:
The 80 million dollar question, a ledger for Belizeans to judge the BTL Speednet deal

By Horace Palacio:

This week, the board of Belize Telemedia Limited approved spending 80 million dollars to buy Speednet, the company Belizeans know as Smart. It did so one day after the Chamber of Commerce publicly begged it to halt. The final agreement still must return to the board before signing, which means one thing.

There is still time for you to think. And you must, because this is not somebody else’s transaction.

BTL is majority owned by the Government of Belize, which is to say, by you. The Social Security Board, holding the retirement contributions of every working Belizean, owns another 34.2 percent. When BTL spends 80 million dollars, it is your company spending what is ultimately your money, with your pension fund along for the ride. You are the shareholder here. So today I will not hand you a verdict. I will hand you the ledger, both columns, honestly weighed, and then I will hand you the gavel.

First, the case for the deal, and let me make it properly, because it is not foolish.

Belize is a nation of 420,000 people carrying two complete, parallel telecommunications networks. Two sets of towers climbing the same skyline. Two fiber networks running down the same streets. Two billing systems, two headquarters, two of everything, serving a market smaller than a single foreign city. The case says this duplication is waste a small country cannot afford, and that one consolidated network could finally achieve the scale to modernize seriously, push fiber and coverage into the villages that neither company found profitable to serve, and strengthen reliability nationwide. BTL says the purchase needs no borrowing and not one new dollar from Social Security, paying for itself from Speednet’s own cash flows in roughly 4.2 years, with the profits of a unified telecom flowing to public hands instead of private ones. And there is a quieter argument some will weigh, that this deal ends Lord Ashcroft’s presence in Belizean telecommunications once and for all. That is the case for. Taken at face value, it is a vision of efficiency, inclusion, and sovereignty.

Now the other column, and it is heavy.

Start with what we already lived. Belizeans of a certain age remember the old single-provider era, and what it delivered, some of the region’s most expensive and slowest service, because a customer with nowhere to go is a customer who need not be pleased. Then competition arrived, and in the PUC’s own public comment file on this very deal sits a citizen pointing to the large price gap between BTL and Speednet as exactly what stands to be lost. Competition is not a theory in Belize. It is the reason your phone plan got better. This deal ends it.

Then the law. Section 42(4) of the Telecommunications Act prohibits agreements that significantly lessen competition in telecommunications. Buying your only major competitor is about the purest example imaginable. The Chamber adds a deeper alarm, Belize has no comprehensive competition or merger control legislation at all, no guardrails, meaning this would be a state-backed monopoly overseen only by a regulator, and the Chamber’s blunt warning is that regulation can never truly replace competition. Which raises the question no one has answered. When government owns the only telecom, and government appoints the referee, who exactly protects you?

Then the valuation. The financial model that justified the 80 million figure was prepared by Moore, a firm the unions say holds established ties to the BTL board, and it was paid for by BTL, the buyer, and reports indicate it stands among the only documents board members received. The unions call that a conflict of interest that renders the number inherently suspect, and demand what any buyer of a used car would demand, an independent inspection.

Then the arithmetic itself, because analysts who have studied the projections raise eyebrows at every line. The model reportedly projects Speednet earning a 66.5 percent profit margin, far above BTL’s own 44 percent, on revenue of 69 million dollars. Skeptics who place Speednet’s realistic revenue nearer 28 to 32 million calculate that the payback stretches not to 4.2 years but to somewhere between 13 and 25. The company’s own slides reportedly show combined revenue going flat, growing under one percent yearly once the deal closes, meaning the promised leap in profits rests almost entirely on cutting costs. And the seller’s own press release confirms where the knife lands, power, software, maintenance, and the duplicated departments, sales, marketing, human resources, finance, IT, purchasing. Behind every one of those words sit Belizean employees whose futures nobody has yet disclosed. BTL claims its payback is calculated on a discounted basis, yet the standard tools of any public investment of this size, the net present value, the internal rate of return, the formal schedules, have not been published for the shareholders, meaning you, to see.

Now count the voices, because the scorecard on this deal is unlike anything in recent memory. In favor, the BTL board and management. Urging halt or answers, the Chamber of Commerce speaking for over six thousand employers, the National Trade Union Congress speaking for organized labor, the parliamentary Opposition, and all four independent senators in a joint statement. Stop and appreciate the rarity. The employers and the unions of this country agree with each other about once a decade. They agree on this. When both the boss and the worker smell the same smoke, wise citizens check for fire.

So, Belize, was 80 million dollars for a national telecom monopoly worth it, or not? That verdict belongs to you. But hear me carefully, because this is the entire point of today’s column.

No honest verdict can be rendered on sealed evidence. Before any Belizean, for or against, can truly judge this deal, six things must be put on the table. Speednet’s audited financial statements for the past five years, so the revenue dispute dies on facts. A second, fully independent, internationally credible valuation, so the price stands on neutral ground. The full financial workings, published, so the payback claim can be tested by any accountant in the country. The honest scope of planned redundancies, so workers stop learning their futures from press releases. A public, rigorous PUC merger review under Section 42(4), conducted as law, not formality. And binding, enforceable consumer protections, in writing, before signing, not promises after.

If this deal is as good as its backers insist, none of that sunlight costs them anything. Good deals survive audits. Only bad ones fear them. And a transaction this size, by a publicly owned company, in a country still raw from the Mira Millions lesson about what happens in the dark, must be concluded in daylight or not at all.

The board has voted. The ink is not dry. You are the shareholder, Belize, all 420,000 of you.

Demand the books. Read the ledger. Then judge.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Jorge Messi, father and lifelong architect of Lionel’s career, dies at 68
World.content:
Jorge Messi, father and lifelong architect of Lionel’s career, dies at 68

By Breaking Belize News Staff ( HP): Jorge Messi, the father of Argentina captain Lionel Messi and the man who guided every step of the greatest career in football history, died Saturday at a hospital in Rosario, Argentina. He was 68.

Club Atlético Newell’s Old Boys, the Rosario club where both father and son once played in the youth ranks, announced his death, saying he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness. The club described him as “the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigor and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini.”

The announcement casts the recent World Cup in a new and poignant light. After scoring against Algeria in Argentina’s opening match, Messi was visibly emotional, later saying he wept for “a reason unrelated to sports” and that he had endured “difficult, complicated days.” Media speculation at the time drew a sharp statement from the Messi family confirming that Jorge was experiencing a health issue, while insisting that “a person’s health and the peace of mind of their loved ones should not be the subject of speculation.” Messi went on to captain Argentina to the final, where they finished runners-up to Spain, before returning home to rest.

A chemical technician and former steelworker, Jorge Messi played as a midfielder in Newell’s youth system before military service ended his own football path. His life’s work became his son’s. He traveled with a young Lionel to Barcelona in the early 2000s for the trial that opened La Masia’s doors, negotiated the contracts with Barcelona and the later moves to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, and managed his son’s business affairs throughout.

Lionel Messi himself once described what those early days cost them both. “Sometimes I would lock myself in my room to cry when we arrived in Barcelona, or my dad would do the same without me seeing him,” he said in 2007. “My dad even asked me what I wanted to do when we were feeling down, if I wanted to stay or go back, and I wanted to stay, and he stayed with me.”

Tributes flowed Saturday. CONMEBOL offered condolences “with respect and affection for Lionel,” and Argentine federation president Claudio Tapia honoured Jorge “for having raised a person of values: humble, respectful, and deeply committed to others.” The federation ordered a moment of silence at all matches across every category of Argentine football, with players, referees and coaching staff to wear black armbands.

Jorge Messi is survived by his wife Celia and their children. Breaking Belize News extends condolences to the Messi family.

World.title: BDF and University of Belize deepen partnership on education and training
World.content:
BDF and University of Belize deepen partnership on education and training

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Defence Force and the University of Belize are strengthening their collaboration, with the BDF’s Training and Doctrine Directorate visiting the university to meet with President and members of his staff on furthering joint efforts between the Ministry of Defence and Border Security and the nation’s leading academic institution.

The engagement provided an opportunity for discussions on ongoing programs, future initiatives, and the continued growth of the partnership between the two institutions, according to the BDF.

Members of the Force also attended the closing ceremony of the Digital Literacy Program hosted by the University of Belize, a program in which the BDF proudly participated. The Force described the training as another important step in equipping its members with valuable knowledge and skills for both professional and personal development.

With the university preparing for the upcoming academic year, plans were established to continue and expand engagements between both institutions.

The BDF said it remains committed to promoting higher learning, professional development and continuous education as essential components in transforming training and developing a more capable and knowledgeable Force, summing up the effort in its own words: investing in education, strengthening our Force, serving Belize.
