World.title: Iraq oil exports drop 75% amid Hormuz closure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Oil Minister Hayan Abdul-Ghani announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, that the nation’s crude oil exports have plummeted by 75% due to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and regional military escalations. The severe drop in oil revenues has triggered a liquidity squeeze across the federal government, causing widespread delays in state employee salary disbursements.

Speaking at a press conference in Baghdad, Abdul-Ghani revealed that Iraq is currently exporting only a quarter of its pre-war volumes, which stood at approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) prior to the outbreak of regional hostilities on February 28. He noted that while Baghdad has engaged in diplomatic talks with Iran to permit the passage of Iraqi oil shipments through the Gulf, no operational agreement has been activated.

Key financial and operational highlights

Export Collapse: Iraq’s crude exports have fallen to ~25% of pre-war capacity, cutting off the primary source of state revenue.

Fiscal Pressure & Salary Delays: Reduced export volumes and below-budget sale prices have caused acute liquidity shortages, delaying public sector payrolls.

Corporate Damage Compensation: Domestic Attacks: Baghdad has agreed to compensate foreign energy companies for damages resulting from attacks originating inside Iraqi territory. External Strikes: The government declared itself legally exempt from compensating firms for damages caused by foreign strikes or broader military actions beyond state control.

Alternative Export Bypasses: Baghdad is fast-tracking pipeline infrastructure projects bypassing the Persian Gulf, including routes south toward Turkey’s Ceyhan port, Syria’s Baniyas terminal, and Jordan’s Aqaba port.

To maintain minimal cash flows, Iraq is currently forced to sell its crude at deep price concessions below the baseline benchmark set in the national budget, compounding treasury deficits.

In response to the prolonged maritime chokehold in the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of Oil is accelerating infrastructure development along overland export routes.

Priority has been placed on expanding and constructing pipeline corridors connecting southern production hubs to the Mediterranean via Syria and Turkey, alongside long-term transit planning toward the Red Sea via Jordan.

World.title: Iraq activates Kirkuk oil field development contract with BP
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, the official activation of its Kirkuk oilfield development contract with British energy giant BP. The project aims to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day (bpd) to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Ministry of Oil Spokesperson Salim Al-Rikabi stated that the contract—initially signed in September 2025—focuses on expanding crude extraction while capturing associated natural gas to eliminate routine flaring and feed domestic power generation infrastructure.

Key operational targets & metrics

Crude Oil Output: Increasing current production from 320,000 bpd to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Associated Gas Capture: Raising associated gas processing from 255 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) to a peak capacity of 400 million scf/d.

Facility Modernization: Upgrading and expanding infrastructure across North Oil Company fields and North Gas Company processing plants.

Power & Social Infrastructure: Constructing a dedicated 400-megawatt (MW) power plant, expanding local employment, funding community development initiatives, and upskilling North Oil and North Gas workforces.

Environmental Impact: Phasing out continuous gas flaring to redirect captured methane directly into national electricity generation.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major component of Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

By upgrading processing facilities managed by the North Gas Company and constructing a dedicated 400 MW power generation facility, the initiative directly addresses regional electricity shortages while reducing environmental emissions.

The partnership also reinforces BP’s operational footprint in northern Iraq, complementing its long-standing management of the Southern Rumaila field and bolstering state-led efforts to modernize national energy infrastructure.

World.title: India’s Reliance pays record $25 million freight cost for Iraqi crude amid Hormuz crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — India’s Reliance Industries (RELI.NS), operator of the world’s largest refining complex in Gujarat, paid an unprecedented record charter fee of $23 million to $25 million for a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) to transport 2 million barrels of Basrah crude from Iraq, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters on Friday, August 7, 2026.

The extreme freight surge—marking a jump from a pre-war average of $2 million to 12 times the baseline global freight rate—highlights severe shipping chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Daily vessel transits through the strategic waterway have plummeted from a pre-war average of 125–140 ships to a fraction of normal capacity as shipowners avoid military risks.

Key financial & logistics metrics

Soaring Freight Rates: Reliance chartered the VLCC from South Korea’s Sinokor at 1,200 points on the Worldscale freight index—12 times the reference benchmark—up from pre-war levels of 0.8 to 0.9 times ($2 million total).

Deep SOMO Discounts: To offset soaring shipping costs and attract buyers into the Gulf, the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered steep discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel below Dubai regional benchmarks.

Net Margin Offset: Despite the $25 million freight tag, energy analysts estimate Reliance will still save millions on the overall transaction due to Iraq’s heavy crude price reductions.

Limited Carrier Pool: Sinokor remains one of the few international maritime operators willing to navigate the Strait of Hormuz to load cargo at Iraq’s Basra Oil Terminal.

While Asian refiners—particularly across India and China—are actively seeking chartered tankers to capture Iraq’s discounted crude allocations, shipowner reluctance continues to limit available tonnage entering the Gulf.

By offering deep price concessions, Iraq’s oil marketing arm is successfully maintaining crude flow off the Basra coast despite soaring war-risk insurance premiums and maritime transport bottlenecks.

World.title: Kata’ib Sayyid Al Shuhada clarifies delay in retaliatory strikes against U.S.-Saudi targets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Abu Ala al-Walai, Secretary-General of Kata’ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, commented on Saturday, August 8, 2026, regarding the decision by the “Islamic Resistance in Iraq” to pause planned military responses to recent joint U.S.-Saudi strikes.

Speaking via a statement on social media platform X, al-Walai confirmed that the delay was granted at the direct request of Coordination Framework leaders, led by Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri, alongside several independent political figures. However, the paramilitary commander emphasized that options for retaliation—including the reassessment of its timing, scale, and nature—remain fully on the table. He urged state officials to utilize this temporary window to secure Iraq’s rights through diplomatic and legal channels.

Key developments in the escalation pause

The Deferred Response: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq announced on Friday, August 7, the postponement of retaliatory operations originally scheduled for the 23rd of Safar targeting Saudi Arabia and U.S. military bases.

Al-Amiri’s Appeal: Badr Organization leader Hadi al-Amiri issued an urgent video address early Friday urging armed factions to delay military action following American-Saudi strikes on Iraqi territory, prioritizing national stability while pursuing accountability for casualties via diplomatic means.

High Security Readiness: The political appeal followed a volatile night across Baghdad and multiple governorates, prompting high-level security alerts and military deployments across the capital.

Command Structure On Site: In response to directives from Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to elevate combat readiness, senior commanders from Baghdad Operations Command were deployed on the ground to enforce military discipline and secure vital sectors.

The brief pause in military operations provides a critical window for Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s administration to manage state security, navigate delicate diplomatic channels with Washington and Riyadh, and prevent further regional escalation.

World.title: Iraq fish deaths: 7 alarming signs of a deepening water and pollution crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Recurring Iraq fish deaths are becoming an increasingly serious environmental and economic warning, with the Green Iraq Observatory describing the phenomenon as an annual pattern that reflects the accumulation of two interconnected crises: worsening water scarcity and persistent pollution.

Rather than representing isolated incidents caused by temporary changes in river conditions, the repeated deaths of large numbers of fish across Iraq’s rivers, canals and marshlands suggest that the country’s aquatic ecosystems are coming under sustained pressure from declining water flows, untreated wastewater, industrial pollution and weaknesses in water management.

The latest incidents, recorded in April and August 2026, have once again raised concerns about the condition of Iraq’s freshwater resources and the government’s ability to protect them. According to the observatory, more than 1,000 tonnes of fish died in the Tigris and Diyala rivers during April, with particularly heavy losses reported in Wasit province, while a separate incident occurred earlier this month in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan.

Although the two incidents were associated with different immediate circumstances, they demonstrate how vulnerable Iraq’s aquatic ecosystems have become when declining water levels interact with pollution and inadequate environmental controls.

Iraq fish deaths are becoming an annual warning sign

The Green Iraq Observatory argues that the recurrence of mass fish deaths should no longer be treated as a series of unrelated environmental emergencies. According to its assessment, similar incidents have occurred repeatedly across different parts of Iraq over the past several years, yet the underlying causes have not been addressed with sufficient consistency to prevent them from returning.

This pattern is particularly concerning because rivers and wetlands are not only ecological assets; they also support fisheries, agriculture and the livelihoods of communities that depend directly on healthy waterways.

The observatory said the April incident involved more than 1,000 tonnes of dead fish in the Tigris and Diyala rivers, with the largest losses concentrated in Wasit. It attributed the event to severe contamination caused by untreated sewage and industrial waste, while also pointing to increased water releases from Hamrin Dam that reportedly moved accumulated pollutants downstream toward the Tigris.

The organization further said that more than 20 people experienced poisoning or skin-related injuries and were taken to hospital, illustrating how deterioration in water quality can potentially extend beyond damage to aquatic life and become a broader public-health concern.

A second incident was reported at the beginning of August in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan. According to the observatory, the agriculture and water committee of the Maysan Provincial Council attributed the fish deaths to a sharp decline in the water releases allocated to the canal.

This episode is significant because it demonstrates that pollution is not necessarily the only immediate trigger for fish mortality; inadequate water flows can also create conditions in which fish become increasingly vulnerable to high temperatures, reduced oxygen levels and the concentration of pollutants already present in the water.

Water scarcity Is only part of the problem

Iraq’s water crisis is frequently discussed in terms of declining river flows, prolonged drought and reductions in water arriving from upstream countries. Those factors are undoubtedly important, but the recent fish deaths suggest that the country’s environmental problems cannot be explained simply by saying that Iraq does not have enough water. The quality, distribution and management of the water available can be just as important as its overall volume.

The Green Iraq Observatory highlighted this distinction by noting that the country’s total water storage had reportedly risen to around 34 billion cubic meters at the time of the latest incident.

From the organization’s perspective, the fact that fish mortality continued despite an increase in total reserves indicates that administrative decisions concerning water distribution may be contributing to the problem alongside genuine resource scarcity.

This does not mean that Iraq’s wider water shortage is unimportant. On the contrary, prolonged drought and declining inflows can weaken the natural ability of rivers and wetlands to dilute pollutants and maintain ecological balance. However, when available water is distributed unevenly or when polluted water is allowed to enter already stressed waterways, the consequences can become significantly more severe.

In other words, the crisis is not simply about how much water Iraq has, but also about where the water goes, what quality it has and how effectively it is managed.

Pollution can turn a water shortage into an ecological emergency

Untreated sewage and industrial waste are among the most serious threats facing Iraq’s waterways because they can fundamentally alter the chemical and biological conditions required for aquatic life. When large quantities of organic material enter a river or canal, microorganisms consume oxygen while breaking that material down, potentially reducing dissolved oxygen to levels that fish and other aquatic organisms cannot tolerate.

The situation can become even more complicated when water temperatures rise or when algae proliferate excessively. Some forms of harmful algae can contribute to oxygen depletion, particularly when large quantities of organic matter subsequently decompose.

At the same time, reduced water flows can prevent pollutants from being dispersed naturally, leaving them concentrated in particular sections of a river, canal or wetland.

This combination of factors helps explain why pollution and water scarcity should not be treated as completely separate problems. A waterway with strong flows may have a greater capacity to dilute certain pollutants, whereas a shallow and poorly circulated waterway can become significantly more vulnerable to contamination.

Consequently, environmental protection requires both adequate water releases and strict control over what is discharged into the country’s rivers.

Iraq has experienced similar fish mortality events for years

The latest incidents are not without precedent. The Green Iraq Observatory cited a long record of mass fish mortality events in Iraq, including a major incident in the Euphrates in Babylon in 2018, when tens of thousands of tonnes of fish were reportedly affected.

This was followed by the death of millions of fish at the Hindiya Barrage and another major incident in Al-Dalm Marsh in Diwaniyah in 2020.

Further incidents were reported in the Al-Ezz River in Maysan in 2023, while extensive fish deaths occurred in Ibn Najm Marsh in Najaf last year. Particularly worrying is the recurrence of fish mortality in the Maysan area where a similar incident had already been recorded, because repeated events in the same geographic location can indicate that the environmental conditions responsible for the original problem have not been adequately corrected.

The observatory argues that the repeated nature of these incidents is difficult to reconcile with a system that relies primarily on temporary investigative committees after environmental damage has already occurred. Investigations can establish causes and responsibility, but they cannot substitute for permanent monitoring mechanisms capable of identifying dangerous changes in water quality before they result in large-scale ecological losses.

Iraq’s Marshlands face particular risks

The Iraqi marshlands are especially sensitive to changes in water availability and quality because their ecological health depends on a delicate relationship between water flows, seasonal conditions and the surrounding environment. These wetlands provide habitat for fish and birds while supporting communities whose economic and cultural lives have developed around them over generations.

When water levels fall sharply, sections of the marshes can become isolated or excessively shallow, increasing temperatures and reducing oxygen circulation. If polluted water enters these already stressed environments, the damage can become significantly more difficult to reverse.

Protecting Iraq’s marshlands therefore requires a long-term approach that connects water policy with environmental policy. Maintaining adequate ecological flows, reducing pollution and establishing continuous monitoring systems would be far more effective than treating each fish mortality event as an isolated emergency.

What Iraq can do to prevent future fish deaths

The Green Iraq Observatory has called for several measures aimed at addressing the structural causes behind recurring fish mortality. Among its recommendations is the establishment of fair and sustainable water allocations for provinces and marshlands, rather than relying on short-term decisions that may leave some waterways dangerously depleted.

The observatory has also called for stronger environmental oversight of wastewater treatment facilities and industrial establishments located near rivers. Effective enforcement would require more than regulations on paper; authorities would need regular inspections, reliable water-quality testing and meaningful consequences for facilities that discharge untreated or inadequately treated waste.

Another important proposal is the creation of an early-warning system that monitors dissolved oxygen and pollution levels. Such a system could bring together government agencies, universities and civil-society organizations, allowing scientific data to be collected continuously and shared quickly when dangerous changes are detected.

Finally, rapid compensation for fish farmers affected by major environmental incidents could provide essential economic relief while investigations determine responsibility and long-term solutions.

No. Water scarcity is an important contributing factor, but pollution and poor water management can also play major roles. Even when overall water reserves increase, individual rivers, canals or marshes may experience insufficient flows or deteriorating water quality.

World.title: US Fed sends $500 million cash shipment to Iraq amid financial pressures
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The United States Federal Reserve has sent a new $500 million cash cargo to the Central Bank of Iraq, providing additional dollar liquidity as Baghdad grapples with rising financial pressures and disruptions to its oil-dependent economy.

The shipment was announced by Iraq’s national news agency, citing an official source who claimed the dollars will be used for permitted overseas transfers and transactions involving Iraqi citizens.

Further supplies are planned each month, with a government official estimating annual cash delivery of $8 billion to $10 billion.

These cash payments are part of Iraq’s peculiar financial relationship with the United States.

Proceeds from Iraqi oil exports are mostly placed in an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with Baghdad obtaining dollars via permitted transfers and cash shipments administered by the Central Bank of Iraq.

The new supply comes at a critical moment for Iraq’s budget.

The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has increased pressure on a nation that relies significantly on oil exports to support government expenditures and get foreign currency.

Iraq’s enormous public-sector pay bill contributes to this vulnerability.

Millions of Iraqis rely directly or indirectly on government wages, pensions, and social benefits; therefore, stable oil income and liquidity are crucial to the national budget.

Baghdad has lately expressed increased worries about its capacity to fulfill expenditure obligations if oil earnings continue low, strengthening long-standing demands for Iraq to diversify government income and lessen its reliance on petroleum exports.

The most recent dollar cargo should offer further liquidity to Iraq’s banking system, but it also shows the country’s vulnerability to both oil-market shocks and its financial ties with Washington at a time of rising regional tensions.

World.title: Lise Klaveness, the Norwegian thorn in Infantino’s side
World.content:
Oslo – A rare woman in the top echelons of football, the head of Norway’s federation Lise Klaveness has been a thorn in FIFA’s side for years.

Now, some would gladly see her take over the leadership of football’s international governing body from Gianni Infantino.

The 45-year-old lawyer and former footballer who played 73 matches for Norway has been highly vocal about international football’s woes under Infantino.

The Swiss-Italian has been mired in controversy since his plan to open FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors was swiftly rejected last week.

On Friday she called for him to resign.

When he was elected FIFA president in 2016, “he was a candidate who had been elected on a reform programme focused on good governance,” she told AFP.

“Then things quickly deteriorated: from keeping a distance, we moved to giving up, and even backtracking, all against a backdrop of a lack of independence from heads of state and other influential figures, particularly from World Cup host countries,” she said.

She fired her first salvo at Infantino in 2022, just after she was appointed head of the Norwegian federation, about the conditions under which the World Cup was awarded to Qatar.

From Doha, she publicly lamented that “human rights, equality, democracy, the core interests of football, were not in the starting 11”.

The following year, Norway refused to back Infantino in his re-election bid, signalling its dissatisfaction with his leadership.

Klaveness “was in a way the first standard-bearer for much of this criticism that many others now share when it comes to the way Infantino runs FIFA,” said Mina Finsted Berg, a sports commentator for Norwegian channel TV2.

She “is very committed to ensuring that rules and decisions are respected,” she added.

– Trump, Balogun and investors –

The reasons for her outrage against Infantino have piled up in recent months: FIFA’s decision to award a “Peace Prize” to US President Donald Trump, with whom Infantino has a conspicuously close relationship; the lifting of the suspension of US player Folarin Balogun at the 2026 World Cup following an intervention by Trump; and the aborted plan to open FIFA to private investors.

The Norwegian federation has decided to bring all three issues before the Ethics Committee of the world football governing body.

Klaveness’s voice carries all the more weight after Norway, long absent from major international tournaments, enjoyed a strong run in this year’s World Cup before being knocked out in the quarter-finals by England.

Internationally, commentators have praised her “strong moral compass” and consider her a serious candidate to replace Infantino if he were to step down.

He is standing for re-election for a fourth and final term next March and is currently the only declared candidate.

“She was the only one who always took a clear stand and did not go along with the mainstream. And at FIFA, the time is right for a woman to take the lead,” former FIFA head Sepp Blatter — himself disgraced after a corruption scandal — wrote on social network X.

– Ballot box obstacles –

Klaveness herself has insisted that the crisis in world football should not be reduced to a simple “Game of Thrones” power struggle and has instead called for a renewed focus on good governance.

“For us, it has never been a personal issue against Gianni Infantino,” she told AFP. “The problems go beyond the person of the president.”

And while she “has registered” that her name is being tossed around as a possible successor, she brushed aside questions about whether she was a candidate: “We’re not there yet.”

Many obstacles remain.

“In addition to being seen as extremely radical in many places, especially outside Europe, she is a woman. That is also likely to count against her in many regions of the world,” Mina Finsted Berg said.

Even within Europe’s governing body UEFA, which one could presume would be most favourable to her, Klaveness failed to win election to the Executive Committee in 2023.

She only joined in 2025, when she was the sole candidate for the seat reserved for women.

“If she already has such a hard time getting elected in Europe, how could she convince Africans and South Americans?” asked Erik Thorstvedt, a former goalkeeper for the Norwegian national team turned commentator.

World.title: Clinton compares Trump’s White House to former Iraqi dictator Saddam’s palaces
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has compared President Donald Trump’s White House renovations to former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s palaces, remembering her own travels to Baghdad after his ouster.

Clinton, speaking on journalist Kara Swisher’s podcast, compared Trump’s White House decor to meetings she attended in Saddam Hussein’s former palaces while serving as a US senator.

“They were quite reminiscent of what we are seeing in our own White House,” she said.

Her remarks come amid wider criticism of Trump’s renovations and architectural decisions, such as heavy gold décor within the Oval Office, plans for a new White House ballroom, and a projected triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Clinton called the improvements “tacky” and suggested that the president was focusing too much on cosmetic initiatives when the US confronts substantial foreign policy, economic, and technological issues.

She also criticized the process around Trump’s planned ballroom, stating that she was not opposed to the White House having such a facility but was concerned about the architecture and how the project had been handled.

Given Clinton’s past with Iraq, the connection to Saddam was especially relevant.

She was a member of the United States Senate during the 2003 war that deposed Saddam Hussein and subsequently became Secretary of State under President Barack Obama.

During his reign, Saddam was noted for building multiple extravagant presidential palaces around Iraq, many with elaborate interiors and significant use of marble, chandeliers, and gold-colored décor, despite the country’s international sanctions and economic difficulty.

Trump has defended his White House restoration plans, which are part of a larger push to renovate and enhance Washington’s important federal buildings and sites.

Clinton’s parallel brings Iraq and one of Saddam’s most recognizable emblems into the increasingly heated political argument over Trump’s White House moves.

World.title: 'Anti-people': Congress vows to oppose FCRA Bill, Venugopal accuses Centre of targeting NGOs
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday stepped up its opposition to the proposed Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, with AICC general secretary KC Venugopal warning that the party and other opposition parties would strongly protest if the legislation is introduced in Parliament.

Venugopal, speaking to reporters in Alappuzha, alleged that the proposed legislation was aimed at targeting minorities and NGOs and said the Opposition would not allow it to be passed.

"If the Central Government thinks they can cook up and introduce the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill within these two or three days, they should keep that wish to themselves," Venugopal said.

He described the proposed legislation as "unconstitutional and anti-people", adding, "We will not allow such an anti-people and unconstitutional bill to be passed."

The FCRA Amendment Bill, which seeks to amend the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, is expected to be taken up in the final week of the Monsoon Session.

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge also said on Saturday that the party would oppose the measure and that its strategy would be discussed at a meeting of Opposition floor leaders on Monday.

Congress raises questions over student protests, Amit Shah

Venugopal also sought answers from Union home minister Amit Shah over the alleged use of force against students protesting in Delhi against irregularities in competitive examinations.





He asked Shah to respond to allegations concerning the use of pellet guns, lathi charges and tear gas during the protests, and questioned his absence from Parliament.

"When students in India ask the crucial question of who ordered the use of pellet guns, lathi charges and tear gas shells against them to suppress their protest, Amit Shah would not come forward to answer it," Venugopal said.

His remarks came amid a broader opposition campaign over the July 20 protests in Delhi, during which student protesters have alleged excessive use of force.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had also raised the issue during an interaction with protesters earlier.

Opposition prepares for key Bills in Parliament

The Congress' opposition to the FCRA Bill comes ahead of the final three days of the Monsoon Session, with the party issuing a whip asking its MPs to remain present in both Houses on August 10, 11 and 12.

Congress chief whip in the Rajya Sabha Jairam Ramesh said the party wanted to ensure that "history should not repeat itself", recalling the suspension of 146 Opposition MPs during the 2023 Winter Session.

Ramesh said that after the suspensions, several major pieces of legislation, including the three new criminal laws, were passed with minimal Opposition presence.

The Congress has also asked its INDIA bloc allies to ensure their MPs remain present during the final days of the session.

The FCRA Bill requires a simple majority for passage, while any Constitution amendment bill on delimitation would require a two-thirds majority, according to the background information provided by the party.

Venugopal questions FCRA restrictions, delimitation proposal

Venugopal also questioned the proposed restrictions on organisations receiving foreign contributions and raised the issue of foreign funding received by organisations associated with the RSS.

"If you have the courage, try controlling the RSS," he said.

He also opposed the proposed delimitation legislation, arguing that it could disadvantage states that had successfully implemented population-control measures.

"This bill effectively chokes states that have successfully implemented population control," Venugopal said, referring to the proposed legislation.

On the FCRA Bill, several Opposition parties have expressed concerns. NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule has called for the legislation to either be withdrawn or referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, while DMK president MK Stalin has also urged the Centre to withdraw it.

World.title: What happens after you apply for an organ transplant?
World.content:
For a patient facing end-stage organ failure, being told that a transplant may be required is only the beginning. The journey from a hospital referral to an actual transplant involves medical evaluation, registration, documentation, waitlist management, organ matching, allocation and, eventually, surgery and long-term follow-up.

In India, the process is coordinated through a network involving the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation (NOTTO), regional and state-level bodies, registered transplant hospitals and transplant coordinators.

The scale of that system has changed sharply. In a February 2026 release, the Press Information Bureau said India recorded nearly 20,000 organ transplants in 2025, compared with fewer than 5,000 in 2013.

More than 1,200 families donated the organs of loved ones after death in 2025, the release said.

Yet the numbers tell only part of the story. Behind every transplant is a sequence that begins long before the surgeon enters the operating theatre â and, for the recipient, often long before an organ is ever offered. Nottoâs says patients are evaluated by a multidisciplinary team, registered through a transplant centre, verified by the relevant allocation body and, once cleared, placed on the appropriate waiting list.





The process starts at the transplant centre

A patient with advanced organ failure is first referred to a licensed transplant centre. Doctors assess the underlying disease, the extent of organ damage and whether transplantation is medically appropriate.

Not every patient with end-stage organ failure will necessarily be fit for transplantation.

Talking about the initial evaluation before transplantation, Dr Manoj Gupta, senior director and HOD, liver transplant, Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital, said, âIt typically includes a review of the patientâs medical history, physical examination, blood and tissue tests, imaging, assessment of organ function, infection screening and evaluation of any underlying conditions.

Eligibility is determined by several factors, including the patientâs overall health, the extent of organ failure, surgical suitability, the likelihood of benefiting from transplantation and the ability to adhere to the post-transplant treatment regimen.

â

However, other factors can also determine eligibility. Dr Goutham Kumar, consultant, HPB & liver transplant services, SPARSH Hospital, added that eligibility also depends on the âabsence of absolute contraindications, including active systemic infections, untreated malignancies, severe substance abuse or irreversible co-morbidities.â

The hospital and transplant coordinator then compile the information required for registration.

Once the application is accepted, the patient's details enter the relevant transplant registry and waiting list. The waiting period can range from the same day to several years.

What being on the waiting list actually means

Being on a transplant waiting list is not simply being in a queue. Notto says patients are listed according to medical criteria, with regular and urgent categories, while priority varies by organ.

For kidney transplants, time on regular dialysis is among the factors considered; other organs follow different criteria.

Dr Kumar explains how these organ-specific criteria work in practice, âLiver allocation often uses the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score, while heart allocations prioritize patients on mechanical support. Pediatric patients and high-urgency acute cases frequently receive priority.â

Nottoâs manual also provides for urgent or âPriority Oneâ categories for patients meeting organ-specific requirements. Such cases may be reviewed by an expert committee before priority is granted, with hospitals required to provide regular clinical updates.

Registration does not freeze a patientâs status. Their medical condition continues to be monitored and records updated. Depending on their health, a patient may remain active, be made inactive or become medically unfit for transplantation.

Live Kidneys lead Indiaâs transplant numbers

When a donor organ becomes available

The next turn in the journey comes when an organ becomes available. It may come from a living donor, commonly a kidney or part of a liver, or from a deceased donor after certified brain-stem death. At that point, Organ India says, âthe transplant coordinator of the hospital will counsel the family and give them the option of donating organs and tissues.â

The next of kin must consent before retrieval. That makes a donor pledge only at the beginning of the conversation.

Organ India puts it plainly: âIn India it's more important to talk to your family about your decision than it is to pledge your organs and get a donor card.â

Once a donor organ is identified, a rapid, highly coordinated race against time begins. Blood group compatibility and cross-matching are verified between the donor and potential recipient, while the organ is assessed for suitability.

Dr Kumar explains, âA surgical retrieval team harvests the organ and preservation solution is administered.

Transport logisticsâoften utilising dedicated âgreen corridorsâ or air transportâare activated to move the organ immediately.â

The recipient is called to the hospital, re-evaluated and prepared for surgery, with the surgical team ready to proceed as soon as the donor organ arrives.

From brain-stem death to retrieval

A deceased donor is medically maintained while permissions and retrieval arrangements are completed, helping preserve viable organs until they can be recovered.

Once retrieved, however, the clock begins to run: each organ has a limited preservation window.

4â6 hours for heart and lungs, 6â10 hours for intestine, 12â15 hours for liver, 12â24 hours for pancreas and 24â48 hours for kidneys

Cost remains another major barrier to transplantation in India. Dr Kumar said the âinitial surgical costs range from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 35 lakh depending on the organ (kidney vs. liver/heart) and hospital sector (public vs. private).â But the financial burden does not end with the operation. Lifelong immunosuppressants, anti-rejection treatment and âregular diagnostic monitoring add Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 monthly.

â

That narrow window makes allocation a tightly coordinated process. Organs are assessed, potential recipients identified and transport arranged.

India's transplant numbers are rising

The national system has expanded significantly over the past decade.

The ministry said more than 1,200 families came forward to donate the organs of loved ones after death in 2025.

"More than 4.8 lakh citizens have registered to donate organs and tissues after death through a Aadhaar based verification system, since 17th September 2023," the PIB release said.

The release also said India had developed expertise in complex heart, lung and pancreas transplants and claimed the country "leads the world in hands transplants and performs a greater number of hand transplants than any other country."

The government said the increase reflected improvements in deceased donation, transplant coordination and national organ sharing.

The gap between demand and supply remains

Even after surgery, the process continues. Recipients need lifelong follow-up and immunosuppressive medication, which can also carry long-term risks.

Dr Jagriti Yadav, medical director â lab operations, Cryoviva Life Sciences, said, âThe major long-term risks include acute or chronic graft rejection, opportunistic infections, cardiovascular complications, kidney toxicity, and metabolic side effects related to immunosuppressive medicines.â

The increase in transplant numbers has not eliminated the shortage of organs.

How Indiaâs transplant numbers have surged

A 2024 article published in the National Library of Medicine's PubMed Central noted that India was performing around 17,000-18,000 solid organ transplants a year, making it the world's third-largest transplant country by volume after the United States and China, while transplant rates per million population remained lower than in several high-income countries.

Organ India's data and awareness material has similarly highlighted the disparity between the number of patients requiring organs and the number of deceased donors available. The organisation has estimated that India has a large pool of potential brain-stem-death donors but a much smaller number of actual deceased donors.

For a patient on a waiting list, that gap translates into uncertainty: being medically eligible and registered does not guarantee that a suitable organ will become available in time.

Delhi remains one of the country's major transplant centres.

The Delhi government's organ-donation portal provides information on registered hospitals and transplant services and operates under the Health & Family Welfare Department and the State Appropriate Authority. The department's published information lists registered facilities for kidney, liver, heart, lung and pancreas transplantation, as well as eye and cornea services.

Foreign recipients are also part of the system

Indiaâs transplant system also treats foreign nationals, subject to additional safeguards. Government guidance says an Indian living donor may donate to a foreign recipient only if they are near relatives; donors must be at least 18, with medical-visa and registration requirements applicable to both parties.

Data shows organ transplants for foreign recipients in India

In 2023, India recorded 18,378 transplants and 18,336 individual recipients, including 1,851 foreign nationals, according to Notto data reported in 2024.

Delhi recorded the highest number involving foreign recipients at 1,445, followed by Rajasthan at 116 and West Bengal at 88. Only nine involved unrelated deceased-donor organs.

For a transplant recipient, perhaps the least visible part of the process is the period between registration and an organ offer.

During this period, the patient's condition can change. Tests may have to be repeated, treatment may need adjustment and the transplant centre may update the patient's status on the registry.

The patient therefore remains under the care of the transplant team while the allocation system searches for a medically suitable organ.

Notto says special requests do not guarantee an immediate organ or override the established rules for matching and allocation.

The next stage is a more connected transplant system

Indiaâs transplant system is becoming more digitally connected, with national coordination and data-sharing expanding alongside transplant numbers.

Aadhaar-verified donation registrations crossed 4.8 lakh, while nearly 20,000 transplants were recorded in 2025.

The next challenge is ensuring potential donors are identified, families counselled and organs retrieved, transported and allocated efficiently. For recipients, that means staying medically fit, updating the transplant centre and following clinical advice.

World.title: ‘Stones, shoes thrown at my car’: Mamata faces protest during visit to kin of dead TMC worker
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister

on Sunday alleged that her car was pelted with stones after protesters intercepted her convoy while she was visiting the family of deceased

worker Birju Keot in North 24 Parganas.

According to Mamata, protesters raised "thief" slogans and threw water bottles and footwear.

World.title: Three incidents that shaped Kailash Satyarthi’s life and work
World.content:
Shoeshine boy outside school

In 1959, on his first day to school as a five-and-a-half-year-old in Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh,

(he was Sharma then) spotted a shoeshine boy sitting quietly outside the gate.

Curious and confused, he asked a teacher, âWhy is a child sitting outside the school?â He was told that it is not uncommon for poor kids to work.

Satyarthi was not satisfied. Every day, he would see the boy, roughly his own age, sit there with his father until one day he gathered courage and asked his father why his son was not at school. The man spoke with a deep hopelessness, recalls Satyarthi. He said, âBabu, school jaane ke liye aap log to hain.

Hum to yehi kaam karne ke liye paida hote hain (There are people like you who go to school. We are born to do this kind of work).

â

As a child, Satyarthi felt there was something wrong in this, but he couldnât understand what. âI was taught that God has made us all equal. Why this inequality, I wondered,â he recalls.

This encounter gave him a different perspective on life at a very early age.

Friend who dropped out

Satyarthi was just 11 when he found that his best friend and some other students had stopped attending classes in the new session.





He was told that such dropouts happened because the poor could not afford even nominal fees and textbooks.

Satyarthi wanted to do something. He got an idea and shared it with a friend. âMy father had given me some money to buy sweets after I had cleared the examination. We went to a vegetable vendor, gave him the money and rented his pushcart,â he says.

They went around the neighbourhood, urging people to donate the used books of their children, so that the needy could use them.

âWithin a few hours, the cart was full and we had to take a second turn. We collected 2,300 books that day,â he remembers.

Soon, another idea â a permanent book bank for needy kids â was born, in which even headmasters and bookstore owners joined in. About 10,000 books were collected.

Decades later, when Satyarthi went to Vidisha after winning the Nobel in 2014, he heard someone call out his name during an open-jeep parade.

âThe gentleman said, âI am a retired headmaster. I had almost quit my studies due to lack of money. But your book bank initiative allowed me to continueâ,â Satyarthi recalls.

It was quite a moment for both.

Wasal Khan and Sabo

At 27, Satyarthi had started a journal, âSangharsh Jaari Rahegaâ, which spoke up for the marginalised and oppressed. The office was near Mandi House in central Delhi. One day, a sickly person in a lungi knocked on his door and passed out after a few words.

He was carrying a copy of the magazine.

When he regained consciousness, the man started whimpering, âBabuji, please save my daughter.â His name was Wasal Khan. Over the next few minutes, he poured out his life story. His wife and he were lured away from a village in Aligarh district, taken to Punjabâs Sirhind, where they had been enslaved in a brick kiln for 17 years. They worked without pay, given just food and used clothes to wear.

âHe said the owners were planning to sell Sabo, his 15-year-old daughter, to brothel agents from Delhi,â says Satyarthi.

Wasal had escaped on the back of a truck and reached Chandigarh, where a magazine subscriber had given him an old copy and asked to go to Delhi for help.

Satyarthi was faced with a tough choice: write an article or take action. He opted for the latter. He organised a truck and, on reaching the spot, he and his friends from Punjab â one of them had a camera â boldly told the lone gun-wielding chowkidar that they were journalists from Delhi.

The watchman ran away. âWe were about to leave with 36 men, women, and children when a police jeep arrived with the owners. They started slapping us and forcing the labourers to get down from the truck,â Satyarthi recalls.

The truck driver had run away. Satyarthi and his friends too had to flee. âOur slippers were lost, our clothes torn.â

Somehow they reached Chandigarh and then Delhi. âThey had taken away the camera. But two reels, which vividly captured the labourers on camera, were with us.

We had good evidence,â he says. Satyarthi approached Swami Agnivesh and, through him, renowned lawyer Gobinda Mukhoty, who filed a habeas corpus petition in Delhi high court. Since nobody knew the name of the brick kiln owners, a notice was sent to Punjab Police and the state.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Eventually, Wasal Khan, Sabo and the rest were produced in court and freed.

The children, who had grown up inside the brick kiln, had no idea of life outside.

âAs we walked from the high court towards our office, they were jumping like frogs released from a bucket, oblivious to the traffic. That day, I realised what true freedom really meant. I could feel God in their joy. We also knew this was the field where we have to work. Over the decades, our organisation, Bachpan Bachao Andolan, has rescued over 1,40,000 men, women and children,â he says.

Compassion and

AI ethics

This is the age of AI and Satyarthi believes that technology should factor in compassion (karuna), which he defines as âa force born from feeling the suffering of others and drives us to take action.â Satyarthi feels that AI technology must be governed by a sense of responsibility during its designing, development and deployment. âAI should have a moral compass. It cannot just be profit-hungry,â he says.

World.title: Watch: Trainer aircraft crashes near Baramati airstrip in Maharashtra
World.content:
Visuals from the crash site showed the aircraft's wreckage, with local villagers and emergency responders gathering at the spot.

What happened during the exercise?

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A trainer aircraft operated by private aviation academy Carver Aviation veered off the runway during a training exercise at the Baramati airstrip in Maharashtra's Pune district on Sunday, police said.The incident occurred around 12.30 pm when the aircraft, carrying a pilot and a cadet, was conducting a circuit and landing emergencies exercise, officials said. No casualties were reported, as reported by news agency PTI.The aircraft, identified as VT-SEX, was unable to come to a complete stop at the designated point while taxiing on the runway. It continued about 20 feet beyond the runway before entering a grassy area, police said.Visuals from the crash site showed the aircraft's wreckage, with local villagers and emergency responders gathering at the spot.According to a senior police official, the aircraft initially lined up at the threshold of Runway 29 and carried out a rejected take-off. It was then positioned at the threshold of Runway 11, where another rejected take-off was conducted."During the course of this exercise, the aircraft could not be brought to a complete stop on the runway and continued beyond the threshold of the runway.Subsequently, it veered off the extended paved surface to the right side beyond the Runway 29 threshold. No injuries have been reported," the official said, as quoted by PTI.The aircraft sustained a runway excursion during the training exercise, while further details about the incident were awaited.The incident comes months after a fatal aircraft crash near the same airstrip. On January 28, a Learjet 45 operated by VSR crashed while attempting an emergency landing near Baramati. Maharashtra's then deputy chief minister and NCP chief Ajit Pawar and four others on board were killed in the crash.Earlier, on May 13, another trainer aircraft operated by a private company made a crash landing near the Baramati airstrip after developing a technical snag. However, no casualties were reported in that incident.

World.title: AI can help bridge India's healthcare gap: Report
World.content:
AI is not intended to replace doctors but to multiply specialist capacity by assisting in diagnosis

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's healthcare system is coming under growing pressure from an ageing population, rising burden of chronic diseases and shortages of doctors, nurses and hospital beds, according to a knowledge paper released by Union Health Minister J P Nadda on Saturday. The report says artificial intelligence (AI) can help bridge this widening gap by extending specialist expertise, improving diagnosis and expanding access to quality healthcare, particularly in smaller hospitals and underserved areas.Nadda released the knowledge paper, "AI in MedTech: Revolutionizing Healthcare Through Artificial Intelligence," at the 9th edition of India Medical Device 2026, organised by the Department of Pharmaceuticals in association with FICCI.The report estimates India's population at 1.47 billion in 2026 and says more than 65% of deaths are now due to non-communicable diseases such as heart disease, diabetes and cancer. It projects the population aged 60 years and above to cross 230 million by 2036, further increasing demand for long-term healthcare.Despite expansion in healthcare infrastructure and medical education, shortages persist. India has 9.6 doctors per 10,000 population, compared with the global average of 18.3.It has 27.2 nursing personnel per 10,000 against 40.5 globally, 15.9 hospital beds per 10,000 compared with 33, and only 4 MRI scanners per million people, against the global average of 19, the report says.According to the report, AI is not intended to replace doctors but to multiply specialist capacity by assisting in diagnosis, clinical decision-making and screening. AI-enabled diagnostics are expected to be the first large-scale application, helping extend specialist expertise to primary and secondary healthcare, improve productivity and reduce inequalities in access to care.The report says India has already built the foundations for AI in healthcare through initiatives such as the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, IndiaAI Mission, SAHI, BODH and the National Medical Devices Policy, 2023. It says the next challenge is to move AI from successful pilot projects to routine clinical use by creating AI-ready health data, a predictable regulatory framework and reimbursement mechanisms for AI-enabled technologies.

World.title: NIA arrests main conspirator in Kerala illegal explosives seizure case; tenth arrest so far
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) has arrested another accused in connection with the seizure of a large consignment of illegal explosives in Keralaâs Malappuram district, taking the total number of arrests in the case to 10, officials said on Sunday.

The accused, identified as Haris TA, was arrested on Saturday from Manjeri in Malappuram. According to the NIA, Haris is a main conspirator and was involved in the illegal procurement of the explosives seized in the case.

The case relates to the seizure of 89,600 explosive sticks and 10,500 shock tubes (NONEL) from a lorry parked at the compound of Farha Hollow Bricks Company on the Chemmad-Thalappara Road in Malappuram on February 7, 2026.

The lorry was intercepted by Kerala Police, who arrested three people linked to the consignment. The NIA said the accused did not have the required licences or permissions to possess or transport the explosives.

The agency subsequently re-registered the case and took over the investigation in April 2026. During the probe, the NIA conducted searches at 19 locations across Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, and recovered digital devices, documents and other material, including gelatin sticks.

World.title: NIA arrests alleged mastermind in illegal explosives case from Kerala’s Manjeri

The National Investigation Agency (NIA) has reportedly arrested T.A. Harris, the alleged mastermind in a case involving the seizure of a huge cache of explosives from Chemmad, near Tirurangadi, in Kerala’s Malappuram district. He was reportedly arrested from Manjeri in the district.

According to the NIA, Mr. Harris played a key role in illegally procuring, stockpiling and distributing the explosives.

The case relates to the seizure of 89,600 gelatin sticks and 10,500 non-electric detonators from a hollow bricks factory compound at Chemmad on February 7, 2026. They were stored in boxes and were found hidden among onion sacks.

The case was handed over to the NIA after the explosives were found to have been brought without a licence. The NIA took over the investigation citing its national security implications.

The NIA conducted searches at around 19 locations across Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, recovering digital devices and documents. Three people were arrested in Karnataka earlier, while the total number of arrests in the case has now reached 10.

The agency had also searched quarry-related locations in Kozhikode, Kasaragod and Kannur districts before arresting the suspects.

World.title: BJD sees potential opportunity to regain political ground
World.content:
The resignation of former Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, following protests led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) last month, may have marked a notable development in national politics. In Odisha, however, it appears to have had implications for the political landscape, with the Biju Janata Dal (BJD), one of the country’s strongest regional parties, viewing it as a potential opportunity to regain political ground.

The party’s renewed confidence appears to stem from ground-level conversations that are critical of the pace of development under the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government, which is now well past its “honeymoon period” in office. Moreover, the Mohan Charan Majhi Government is yet to clearly articulate a narrative around its governance model.

After the setback in the 2024 Assembly election, the regional party has ceded ground to the BJP, losing three Rajya Sabha MPs, while its strength in the Odisha Legislative Assembly has dropped from 51 to 42, following the defection of eight MLAs during the Rajya Sabha elections.

Despite shifts in political dynamics across rural and urban local bodies over the past two years due to defections, the overall impact has been limited for a party that had secured nearly 70% of seats in the three-tier Panchayati Raj Institutions and urban bodies in 2022.

Political observers note that the scale of disintegration within the BJD remains contained, far below the levels anticipated after 24 years of uninterrupted rule and the weight of accumulated anti-incumbency. The exodus, though notable, also falls short of the turbulence seen in other regional parties such as the Trinamool Congress and the Shiv Sena (UBT).

“We were never in doubt about our ability to bounce back as a strong regional force. We knew the new BJP government would eventually struggle under the weight of public expectations. It clearly lacks the capability to sustain the pace of development Odisha witnessed under Naveen Patnaik,” said Debi Prasad Mishra, senior vice president of the BJD.

Mr. Mishra further argued that the State’s economy has “lost direction”. “We inherited a situation where the government struggled to pay salaries. From there, we expanded the State’s annual budget to over ₹2 lakh crore. When we left office, Odisha ranked among the States with fiscal surpluses. Within just a couple of years, borrowing has surged, while progress on major projects has been negligible,” he said.

Veteran journalist Rabi Das echoed similar concerns, stating that the Mohan Charan Majhi government has failed to resolve key crises, allowing them to persist. “One of the most glaring administrative failures is the error-ridden school textbooks affecting lakhs of students. The situation demanded innovative intervention. Instead, the government appears to be buying time by handing the matter over to the Crime Branch after terming it a possible conspiracy,” he said.

The deteriorating law and order situation, particularly crimes against women and instances of mob violence, has further dented the government’s image. In response, the BJP has placed heavy emphasis on investment announcements. However, political observers note that such announcements have had limited impact on public perception, as they do not translate into immediate, lived improvements such as better roads, adequate teachers in schools, or effective delivery of welfare schemes.

Lack of strong alternative

Even as the BJP appears to be losing momentum in the State and, to some extent, at the Centre in the wake of protests such as those at Jantar Mantar in Delhi, the absence of a credible political alternative remains striking. The Congress has failed to revive itself, with frequent leadership changes dampening cadre enthusiasm and internal factionalism persisting. For the BJD, this vacuum has aided a gradual revival.

“Some leaders who joined the BJP have not received the prominence they expected, nor have they been able to bring their cadres along,” Mr. Mishra said.

A key positive for the BJD has been the renewed energy of party supremo Mr. Patnaik. Though advancing in age, he has notably changed his style of engagement with party workers. Earlier interactions were largely limited to formal appearances and clicking photographs with party workers. After his defeat, he has been more accessible at Sankha Bhawan, the party headquarters. In one such meeting, he was seen sitting patiently for over two hours and engaging directly with 42 leaders. The impromptu interaction had surprised many within the party.

Of late, Mr. Patnaik has taken an unambiguous political stance, clearly distancing himself from the BJP. He demanded the resignation of Mr. Pradhan in the wake of the NEET controversy and also came down heavily on the BJP over the change of the colour of the Indian Hockey team’s jersey to saffron. The former Chief Minister has announced that the party will fight the next election under his leadership.

The induction of Sujata Rout, wife of V.K. Pandian, into the BJD has also drawn attention. Party sources say Ms. Rout has shed the baggage of her bureaucratic background and her association with Mr. Pandian, and is now functioning independently. Her low-key and approachable style has helped her connect with district-level leaders and cadres, with some viewing her as a unifying presence within the party.

At the same time, the BJP government’s challenges are seen as stemming from internal and administrative constraints. “Mr. Majhi’s personal image as a clean politician remains intact. However, he is yet to be seen as an effective administrator,” said Mr. Das, adding, “He has neither reshuffled portfolios of underperforming Ministers nor acted decisively against bureaucratic lapses, even in the face of clear governance failures.”

Above all, the regional party has kept itself afloat by regularly presenting its views on important issues in the media, organising public agitations and strengthening its connection with cadres through organisational rejuvenation. The party has kept its fingers crossed for the rural and urban local-body polls scheduled next year.

तेरह दिन हो गए - गृह… — Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) August 9, 2026

Several days have passed since the students protesting at Delhi's Jantar Mantar over alleged paper leaks have called off their agitation, yet not a single word has come from Shah on the action taken by the Delhi Police against them, he said.

"Instead of apologising, Modiji is busy dispensing 'forgiveness'," Mr. Gandhi said.

"Amit Shahji, do not think for a moment that we will stop demanding accountability. Batons and pellets were used against young people on the streets of the capital -- and you did not utter a single word. Sooner or later, you will have to answer for this crime," he said.

Mr. Gandhi asserted that students are the light of the nation, and said he stands with them with all his might.

Both Houses of Parliament remain deadlocked over the opposition's demand that Mr. Shah should make a statement in both Houses on the alleged police brutalities during the students' July 20 protest over the paper-leak issue.

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge slammed Mr. Shah last week for not making a statement in Parliament over the alleged police brutalities on students and said the home minister did not come to the Rajya Sabha despite Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan noting that he should speak in the House.

Earlier in the day, Mr. Gandhi greeted Indian Youth Congress members on the organisation's foundation day.

"India's greatest strength is its youth, and IYC has a proud legacy of giving young Indians a platform -- amplifying their voices, raising their concerns, and fighting for their rights, dreams and aspirations," he said in a post on X.

"Today, when our youth are fighting against a system that is rigged against them, IYC is standing with them every step of the way," he added.

World.title: Pilot disoriented by laser light, flight circles mid-air before landing at Kolkata airport
World.content:
A Malaysia Airlines flight MH-184 from Kuala Lumpur carrying 159 passengers faced problem while approaching the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport for landing as the pilot was distracted by a laser beam, airport sources said on Sunday (August 9, 2026).

The flight was scheduled to land at 11.20 p.m. on Saturday (August 8), but when the aircraft was approximately eight nautical miles from the runway, the pilot reportedly noticed a bright laser beam flashing towards the cockpit from the Madhyamgram-Barasat side, the sources said.

The aircraft finally landed safely at around 11.25 p.m. and all passengers and crew members were reported safe, they said.

The sudden laser flash reportedly affected the pilot's vision, momentarily disorienting him, owing to which the aircraft could not land at the scheduled time and had to circle in the sky before making another approach.

Following the incident, the airline informed the airport authorities. The Kolkata airport authorities also lodged a complaint with the NSCBI Airport Police Station, the sources said.

Kolkata airport director Vikram Singh said the use of laser lights around the airport is prohibited, but such incidents occur occasionally and can potentially affect aircraft operations.

He said the matter has been brought to the notice of police authorities, who are investigating the case.

Pilots have previously complained about laser beams affecting their vision during take-off and landing on earlier occasions as well.

During the 2025 Durga puja festival, laser lights used near the Sreebhumi Sporting Club pandal reportedly caused concern among pilots, following which the laser show was stopped.

Intense laser beams can temporarily impair a pilot's vision, causing distraction and even temporary blindness-like effects, posing a risk during the critical stages of take-off and landing, the sources said.

The Trinamool Congress chairperson stated that bricks were thrown at her vehicle by Bharatiya Janata Party supporters and blamed the police for the attack. Ms. Banerjee was accompanied by Trinamool Congress MPs Kalyan Banerjee and Dola Sen.

Birju Keot, husband of former Trinamool Congress councillor Jenny Sharma Keot, was arrested by Halisahar police on Friday on allegations including extortion and corruption. He was presented before a Barrackpore sub-divisional court, which remanded him to five days of police custody. On Saturday, Birju Keot was taken to a state-run hospital from police lock-up, where he was pronounced dead.

“I condemn this. Even after a custodial death, they are threatening the family of the deceased,” the former Chief Minister said, adding that instead of providing security to her, the police allowed “lumpens from outside” to attack her vehicle. The Trinamool Congress chairperson stated that her party will appeal to the court over the custodial death.

This was the first occasion after the defeat in the West Bengal Assembly polls that the former Chief Minister reached out to a party worker. Trinamool Congress general secretary Abhishek Banerjee was attacked on May 30 when he visited Sonarpur to meet the family members of a deceased Trinamool Congress worker.

After the defeat of the TMC in the recently concluded Assembly polls, there have been several incidents of arrest of party workers and in many cases people have attacked local leaders of the party.
