World.title: For weary Luzon, still no letup in rain due to southwest monsoon
World.content:
The southwest monsoon will still trigger significant rainfall in the next few days, PAGASA warns the public on Sunday afternoon, August 9

MANILA, Philippines – The southwest monsoon or habagat continued to batter much of Luzon on Sunday, August 9, and it appears there may be little to no relief yet going into a new week.

In a briefing past 5 pm on Sunday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said the southwest monsoon will still trigger significant rainfall in Metro Manila and more than 20 provinces in the next 24 hours.

The province of Benguet, located in the Cordillera Administrative Region, may be worst-hit.

Here is PAGASA’s full 72-hour outlook for rainfall from the southwest monsoon, as of 5 pm on Sunday:

Sunday afternoon, August 9, to Monday afternoon, August 10

Intense to torrential rain (above 200 millimeters): Benguet

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Ilocos Sur, La Union, Zambales, Bataan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Pangasinan, Abra, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Ifugao, Nueva Vizcaya, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Bulacan, Batangas, Laguna, Oriental Mindoro, Antique

Monday afternoon, August 10, to Tuesday afternoon, August 11

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): La Union, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan, Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, Abra, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Cavite, Batangas, Oriental Mindoro, Antique

Tuesday afternoon, August 11, to Wednesday afternoon, August 12

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Zambales, Bataan, Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): La Union, Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, Benguet, Tarlac, Pampanga, Nueva Ecija, Cavite, Batangas

For Sunday evening, other areas in Luzon and Western Visayas not mentioned above, as well as the Negros Island Region, may also see scattered rain and thunderstorms due to the southwest monsoon.

The persistent rain has brought floods and landslides to various regions, including Metro Manila.

In Marikina City, the water level of the Marikina River was at 17.2 meters as of 7 pm on Sunday, down from 17.5 meters as of 6 pm but still equivalent to the second alarm. The second alarm means there should be preemptive evacuation for residents of areas which may be affected if the river overflows.

If the Marikina River’s water level reaches 18 meters, the third alarm would be raised and mandatory evacuation would be enforced.

Meanwhile, the water level of the La Mesa Dam in Quezon City was at 79.87 meters as of 7 pm on Sunday, breaching the critical level of 79.50 meters.

The dam would overflow if it reaches the spilling level of 80.15 meters. This could affect communities in Quezon City, Caloocan City, Malabon City, Navotas City, and Valenzuela City, especially those near the Tullahan River.

PAGASA is also monitoring a tropical cyclone outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) — a tropical storm with the international name Peilou.

Peilou was located 2,200 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 pm on Sunday, moving east southeast or away from PAR at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

The tropical storm has maximum sustained winds of 65 km/h and gustiness of up to 80 km/h.

While Peilou is unlikely to enter PAR, it could enhance the southwest monsoon in the coming days, according to PAGASA Weather Specialist Charmagne Varilla.

The weather bureau earlier predicted that two to four tropical cyclones could develop within or enter PAR in August. So far, there have been two: Tropical Depression Luis and Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira).

Another tropical cyclone that was previously being monitored, Typhoon Dolphin, did not enter PAR but enhanced the southwest monsoon.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council on Sunday morning reported that the enhanced southwest monsoon, Luis, and Maymay combined have left at least six people dead and seven others injured. – Rappler.com

World.title: UNIQLO’s new patches champion artisans from Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao
World.content:
The Japanese brand that has become well-loved among Filipinos partners with creative director Wilson Limon to introduce handmade patches by Itneg, Panay Bukidnon, and T'boli artisans

In the Philippines, indigenous weaves and textile patterns aren’t just for aesthetic appeal. They carry centuries’ worth of our ethnic groups’ oral tradition and heritage, and hold stories that run deep into our culture.

These are handwoven by local artisan communities whose craft was passed down from generation to generation — rendering the final products as invaluable pieces of art.

When it comes to these embroidered goods, however, people are often quick to think that they’re only meant to be used on special occasions, or that it’s difficult to get their hands on them. But in one of UNIQLO’s latest collections, artisan communities from Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao handcraft one-of-a-kind patches using traditional embroidery techniques and fabric scraps from Re.UNIQLO, a sustainability program that reuses and recycles old UNIQLO clothing.

In celebration of 70 years of Japan and the Philippines’ friendship, the beloved Japanese fashion brand partnered with Davao-based creative director Wilson Limon to bring these patches to life.

Limon has been working with ethno-linguistic groups for more than 10 years. He was connected with UNIQLO by the National Commission of Culture and the Arts (NCCA) to produce the collaboration under its flagship program, the School of Living Traditions (SLT) — a series of community-based learning centers dedicated to preserving traditional art, oral history, and heritage.

“Working with ethno-linguistic groups, my main mission is to recreate the traditional and the ethnic to make it more relatable to Filipinos,” Limon said during the launch in a mix of English and Filipino.

Each patch is handmade — so no two are exactly the same.

Representing Luzon are the Itneg artisans of Barangay Namarabar in Peñarrubia, Abra, whose embroidery style leans toward designs that are geometric, and take inspiration from nature, animals, and human figures. These patches feature the Kukko pattern, which holds stories of abundance, fertility, productivity, hard work, and agriculture.

LUZON PATCHES. All photos courtesy of UNIQLO Philippines

Over in Visayas, you will find the Panay Bukidnon artisans from Calinog, Iloilo, whose centuries-old embroidery technique is called Panubok, which, according to the National Museum of Iloilo, was once sewn using abaca fibers sourced from the lowlands before being replaced with more widely available threads. The patches they created for UNIQLO take the shape of floral motifs, which are meant to signify nature, oral traditions, and ancestral beliefs.

VISAYAS PATCHES. All photos courtesy of UNIQLO Philippines

Mindanao, meanwhile, is represented by the T’boli artisans of Sitio Lem-ehek, Barangay Poblacion, Lake Sebu from South Cotabato. This community drew inspiration from nature, mountains, and fauna to create their UNIQLO patches — which reflect their daily life and surroundings.

MINDANAO PATCHES. All photos courtesy of UNIQLO Philippines

“Each patch is thoughtfully created by our very own Filipino artisans to reflect the artistry, culture, and heritage of their communities,” Limon explained.

The patches are priced at P300 each, and all profits go back to the specific artisan communities that created them. As a part of the brand’s sustainability efforts, customers can bring their old UNIQLO LifeWear apparel in to have the patches sewn onto them at the brand’s flagship store in Glorietta in Makati City, at the Mall of Asia branch in Pasay City, at the BGC branch in Taguig City, as well as in Cebu and Davao.

NEW LIFE. An old UNIQLO jacket is given new life with these artisan patches. Juno Reyes/Rappler

These patches mark a first for UNIQLO in the Philippines.

While the Japanese apparel brand has focused more on connecting with Filipinos by forging collaborations with brands like Jollibee and Potato Corner, and even schools like ICA, Xavier, and La Salle Green Hills — this is the first time the brand has ever come out with merchandise that champions indigenous culture.

“We want to reach out and partner with local communities,” UNIQLO chief operating officer Geraldine Sia told Rappler. “This is something that we are really aiming for so that we can give back to them.”

The artisan patches are also a way for UNIQLO to dive deeper into Filipino culture, and the best way the brand thought to do that was to trace the country’s roots across the regions by connecting with local artisan communities. – Rappler.com

Patches are limited in quantity and are available until supplies last.

World.title: Accused Thai school shooter had watched violent content online, police say
World.content:
PAYING RESPECTS. A woman pays her respect outside Debsirin Nonthaburi School following a deadly shooting at the school, in Bang Kruai district in Nonthaburi province, on the outskirts of Bangkok, Thailand, August 9, 2026.

Thai police say the boy had used social media to learn how to use a firearm

BANGKOK, Thailand – The Thai teen behind a deadly school shooting outside Bangkok had an air gun confiscated by a teacher last year and had watched violent content online, police said on Sunday, August 9, as the government promised new safety protocols for schools.

As investigations continued into Friday’s rampage, where a 14-year-old boy allegedly shot dead his grandparents at home before killing another six people at his school before turning the gun on himself, police said the boy had used social media to learn how to use a firearm.

“According to witness interviews, the perpetrator had begun showing interest in studying the use of firearms for some time, about one to two years,” Atthapol Anusit, deputy commissioner of the Provincial Police Region 1, told reporters.

Atthapol, who said police had so far interviewed 17 witnesses, said a knife had also been found in the boy’s bag and other evidence found at the crime scenes included a firearm, spent cartridge cases, and a personal computer.

“After examining the PC, it was found that the child had watched social media content involving violence,” the deputy commissioner said, but added there was no evidence yet that he had practiced shooting.

He said that last year a teacher had confiscated a BB gun, a type of air gun, that the boy took to school. The boy had lived with his grandparents for 12 years after his parents had separated, Atthapol said.

The Ministry of Education said it would develop new safety protocols over the next three months, including mental health screenings and a system to refer at-risk people to specialists, drills for emergency response plans, a drive to stamp out bullying and better detection to stop items from being taken into schools.

Along with those who died, more than 20 people were injured in Thailand’s worst mass shooting since 2022, which has reignited debate over firearms control in Southeast Asia’s largest gun-owning nation. – Rappler.com

World.title: Meet the Ilonggo band that took Philippine metal to Germany
World.content:
THE FREAK SHOW. Sentient Void performs as the country’s only representative at the Wacken Metal Battle 2026 Final, a showdown of competing bands from 31 different countries.

From small gigs across Panay to representing the Philippines in Germany, Sentient Void brings its heavy metal to the Wacken Metal Battle

Sentient Void is used to playing for crowds of 20 to 50 people at small venues around Panay. On July 30, the Ilonggo band took that experience to Wacken, Germany, and represented the Philippines at the 2026 Wacken Metal Battle Final after winning the local leg of the competition.

The band is composed of vocalist Richard Arengo, guitarist and vocalist Kevin Sombero, bassist Stephen Benedicto, guitarists Dr. Alfred Gregore and Atty. John Paul Ernest “Jope” Ravena, and drummer Lemuel Anthony Gadong. Five members are from Iloilo, while Gadong is from Roxas City, Capiz.

Performing in Wacken is a dream that started years before the band existed.

From internet cafés to Germany

As high school friends, Arengo and Sombero spent time at internet cafés after school, watching livestreams of bands performing at the biggest metal festival in the world — Wacken Open Air in Germany.

“[We were] just two best friends in high school who couldn’t sing and play guitar properly. Two kids who would go to internet cafes after school to watch live performances of our favorite bands playing at Wacken and hoping that someday we could go there and enjoy the festival,” Arengo said.

Arengo and Sombero eventually formed Sentient Void in 2022 with four other musicians from Iloilo and Capiz. The six members bonded over their shared interest in heavy and dark music, drawing influences from bands such as Meshuggah, Orbit Culture, Emperor, Nails, and Slipknot.

BACKSTAGE. Sentient Void prepares to perform at the Wacken Metal Battle 2026 Final in Germany, on July 30. Photo from Wacken Metal Battle – Philippines Facebook page

Sombero said the band brings its own twist to heavy metal, combining chainsaw-style Swedish guitar tones, low-end bass, grooving drums, and bellowing vocals.

“Our goal was to create music that would elicit a dreadful yet enjoyable feeling,” Sombero added.

Beyond their sound, Arengo said the band also puts emphasis on its live performances, using theatrics in their sets to make the experience memorable.

“We pride ourselves on making sure that people who watch us, remember exactly who we are and not just another band that played,” said Arengo.

The band’s name was inspired by the “Warp” in Warhammer 40,000, a fictional realm where thoughts and emotions can manifest into physical forms. Sombero said the name fit the atmosphere they wanted for the band and echoed Friedrich Nietzsche’s reflection about gazing into an abyss.

In 2024, the band released its debut EP, Aberrant, which features the singles “Voidwalker” and “The Freak Show.”

The band’s members continue to work regular jobs while making time for rehearsals and performances, playing on weekends as a break from their careers.

The members jokingly call themselves “the 6 angry salarymen,” a reference to their full-time jobs and their shared pursuit of heavy music on the side.

“Considering that all of us have our respective jobs with different working hours and in different places across Panay, proper time management and committing to agreed schedules have always worked for us,” said Ravena.

For Benedicto, the band has become an escape from their 9-to-5 jobs and an outlet for their passion for music and performing.

“It’s not just about the music, but performing as a whole as well. That drives us to create more music, and to perform onstage,” Benedicto said.

The road to Wacken

After establishing itself in the local music scene, Sentient Void entered Wacken Metal Battle Philippines, the local leg of the worldwide competition, spotlighting unsigned metal bands and giving them the chance to perform at Wacken.

Sentient Void went through several qualification rounds before reaching the national finals, where bands representing Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao competed for the chance to represent the country. After the competition in Marikina City, the band emerged as the national champion.

However, preparing for the international competition brought another set of challenges.

As an independent band based in the region, Sentient Void had to work around financial constraints while preparing for the performance.

“Like many independent musicians, we faced significant financial constraints, which limited our preparation. We had to make last-minute upgrades to our equipment just to ensure we could compete at an international level,” Gregore said.

When the band arrived in Germany, it experienced more than just the chance to perform. For Benedicto, being able to experience the festival firsthand was his favorite part of the trip.

“We didn’t expect that one day we’d be in Wacken, let alone to be able to play in it,” said Benedicto.

WACKEN. Sentient Void poses at Wacken Open Air in Germany on its fifth day, August 1. Photo from Wacken Metal Battle – Philippine Facebook page

The members also met bands, promoters, and producers from different parts of the world, including some of their favorite artists.

“We were fortunate enough to connect with different nationalities with just music. Even if everyone didn’t speak the same language, everyone connected through their love of metal,” Benedicto said.

A win built on community

Sentient Void won the Wacken Metal Battle’s first-ever Online Fan Vote Award, along with a €2,500 cash prize.

“We made it to the competition because of the incredible support we received from our families, friends, fans, and the local music community,” Gregore said.

ONLINE FAN VOTE. Sentient Void receives the Online Fan Vote Award at the Wacken Metal Battle 2026 Final in Germany, on August 1. Photo from Wacken Metal Battle – Philippines Facebook page

Arengo said the opportunity to perform in Wacken carried particular significance for the group because all six members come from Iloilo and Capiz.

“It gave us so much joy and pride that we are the first full Ilonggo, born and raised, metal lineup that played at an international event,” Arengo said.

For Arengo, the band’s experience in Wacken has also changed what the members see as possible for Sentient Void.

“This whole band thing we started was only just so we can make the heavy sound we always wanted to do before we retire from playing music altogether. Maybe do this for another 5-7 years and hang our instruments and move on with our lives, because Father Time isn’t slowing down on anybody,” Arengo said.

But after coming into the spotlight, they don’t see themselves stopping anytime soon.

“But since we have garnered national attention from our recent accolades, our paths suddenly changed,” said Arengo. “Hopefully, it opens up many more opportunities for us to play our music and reach as many people as possible.” — Rappler.com

World.title: Gilas Pilipinas faces early China test in Asian Games title defense
World.content:
HERO. Justin Brownlee in action for Gilas Pilipinas against China in the 19th Asian Games.

Adding a new chapter to their rivalry, Gilas Pilipinas and China face each other for the fourth straight Asian Games edition after being bunched in Group C

MANILA, Philippines – Gilas Pilipinas defends its Asian Games crown in Nagoya, Japan, with an early clash with China.

Adding a new chapter to their rivalry, the Philippines and China face each other for the fourth straight edition of the continental showpiece after being bunched in Group C together with Bahrain and Kazakhstan.

Their last Asian Games clash proved nothing short of epic as the Filipinos came back from 20 points down behind Justin Brownlee to stun the Chinese before their home crowd, pulling off a dramatic 77-76 win in the semifinals in 2023.

Buoyed by that morale-boosting victory, the Philippines captured its first Asian Games gold medal in over six decades with a convincing 70-60 triumph over Rondae Hollis-Jefferson and Jordan in the final.

While the upcoming Asian Games is officially scheduled to be held from September 19 to October 4, the men’s basketball competition will run from September 10 to 20.

Gilas Pilipinas opens its campaign against Bahrain on September 11, battles Kazakhstan on September 12, before it tangles with China on September 14, with all games to be played at the Aichi International Arena.

Only the top two from each of the three groups and the two best third-placed teams will advance to the quarterfinals.

Host Japan leads Group A that includes South Korea, Saudi Arabia, and Indonesia, while Iran, Jordan, Chinese Taipei, and Qatar make up Group B.

A retooled squad, distinctly different from the usual team that represents the Philippines in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers, will play for head coach Tim Cone and don the national colors in the Asian Games.

With national mainstays from the Japan B. League (Dwight Ramos and AJ Edu) and Korean Basketball League (Kevin Quiambao and Carl Tamayo) expected to miss the Asian Games due to commitments to their mother clubs, Cone will build a rejigged crew from a pool that features PBA standouts.

Brownlee is tipped to once again show the way for the Nationals, hopefully with Bennie Boatwright by his side, as the Philippines looks to become the first team to retain its Asian Games title since China won back-to-back in 2006 and 2010.

On the verge of being naturalized, Boatwright just needs President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to sign the law granting him Filipino citizenship. – Rappler.com

World.title: What Alex Eala, Manny Pacquiao, and Alyssa Valdez can teach us about community
World.content:
Sports is never just about sports

When Alex Eala won her first WTA Tour title this week, history recorded it as a tennis victory.

For millions of Filipinos, it felt like something much bigger.

Suddenly, people who had never watched tennis were debating her second serve, following the rankings, and talking about Grand Slams. Parents began asking about tennis clinics. Social media filled with debates about her chances at the US Open and whether this was the beginning of a golden age for Philippine tennis.

It wasn’t really tennis that had captured the country’s imagination.

FAN FAVORITE. Alex Eala celebrates with her fellow Filipinos after winning the 2025 WTA 125 Guadalajara Open in Mexico. GDL Open Instagram page

It was Alex.

Her historic victory—the first WTA Tour singles title ever won by a Filipino—didn’t simply produce another champion.

It recruited a new generation of tennis fans.

Watching the country celebrate, I remembered a question I heard many years ago inside a television network.

At the time, I thought it was a question about sports.

I later realized it was a question about media.

Growing up in the Philippines, we didn’t need anyone to explain why sports mattered.

We had Manny Pacquiao.

There’s an old joke that whenever Pacquiao fought, crime rates dropped because even the criminals were watching. Whether the statistics ever supported the joke is beside the point. Like all good kuwentong kutsero (tall tales), it survived because it captured something everyone recognized.

The streets became quieter.

Restaurants wheeled television sets into their dining areas.

Families rearranged their Sundays.

Friends delayed lunch until after the main event.

For a few hours, an entire country experienced the same story at exactly the same time.

These weren’t simply boxing matches. They were moments of national gathering.

ICON. Filipino boxing star Manny Pacquiao raises his arms while looking at fans following a boxing match.

Today, our attention is scattered across YouTube channels, TikTok creators, streaming platforms and algorithmic feeds. We have never had more content.

Yet somehow, we have fewer moments that make us feel part of the same audience.

Watching thousands of Filipinos rally behind Alex Eala this week reminded me why sports continues to occupy a unique place in media.

It doesn’t just entertain.

It gathers.

Looking back

Years ago, I had the privilege of helping build ABS-CBN Sports.

Like many people in sports broadcasting, I thought our mission was obvious: Produce the best sports coverage in the country.

Our then-chairman, Gabby Lopez, constantly challenged us to improve the viewing experience.

Better graphics.

Cleaner statistics.

Faster replays.

During one basketball broadcast, he asked a deceptively simple question.

“Why does it take several seconds for the score to change after every basket?”

Someone explained that every basket had to be entered manually by the graphics operator.

Gabby simply asked, “Can’t technology do it faster?”

The question wasn’t really about basketball.

It was about respecting the audience.

If we could make the experience better for the audience, we should.

But another lesson stayed with me even longer.

Gabby often reminded us that if we wanted sports to grow in the Philippines, we couldn’t treat it merely as another business unit.

We had to treat it as an advocacy.

While he was talking about sports, he was really talking about the audience.

Serve them well.

The business follows.

In another meeting, then-ABS-CBN president Charo Santos-Concio asked a question that changed the way we thought about sports.

“Bakit ko mamahalin ang player ninyo?” (Why would I love your athlete?)

There was an uncomfortable silence.

Our first instinct was to push back.

We’re not showbiz.

Sports isn’t scripted.

Games create their own drama.

But Ma’am Charo wasn’t asking us to manufacture emotion. She was asking us to discover it.

Because audiences don’t fall in love with statistics.

They fall in love with people.

That single question changed everything.

We still covered the games.

But we also started telling the stories behind the uniforms.

The student-athlete balancing classes and training.

The boxer training barefoot because his family couldn’t afford shoes.

The parents making impossible sacrifices.

The doubts.

The disappointments.

The dreams.

Then we noticed something interesting.

People who had never watched volleyball suddenly began following Alyssa Valdez.

PHENOMENAL. Creamline’s Alyssa Valdez in the 2024 PVL All-Filipino Conference finals. PVL

They didn’t become volleyball fans first.

They became Alyssa fans.

Somewhere along the way, they became volleyball fans too.

ICONIC. Alyssa Valdez at the 2023 PVL Second All-Filipino finals. PVL

The athlete became the doorway to the sport.

We eventually realized that growing a sport required more than covering the game.

We had to think beyond the broadcast.

So we developed a framework of four expanding circles around every sport.

At the center was The Game—the competition itself.

Surrounding it was what we called Beyond the Paint—everything that helped audiences appreciate the sport more deeply: coaching, tactics, training, nutrition, equipment and preparation.

The third circle was Beyond the Sport—the athletes’ lives beyond the game.

Their families.

Their struggles.

Their dreams.

Their personalities.

But the outermost circle turned out to be the most important.

The Community.

Fan festivals where children finally met the athletes they admired.

Grassroots clinics where national team players taught kids the fundamentals.

Play Video

School visits.

Outreach programs.

Moments where fans didn’t simply watch together. They belonged together.

We called it “building the sports ecosystem.”

What we were really building were communities.

Perhaps that’s why so many great athletes eventually transcend their sport.

Alex Eala has become proof that Filipinos can compete with the world’s best in tennis.

Hidilyn Diaz made millions of Filipinos care about weightlifting.

LEGEND. Weightlifter Hidilyn Diaz in action for the Philippines in the women’s 58kg division in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games. POC Media Pool

Carlos Yulo transformed gymnastics from an Olympic curiosity into a dinner-table conversation.

GOLDEN BOY. Gymnast Carlos Edriel Yulo of the Philippines celebrates on the podium after winning the floor exercise gold in the Paris Olympics. Reuters

The Azkals introduced millions of Filipinos to football—not because people suddenly became interested in formations and tactics, but because they were captivated by the Younghusbands.

SOCCER. Former Azkals football stars James Younghusband and brother Phil Youghusband (right).

People rarely fall in love with a sport first.

They fall in love with a person.

The story comes before the statistics.

The relationship comes before the fandom.

Sometimes I wonder if we’ve made media more complicated than it needs to be.

Today we speak about “building community” as though social media invented the idea.

It didn’t.

Sports figured it out decades ago.

Long before likes, follows and algorithms, sports understood something fundamental about people.

We don’t simply gather around games.

We gather around each other.

BEST FEELING. The Philippines’ Alexandra Eala celebrates after winning her third-round match against Poland’s Iga Swiatek in the Wimbledon Championships on July 4, 2026. Reuters

Looking back, sports gave me one of my earliest lessons about community.

Technology changes.

Platforms change.

Business models change.

But human beings still look for the same things.

Stories.

Heroes.

Shared experiences.

Reasons to belong.

That’s why the game is only the beginning.

The community is the destination. – Rappler.com

Vince Rodriguez has spent more than 30 years in Philippine media, with experience spanning news, sports, content production, channel management, and marketing. He is currently Head of Network Marketing at TV5. His writing explores the intersection of media, culture, audiences, and the stories that shape how we see the world. He is married to journalist Niña Corpuz and is the father of three children, ages 14, 12, and 8, who continually challenge—and reshape—his understanding of the future of media.
