World.title: Take-home assessments to be banned in radical HSC overhaul
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWHSC Take-home assessments to be banned in radical HSC overhaul Christopher Harris August 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A radical overhaul of the Higher School Certificate would bar year 12 students from completing unsupervised take-home assignments as Education Minister Prue Car vows to safeguard the integrity of the NSW education system from the threat of AI. The move comes after it was revealed the use of artificial intelligence was driving a sustained and elevated rate of misconduct in year 12 assessments, with more than 1000 cases of cheating in HSC school-based tasks recorded in 2025. NSW Education Minister Prue Car has asked NESA for a moratorium on take-home HSC assessment tasks due to the threat of AI. Dion Georgopoulos Car has written to the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) to ask for a “moratorium” on take-home assessment tasks. It is subject to advice from NESA, but is expected to start as soon as next term when current year 11 students begin their year 12 studies. “The value of the HSC as a highly trusted credential depends on it accurately reflecting student knowledge, ability, and understanding. That confidence will be undermined if assessment outputs can be produced without students performing the intellectual work that the course requires,” Car said in a letter to NESA chair, Professor Peter Shergold, last month.



Removing take-home assessment would be an interim measure and will form part of a broader review on the impact of AI on student learning, amid concerns that students are outsourcing the most basic of tasks to AI. The removal of take-home tasks makes NSW the first jurisdiction in Australia to do so. Car said the purpose of schooling was to build knowledge, judgment, resilience and critical thinking over time, but that faced being undermined if students were using AI. “The settings for the HSC have an impact on learning throughout high school. Where teachers and students know they face an offline environment in final exams, that will likely impact they way they are prepared for those exams,” she said. “If you want to run a marathon, you don’t practise on a computer. You don’t build grey matter by getting a computer to do the thinking for you.”



While educational analysts have acknowledged the capacity of AI to enhance learning, a report drawing on surveys of 3400 NSW teachers revealed this year students were using it to complete assignments as well as outsourcing thinking to AI to help them perform even low-stakes activities like class discussions. Car said it was better to put sensible safeguards in place as policymakers came to fully understand AI’s long-term impact on student learning. “We need to act now as the evidence continues to emerge,” she said.



Final exams account for 50 per cent of a student’s HSC mark, while school-based tasks comprise the remaining half. Until now, they comprise a mix of both in-class (such as in-class tests and speeches) and take-home assessment. When the interim measures are introduced, it is expected there will be some exceptions for subjects with major projects, such as art and technology. The HSC proposal is set to start at the beginning of next term. Dominic Lorrimer Some principals report moving away from take-home tasks in response to AI, while most have updated their assessment policies to warn students they must be able to prove work done outside the classroom and submitted for assessment is their own. “Teachers will continue to use standard monitoring, draft checkpoints, and oral reflections (viva voce) to ensure all submitted work genuinely reflects a student’s own learning and authentic understanding,” Oakhill College in Sydney’s northwest informed parents earlier this year.



All Saints College in Maitland warns students that teachers “may use a viva voce, examine the digital footprint of the document, ask for research notes and drafts as part of the investigation to discover the authenticity and originality of student work”. Of the 1270 total cases of cheating in HSC assessment tasks recorded last year, the majority of misconduct cases related to take-home tasks. Related Article Education AI poses ‘urgent threat’ to student learning and the HSC The HSC shake-up comes as higher education analysts warn entry to universities in Sydney has become increasingly competitive due to funding changes. Next year will be worse, they say. Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said since the advent of widespread generative AI in 2022, the technology must be part of the education landscape, citing its ability to “personalise education”.



This year, Norway moved to implement a near total ban on primary school students using AI because of the risk pupils could skip important steps in their education. A similar push is under way in Australia. Last week, the Heads Up Alliance – an organisation that spearheaded the push to ban adolescents from using social media – launched a new campaign to stem the widespread use of tablets and laptops in Australian schools. A key principle of their campaign is that “Generative AI has no place in school learning”. “It turns out that Australia’s Digital Education Revolution of 2008 was, in effect, a vast experiment on our children. Today, the results of that experiment have become impossible to ignore,” founder Dany Elachi said. World.title: Paul Kelly, Snoop Dogg and you: A new kind of karaoke hits Melbourne
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Paul Kelly, Snoop Dogg and you: A new kind of karaoke hits Melbourne Carolyn Webb August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Inside one of Melbourne’s best-loved live music venues, a group of five people took a free and easy approach to singing Bruno Mars’ pop song 24K Magic at the weekend. They rapped, howled and laughed through the gently funky tune, making up lyrics while miraculously keeping up with the beat. Rocking good time: Five friends rapped and howled their way through a Bruno Mars song at Rockeoke. Martin Philbey In response, the crowd at St Kilda’s Esplanade Hotel on Saturday danced and cheered along, and took snaps with their phones. This is Rockeoke – a weekly karaoke session where people of all singing abilities get to live out their music dreams on stage with the backing of a live band.



By the end of the night, participants can brag they’ve performed at the Espy, where music royalty such as Paul Kelly, Snoop Dogg and AC/DC have also played. Singers, who can put their names down either online or at the basement bar on the night, have 65 songs to choose from, including INXS’s Never Tear Us Apart, Wonderwall by Oasis, and Billie Eilish’s Ocean Eyes. Dream gig: Niamh Troy (left) and Avalon Johnstone sang in the Espy basement bar, backed by a professional band. Martin Philbey If you request an off-list song such as Enter Sandman by Metallica the band is willing to give it a go, keyboard player Thomas Byrne said. On Saturday, one group took the “where do we go now?” line in Guns N’ Roses’ Sweet Child O’ Mine literally, missing lyrics and sometimes the melody, but they were laughing.



Guitarist Simon Paparo said “it’s not about singing perfectly”, but the band will guide singers towards a chorus or ending. Another performer, Eadiella, of Hampton, who goes by one name, smashed Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black out of the park, giving a tune and word-perfect rendition of the pop classic. Nailed it: Singer Eadiella belts out Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black. Martin Philbey Eadiella channelled Winehouse’s growling voice and threw herself into the song’s dramatic tale of romance gone wrong while the crowd swayed and sang along as if this were the Glastonbury Festival in England. Espy venue manager Dan Lovett said the idea for Rockeoke came after a Gaelic football club held its post-finals Mad Monday party at the Espy, and its karaoke session was a huge hit.



“It went off,” Lovett said. He said the event blended karaoke with the Espy’s strength – live rock music. About 36 singers now sign up to Rockeoke each week. The event is free and runs from 11pm for three hours each Saturday. “Each week the crowd’s getting bigger,” Lovett said. “You never know, in a few months it might be on the [Espy’s] main stage, in the Gershwin Room.”



People aged from 18 to 80 have sung in Rockeoke since it began, he said. One week, an 80-year-old sang the 1968 psychedelic rock song Fire by obscure British band The Crazy World of Arthur Brown – famous for the line “I am the god of hellfire!” Lovett said the nice thing about karaoke and Rockeoke is that “even if it’s bad, it’s good. As long as you get up there and have a crack, you’re going to have a great time.”

World.title: After Elizabeth, Redeemer Baptist Church was banned from taking in children of the state. Instead, it opened a school
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPrivate schools After Elizabeth, Redeemer Baptist Church was banned from taking in children of the state. Instead, it opened a school Emily Kowal August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s gravel from Redeemer Baptist School’s property burrowed deep inside Elizabeth Bradbury’s knee. The 62-year-old only has to touch the gnarled skin to be transported back to the 1970s and ’80s, when at 15, screaming for her mum during a planned visit, as she was pulled away by male members of Redeemer Baptist Church. “I got dragged by my hair because I fought them off,” she said. When she stumbled, she fell into the gravel driveway. Elizabeth Bradbury at the Australian Botanic Gardens in Mt Annan. Elizabeth Bradbury was one of the first children to be placed into the care of Redeemer Baptist Church. Sitthixay Ditthavong In 1976, when Bradbury was 11, she was placed into the care of elders at Redeemer Baptist Church by the Youth and Community Services officers with the consent of her mother, who surrendered her care to Redeemer.



By the time Bradbury left in 1981, aged 16 and in the middle of her HSC year, the department of youth and community services banned Redeemer Baptist Community from caring for children in need of substitute care. But Redeemer did not stop caring for children. Instead, the church became a school, operating at first as an unregistered community school, before being accredited by the Department of Education in 1983. On Monday, the school will be at the centre of a NSW Parliamentary inquiry, after a slew of “disturbing” allegations unveiled by this masthead and 60 Minutes into the academically acclaimed private school. Redeemer Baptist School will face a parliamentary inquiry on Monday. Wolter Peeters The school in North Parramatta is accused of subjecting its students to extreme control, dictating their underwear colour and university choices, and not paying its teachers wages.



The school, which has an extensive property portfolio, had raked in tens of millions in government funding in the past decade – all while its teachers go unpaid, relying on a small stipend and, for some, Centrelink benefits. Since the school began, at least 50 children have lived in the homes of church elders Jonathan Cannon and Russell Bailey. A photo of Elizabeth Bradbury taken at around 15 years old. She was suffering during this time and desperately wished to leave the church. But Bradbury wants the world to know that these allegations are not new. She says Redeemer’s alleged control of children started long before its current leaders, Cannon and Bailey were in power. The church was founded by Noel Cannon, Jonathan’s father and a former science head at The King’s School, who was an esteemed figure within the Castle Hill and Parramatta community. When he died in 2012, his life was described in parliament as one of “uncompromising love”.



Bradbury remembers a much darker picture. Despite her mother giving up her care, both wanted to continue contact. She said she was only allowed to see her mother once or twice a year. Placed inside the Baileys home – alongside a teenage Russell Bailey, now the school’s headmaster – she described a life of strict surveillance and control. She was not allowed to use tampons. The wife of a senior church elder once checked under her skirt to make sure. “I was standing on something, and she ran her hands up and down my legs. She realised I was shaving my legs,” she said. She was reprimanded.“When I got my period, [she] basically said if you use tampons, you’re no longer a virgin,” Bradbury said. At the time, Bradbury recalls, there were a number of foster children living inside Redeemer. One of them was a girl who had schizophrenia. Bradbury remembers watching elders hold the girl down while they performed what she described as an exorcism. “She was resisting, fighting them off, and they just held her down while they prayed for her,” Bradbury recalled. “She was psychotic, and I watched that. I witnessed that.“ Redeemer Baptist School leaders, principal Jonathan Cannon and headmaster Russell Bailey.



Any defiance was dealt with by Noel Cannon. At the time, church members attended nearby Castle Hill High School, allowing them to make friends outside the Redeemer community. Bradbury recalls wanting to leave the church in her senior years. Letters, written during that time and kept by Bradbury, show her pleading with an old friend to help her escape. Labelled “rebellious” because she wanted to return to her mother and study nursing, Bradbury was taken upstairs to Noel’s office. As Bradbury lay crying on the floor, Noel loomed over her. “He pulled me up by my hair and I ended up with my head between his legs, and I said to him, ‘You don’t want to do this’,” she said. He let her go, she said. When Bradbury heard Cannon being praised in parliament, she vomited. “I had my head between that man’s legs,” she said. Sam Gibson has his own memories inside Noel Cannon’s office. Adopted into the church in 1974, Gibson spent much of his childhood terrified of Noel Cannon. For years, he was moved between homes, living with different families, among overseas students and “stragglers”.



He estimates he was caned by Noel Cannon upwards of 50 times. Cannon’s son, a then teenage Jonathan Cannon, would often be in the room, watching on. “If I did something wrong or looked at Jon Cannon the wrong way … I was marched up to his dad and his dad put me over the pew, giving me three of the best,” he said. When Gibson was sexually assaulted by another member of the church as a child, Noel Cannon confronted Gibson. “He came up to me and said, ‘You’ve got a dirty little secret don’t you? You are going to sit over there until you tell me what it is’,” Gibson said. Sam Gibson was adopted into Redeemer Baptist School Wayne Taylor



When Gibson left in 1992, Noel Cannon issued a threat: “Sam, if you ever mention anything of what has happened in here or goes on in here, I’ll come down on you like a ton of bricks,” Gibson recalled. Gibson said Redeemer was “not a place of love, of care. It’s a place of control, fear, humiliation”. Bradbury was horrified to learn the church that “destroyed” her has taken in more than 50 more children since the school began. “This is no different to what happened back then … these people are still succumbing to this thing,” Bradbury said. Bradbury wants the school to sell everything it owns to pay back people she said it has harmed.



“I’m not alone anymore, and there’s people there that need to get out too. They need to be finished,” he said. Redeemer did not respond to the Herald’s questions. In a previous statement, the school said: “Just because our practices are unfamiliar, it does not mean they are unlawful, coercive or abusive, and we reject the attempt to portray us as anything other than a law-abiding community with strong Christian faith and practices”. Related Investigation

Private schools Redeemer Baptist School investigation The NSW inquiry, which Redeemer representatives will not attend, will examine “any use by the school of coercive control in relation to students, families, guardians, employees and volunteers”. The inquiry has received more than 100 submissions, many from current volunteer teachers.



“The flavour of Christianity that was taught was fire and brimstone on acid and as students we were left in zero doubt about where they stood on key issues, particularly on matters such as equal rights for all, and marriage equality as cases in point,” wrote ex-student Danny Nowlan in one submission. “We were told in no uncertain terms if we were to date fellow school students we would be suspended/expelled”. It is not the first time the school has found itself in the halls of parliament. In 2007, Greens MP John Kaye called for an inquiry into the school after accusing the school of an “extraordinary tax sham and welfare fraud” that has cost the federal government more than $1 million, state parliament heard. The chair of Monday’s inquiry, Greens MP Abigail Boyd, said: “This is a school that is supposedly overseen by NSW authorities and has benefited from public funds. Serious allegations and concerns were raised decades ago and never resolved by public officials. The community deserves answers, and that’s what our inquiry will seek to provide.”

World.title: Car clash: Private vehicles and the true price the nation pays
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Car clash: Private vehicles and the true price the nation pays Cassandra Morgan August 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A divisive study has laid bare the true price of Australia’s huge number of private cars, finding they cost the country at least $316 billion a year – and the public foots half the bill. University of Queensland researchers say they are the first to fully quantify the “car economy” across five states, and expose a whopping annual estimated cost of $158 billion to the wider public. The study found drivers directly paid only half the annual cost of the vehicle economy. Pat Scala The huge public bill is the total of everything from congestion to the cost of car parks and roads, emissions, pollution and collisions. “Cars impose all these costs on society,” said Associate Professor Dorina Pojani of the university’s School of Architecture, Design and Planning. “People think of automobility, and they just think of the actual car that they drive. But automobility is a whole system.”



Cars impose hidden costs on society says urban planning expert Dr Dorina Pojani. Pojani said she was motivated to investigate the cost of Australia’s car use after robust discussions with her students, who were adamant that drivers paid their way. “They’d say: ‘Yeah, but drivers, we pay lots of fees and taxes, and for fuel, etc.’” Related Article City life ‘Taking the mickey’: Inner-city council tears up e-bike deal The study, though, revealed drivers directly paid only half the annual cost of the vehicle economy (49.82 per cent, or an estimated $157.48 billion) in fuel, parking, tolls and buying vehicles. The wider public, including people who, like Pojani, don’t drive, bore the remainder of the cost (50.18 per cent, or an estimated $158.64 billion).



The public cost outweighed the private cost in all states except NSW. “To this day, I just never got used to cars,” said Pojani, who grew up in communist-era Albania when private car ownership was banned. She now lives in Brisbane. The direct cost to drivers includes expenses such as buying vehicles and paying for fuel, parking and tolls. Drivers also help foot the public bill. Melbourne resident Luke Sapwell, who relies on public transport. Joe Armao Most people living in cities have a choice to drive or catch public transport. The same can’t be said for trucks, which are necessary to move food and other goods around Australia, Pojani said. They were excluded on that basis from the study, which looked at cars and light commercial vehicles only.



But the point of the research wasn’t to cast blame on drivers, for many of whom cars were also a necessity, Pojani said. Instead, the study used a Harvard University-tested method to encourage Australian governments to “put their money where their mouth is” on sustainability. Related Article Public transport ‘Too many cars, too much traffic’: Fuel crisis puts spotlight on car dependency “If [governments are] going to subsidise transport, they need to subsidise the right kind of transport, which is public transport, micromobility, meaning bicycle lanes, bicycle parking,” Pojani said. “My hunch is that the whole car industry knows that they’re getting a pretty good deal in Australia. The figures are clear.” The subsidisation point rang true for Melbourne resident Luke Sapwell, who supports his tax dollars going to the likes of schools, although he doesn’t have children, or hospitals, even though he’s healthy.



The difference with cars was that, for many, driving is a choice, the 34-year-old finance broker and business owner said. Sapwell doesn’t have a car, works mainly from home and relies on public transport and shared e-bikes to get around. That was until his local council, the City of Yarra, voted last month to tear up a deal with US-headquartered hiring company Lime, ordering e-bikes off the area’s streets in inner Melbourne. “Having half of car user costs being borne by other people – that’s unfair,” said Sapwell. Sapwell says governments should consider taxpayers’ subsidisation of cars when weighing up whether to support greener alternatives, such as shared e-bikes. Joe Armao “The least vulnerable people in our community can afford to use cars.



“So really, I just cannot even comprehend why we would be further disadvantaging vulnerable people in our community by taking away such an obvious mode of transport [share bikes] that has minimal impacts on the environment.” National Roads and Motorists’ Association spokesman Peter Khoury said the University of Queensland research had a fatal flaw. While it analysed the costs of Australia’s car economy, it was silent as to its benefits. Related Article City life Answer in 10 seconds or lose your fleet: The e-bike row dividing Yarra “You wouldn’t let your kids set up a lemonade stand without doing a cost-benefit analysis,” Khoury said. “The benefit to 100 years of investing in infrastructure for the combustion engine has helped basically carry Australia to one of the best standards-of-living nations on the face of the earth.



“Bureaucrats are not going to look at a report that quantifies the cost without quantifying the benefit.” Different approaches could quantify the cost of Australia’s car economy differently, Pojani said. But, even if there was a margin of error, the researchers were talking about billions of dollars. “We’re not talking about pennies,” Pojani said. The researchers’ findings were published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers. World.title: The kids are alt-right
World.content:
Brian Harris of Port Macquarie has been “following with interest the current ICAC inquiry. I don’t understand why the participants went to so much trouble to recruit new members to the Liberal Party. Dominic Perrottet is one of 12 siblings, and he has eight children of his own. Assuming some of the others also have large families they have enough people in their own family to control every branch in New South Wales without the need of outsiders.”

Like Graham Russell’s travelling companion in Ceuta (C8), Ken Hudson of Evans Head also required a haircut to gain entry “in 1973 when I arrived at Singapore Airport from the UK”.

“Regarding the dubious dubbing of English language films (C8) into other tongues, it’s important to acknowledge the influence of the dubbed dialogue in Channel 9’s The Samurai on 1960s Australia,” advises Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “Shintaro and his ninja sidekicks inspired a generation of Australian schoolkids to speak in guttural American accents while flicking potentially lethal homemade star knives (the severed lid from a tin of IXL jam was ideal) and delivering karate kicks at pursuing enemies. All good fun until Mum put an end to it when too many of her good sheets were ruined as we kitted-up.”

“On a recent trip to Poland, my wife and I were amused by the 1968 Omar Sharif movie, Mayerling, which also starred James Mason, disguised behind a huge mo,” recalls Alan Marel of North Curl Curl. “It was in the original English, but with the volume turned right down, and a Polish male basically reading all the parts in a dull monotone. There were Polish subtitles, and also a lady standing in the lower-right corner doing sign language, which didn’t make any sense at all unless included for illiterates. Also hilarious was watching Hogan’s Heroes in Germany, dubbed into German.”

Herman Beyersdorf of Corrimal is familiar with the sound barrier: “Flying in the good old days when international flights still featured movies on a universal screen, the whole plane cracked up when it was announced that passengers should purchase their $2 headset and that the movie would be … Silent Movie!”

World.title: Daicos-inspired Pies down Eagles to lock in finals spot
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Daicos-inspired Pies down Eagles to lock in finals spot Justin Chadwick August 9, 2026 — 8:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brownlow Medal favourite Nick Daicos collected what should be another three votes as injury-hit Collingwood fended off a brave West Coast comeback to post a 19-point win in Perth. The Magpies looked set for an easy victory after opening a 34-point lead late in the third quarter of Saturday’s match in front of 47,609 fans at Optus Stadium. Nick Daicos led Collingwood to victory over the Eagles. Getty Images But the Eagles, led by a hobbled Harley Reid, twice closed to within 10 points in a frantic final quarter that featured plenty of heroic acts from both sides. Collingwood held their nerve more often than not to seal the 17.15 (117) to 15.8 (98) win, with the result sealing the Magpies (12-8-1) a berth in the AFL’s new wildcard round.



Despite dealing with the close attention of tagger Brady Hough, Daicos tallied a whopping 39 disposals, 10 clearances, 12 score involvements, 722m gained, two goal assists and a goal to further tighten his grip on the Brownlow medal. Josh Daicos was also big with 35 disposals and a game-high 884m gained. While the Daicos brothers were shining, West Coast’s star midfielder Reid was hampered from the moment he sustained a huge hit to a quad in the first quarter. The 21-year-old bravely battled through the painful cork to finish with 30 disposals, six clearances and a goal. Reid was particularly crucial during West Coast’s fightback, and he received plenty of help from Elliot Yeo (28 disposals, 11 clearances, one goal) and Jake Waterman (three goals).



Lachie Schultz, Tim Membrey and Daniel McStay kicked three goals apiece for Collingwood, who entered the match missing Scott Pendlebury, Jordan De Goey, Jeremy Howe, Harry Perryman and Patrick Lipinski from the team that lost to Geelong by 25 points last week. Harley Reid is tackled by Angus Anderson. Getty Images West Coast (4-17) have now lost nine games on the trot, but their effort against Collingwood was full of spirit. The opening quarter was an entertaining shootout as both sides kicked six goals. West Coast’s accurate return of 6.1 - with the only blemish being a rushed behind - was in stark contrast to their loss against Richmond a week earlier when they had 3.17 to their name midway through the third term.



Yeo’s 50m running goal with just seconds left in the quarter sent the crowd wild, and the Eagles opened an 11-point lead midway through the second term when Jack Graham kicked truly on the run. A long bomb by Nick Daicos helped spark a three-goal run by the Magpies, helping the visitors enter halftime with a six-point advantage. View post on X The major highlight of the second quarter was a bone-crunching but fair hit by Eagles defender Brandon Starcevich on Ed Allan, with both players unscathed. Nick Daicos racked up 21 disposals, five clearances, one goal and a goal assist in a monster first half, and he continued to dominate in the third term as Collingwood broke the game open. AAP
